Nuh's replies are spread in the same way: his messengership (7:61-62) [c2], his proof and mercy (11:28) [c9], and his refusal to drive away the believers (11:29, 26:114) [c10].
chapters.kids_md: The leaders of Nuh's people said he was only a person like them [c4]. They said that only the lowly followed him [c5]. Nuh said he was a messenger and a warner, that he asked for no reward, and that he would not send the believers away [c2][c10][c13].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The leaders judged the message by who delivered it and who followed it: a human being like themselves, followed by people they looked down on [c4][c5]. One reading is that the passage warns against judging a message by the standing of those who follow it [c5][c10].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name the leaders of Nuh's people or any individual among them or among the believers.
- It does not say how many followed Nuh or how many opposed him.
- It does not date these exchanges or give their order; the same arguments are reported in different surahs, and this chapter groups them by theme, not by time.
- The verse 11:35 (a question whether they say he invented it) is a separate aside whose speaker is not clear from the verse; it is not used here and a reviewer should decide.

claims.statement_en: Nuh stayed among his people a thousand years less fifty years.
Nuh told God that he had called his people night and day, and that his calling only increased their flight.
Nuh said that each time he called them so that God might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and were extremely arrogant.
Nuh said that he called them openly, and also spoke to them publicly and in private.

Nuh told them to ask their Lord for forgiveness, for He is ever forgiving, and said that He would then send rain upon them in abundance, increase them with wealth and sons, and give them gardens and rivers.
Nuh asked what was the matter with them that they did not look for dignity from God, when He had created them in stages.
Nuh pointed to the heavens, seven one above another, and to the moon as a light and the sun as a lamp.
Nuh reminded them that God caused them to grow from the earth, will return them into it and bring them out again, and has spread the earth for them so that they may walk its wide paths.

In another passage Nuh told his people that if his standing among them and his reminders of God's signs weighed on them, he relied on God, and they could gather their plan with their partners and act against him without giving him respite.
Nuh told them that if they turned away, he had asked them for no reward, that his reward was only with God, and that he was commanded to be among those who submit.

chapters.summary_md: Nuh stayed among his people a thousand years less fifty years, called them night and day, openly and in private, and reminded them of God's signs, but they turned away [c1][c2][c4][c7][c3].
chapters.body_md:
The Quran says Nuh stayed among his people a thousand years less fifty years [c1]. He told God he had called his people night and day, and that his calling only increased their flight [c2]. Each time he called them so that God might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and were extremely arrogant [c3]. He called them openly, and he also spoke to them publicly and in private [c4].

He told them to ask their Lord for forgiveness, for He is ever forgiving, and said that He would then send rain upon them in abundance, increase them with wealth and sons, and give them gardens and rivers [c5]. He asked what was the matter with them that they did not look for dignity from God, when He had created them in stages [c6]. He pointed to the heavens, seven one above another, and to the moon as a light and the sun as a lamp [c7]. He reminded them that God caused them to grow from the earth, will return them into it and bring them out again, and has spread the earth for them so that they may walk its wide paths [c8].

In another passage Nuh tells his people that if his standing among them and his reminders of God's signs weigh on them, he relies on God, and they may gather their plan with their partners and act against him without giving him respite [c9]. If they turn away, he has asked them for no reward; his reward is only with God, and he was commanded to be among those who submit [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The people's refusal is described by fleeing (71:6) [c2] and by blocking their ears and covering themselves (71:7) [c3]. Nuh's reminders move from his words about forgiveness and its fruits (71:10-12) [c5] to signs in the heavens and on the earth (71:15-20) [c7][c8].
chapters.kids_md: Nuh called his people for a very long time, night and day, in public and in private [c1][c2][c4]. He reminded them of the sky, the sun, the moon and the earth as signs of God [c7][c8]. But they put their fingers in their ears and would not listen [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage shows calling done in more than one manner: by night and by day, openly and privately, with encouragement and with reminders of God's signs [c2][c4][c5][c7]. One reading is that persistence in a sincere call does not depend on how it is received [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran says Nuh stayed among his people a thousand years less fifty years. It does not say whether this is his whole life or only the time he spent calling them.
- It does not say when the calling began or ended, or how the time divides among the ways of calling described here.
- The Arabic word in 71:13 (rendered 'dignity') is read in more than one way, for example as dignity given by God or as God's own majesty; this draft does not decide.
- The promises of rain, wealth, sons, gardens and rivers are reported as Nuh's words to his people; the verses do not say that anyone received them.
- The order of 10:71-72 relative to the rest is not stated.

claims.statement_en: It was revealed to Nuh that none of his people would believe except those who had already believed, so he should not be distressed by what they did.
Nuh told God that his people had disobeyed him and followed one whose wealth and children only increased his loss, and that they had plotted a great plot.
They told one another not to abandon their gods, and not to abandon Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Yauq and Nasr; Nuh said they had led many astray, and asked that the wrongdoers increase only in error.
Because of their wrongs they were drowned and then made to enter a fire, and they found no helpers besides God.
Nuh asked God not to leave on the earth anyone of the disbelievers dwelling there, because if God left them they would mislead His servants and beget only wicked, ungrateful children.
Nuh asked forgiveness for himself, his parents, whoever entered his house as a believer, and the believing men and women, and asked that the wrongdoers increase only in ruin.
Nuh said that his people had denied him, and asked God to open a decisive judgement between him and them and to save him and the believers with him.
Nuh called on his Lord that he was overcome and asked for help, because they had denied him.

chapters.summary_md: God told Nuh that no more of his people would believe; Nuh complained to God of their refusal and their plotting, prayed for the believers, and asked for help [c1][c2][c6][c8].
chapters.body_md:
God revealed to Nuh that none of his people would believe except those who had already believed, and that he should not be distressed by what they did [c1]. Nuh told God that his people had disobeyed him and followed one whose wealth and children only increased his loss, and that they had plotted a great plot [c2]. They told one another not to abandon their gods, and named Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Yauq and Nasr [c3]. Nuh said they had led many astray and asked that the wrongdoers increase only in error [c3].

The Quran adds that because of their wrongs they were drowned and then made to enter a fire, and that they found no helpers besides God [c4].

Nuh asked God not to leave anyone of the disbelievers dwelling on the earth, since, he said, if God left them they would mislead His servants and beget only wicked, ungrateful children [c5]. He asked forgiveness for himself, his parents, whoever entered his house as a believer, and the believing men and women, and asked that the wrongdoers increase only in ruin [c6]. In other passages he says that his people had denied him and asks God to judge decisively between them and him and to save him and the believers with him [c7]; he calls on his Lord that he is overcome and asks for help [c8].
chapters.deep_md: Nuh's requests are worded in different ways: that God judge between them and him [c7], that God help him because he is overcome [c8], and that God not leave anyone of the disbelievers dwelling on the earth [c5]. The names of the gods are given only in the passage at 71:23 [c3].
chapters.kids_md: God told Nuh that no more of his people would believe, so he should not be sad about what they did [c1]. Nuh asked God for help and to save him and the believers [c7][c8]. He asked God to forgive him, his parents and the believers [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage shows Nuh bringing his distress to God in words [c7][c8]. One reading is that taking hardship to God in prayer is presented here as the answer to rejection [c8]. In his prayer he also asks forgiveness for himself and for the believers, and not only relief [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say when, within the long period of calling, these prayers were made, or whether they came before or after the order to build the ship. This chapter groups them by theme.
- It does not say who or what these names were; the verse gives only the names as the gods the people held to. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts say who they were; none is used here.
- It does not say whom the phrase 'one whose wealth and children only increased his loss' points to; it may mean a person or a kind of person.
- It does not name Nuh's parents.
- The verse 71:25 says they were drowned and then made to enter a fire; it does not say when this fire is entered or describe it.

claims.statement_en: God revealed to Nuh that none of his people would believe except those who already had, and told him to build the ship under His watch and by His revelation.
God told Nuh not to speak to Him about those who had done wrong, for they would be drowned.
While Nuh was building the ship, each time leaders of his people passed by him they mocked him.
Nuh said that if they mocked him, he would mock them in the same way, and that they would come to know who would receive a punishment that disgraces and a punishment that lasts.

chapters.summary_md: At God's command Nuh built the ship, and the leaders of his people mocked him as he built it [c1][c3].
chapters.body_md: God revealed to Nuh that none of his people would believe except those who already had, and told him to build the ship under His watch and by His revelation [c1]. He told him not to speak to Him about those who had done wrong, for they would be drowned [c2]. As Nuh built it, whenever leaders of his people passed by they mocked him [c3]. He said that if they mocked him, he would mock them in the same way, and that they would come to know who would receive a punishment that disgraces and a punishment that lasts [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The command to build the ship is worded almost alike at 11:37 and 23:27 [c1][c2]. It comes with a prohibition: Nuh is not to plead for the wrongdoers [c2].
chapters.kids_md: God told Nuh to build a ship [c1]. The leaders of his people laughed at him as he built it [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Nuh keeps building while he is mocked [c3][c4]. One reading is that a task given by God is carried on in spite of ridicule [c1][c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not give the ship's size, its shape, the materials beyond those named in the next chapter, the place where it was built, or how long it took.
- It does not say what the people did, apart from mocking, while the ship was being built.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts give dimensions, a building place and a timeline for the ship; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: When God's command came and the tannur (a word usually rendered oven) boiled over, God told Nuh to carry on the ship a pair of every kind, and his family, except those against whom the word had already gone out, and those who believed; few had believed with him.
Nuh told them to embark and said that in God's name was its sailing and its anchoring, for his Lord is forgiving and merciful.
God told Nuh to say, once he and those with him were settled on the ship, that praise belongs to God who had saved them from the wrongdoing people, and to ask to be landed at a blessed landing place.
God opened the gates of heaven with pouring water and made the earth burst with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed.
God carried Nuh on a vessel of planks and dusur (a word often rendered nails or fibres), which sailed under His watch, as a reward for one who had been rejected.
The ship sailed with them through waves like mountains.
God saved Nuh and those with him in the laden ship and drowned the rest, who had denied His signs.

chapters.summary_md: When God's command came, Nuh carried on the ship a pair of every kind, his family (except those against whom the word had gone out) and the believers; water poured from the sky and burst from the earth, and the ship sailed through waves like mountains [c1][c4][c6]. God saved Nuh and those with him and drowned the rest [c7].
chapters.body_md:
When God's command came and the tannur (a word usually rendered oven) boiled over, God told Nuh to carry on the ship a pair of every kind, and his family, except those against whom the word had already gone out, and those who believed; few had believed with him [c1]. Nuh told them to embark and said that in God's name was its sailing and its anchoring, for his Lord is forgiving and merciful [c2]. God told Nuh to say, once he and those with him were settled on the ship, that praise belongs to God who had saved them from the wrongdoing people, and to ask to be landed at a blessed landing place [c3].

The Quran describes the flood in these terms: God opened the gates of heaven with pouring water and made the earth burst with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed [c4]. He carried Nuh on a vessel of planks and dusur (a word often rendered nails or fibres), which sailed under His watch, as a reward for one who had been rejected [c5]. It sailed with them through waves like mountains [c6]. God saved Nuh and those with him in the laden ship and drowned the rest [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The flood is told from different sides: the sign and the command to embark [c1], Nuh's words on boarding [c2][c3], the description of the waters [c4], the vessel [c5] and the waves [c6]. The outcome is the same in every passage that tells it: Nuh and those with him are saved and the rest are drowned [c7].
chapters.kids_md: When God's command came, water poured from the sky and sprang up from the earth [c4]. Nuh took on the ship a pair of every kind, his family (except those about whom God's word had gone out), and the believers [c1]. The ship sailed through waves like mountains [c6]. God saved Nuh and those with him [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Nuh's words on boarding give thanks to God for rescue and ask for a blessed landing [c2][c3]. One reading is that gratitude and prayer are joined at the moment of safety [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say what the tannur was or where it was; 'oven' is a common rendering and its sense is discussed.
- It does not say how many people were on the ship, which animals were carried or how many kinds, or how they were gathered and cared for.
- It does not say how long the flood lasted, how deep the water rose, or whether the water covered the whole earth or only the region of Nuh's people. A scholar should decide how to word the extent for readers.
- The Arabic word dusur is explained as nails and as fibres; this draft does not decide.
- Which members of Nuh's family were taken and which were not is not stated beyond 'those against whom the word had gone out'; the next chapter tells of his son.
- The Quran does not name the passengers.

claims.statement_en: Nuh called out to his son, who was standing apart, to come aboard with them and not to be with the disbelievers.

The son said he would take refuge on a mountain that would protect him from the water; Nuh replied that nothing that day protects from God's command except for the one on whom He has mercy; the wave came between them, and the son was among the drowned.
Nuh called to his Lord, saying that his son was of his family, that God's promise is true, and that He is the most just of judges.
God answered that the son was not of Nuh's family, that his deed was not righteous, and that Nuh should not ask Him about what he had no knowledge of; God advised him not to be among the ignorant.
Nuh said that he sought refuge in God from asking what he had no knowledge of, and that unless God forgave him and had mercy on him he would be among the losers.

chapters.summary_md: Nuh called to his son to board; the son refused, the wave came between them and he was drowned [c1][c2]. Nuh appealed to God about him, God answered that he was not of Nuh's family because his deed was not righteous, and Nuh asked forgiveness [c3][c4][c5].
chapters.body_md:
As the ship sailed through the waves, Nuh called out to his son, who was standing apart, to come aboard with them and not to be with the disbelievers [c1]. The son said he would take refuge on a mountain that would protect him from the water [c2]. Nuh replied that nothing that day protects from God's command except for the one on whom He has mercy; then the wave came between them, and the son was among the drowned [c2].

Nuh called to his Lord, saying that his son was of his family, that God's promise is true, and that He is the most just of judges [c3]. God answered that the son was not of Nuh's family, that his deed was not righteous, and that Nuh should not ask Him about what he had no knowledge of; God advised him not to be among the ignorant [c4]. Nuh said that he sought refuge in God from asking what he had no knowledge of, and that unless God forgave him and had mercy on him he would be among the losers [c5].
chapters.deep_md: God's answer in 11:46 gives a reason for the statement that the son is not of Nuh's family: his deed was not righteous [c4]. The passage ends with Nuh asking forgiveness for the question itself [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Nuh called to his son to come on the ship, but the son would not come and was among those drowned [c1][c2]. Nuh asked God about his son, and God told him not to ask about what he did not know [c3][c4]. Nuh asked God to forgive him [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage shows a father asking on behalf of his son, and the answer given to him [c3][c4]. One reading is that family ties are not treated here as a ground of rescue by themselves, since the verse gives the son's deed as the reason [c4]. Another is that a prophet, on being corrected, turns to seeking God's forgiveness [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name Nuh's son, or say why he stood apart or what he believed. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts give the son a name; it is not used here.
- It does not say how old the son was or whether he had a family.
- The wording of 11:46 ('his deed was not righteous') can be read in more than one way in the Arabic; this draft keeps the plainest rendering and a reviewer should check it.
- It does not say whether other relatives were among those not carried.

claims.statement_en: A command was given that the earth swallow its water and the sky hold back; the water subsided and the matter was decreed.
The ship settled on Judi (with the Arabic article, al-Judi), and it was announced that the wrongdoing people were to be far removed.

Nuh was told to come down in peace from God and with blessings upon him and upon communities from those with him; and there would be other communities whom God would let enjoy life for a time, and then a painful punishment from Him would touch them.

chapters.summary_md: At God's command the water subsided and the ship settled on Judi; Nuh was told to come down in peace and with blessings [c1][c2][c3].
chapters.body_md:
A command was given that the earth swallow its water and the sky hold back; the water subsided, the matter was decreed, and the ship settled on Judi (with the Arabic article, al-Judi) [c1][c2]. It was announced that the wrongdoing people were to be far removed [c2].

Nuh was told to come down in peace from God and with blessings upon him and upon communities from those with him [c3]. There would be other communities, God said, whom He would let enjoy life for a time, and then a painful punishment from Him would touch them [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The ending in 11:44 is told in short successive clauses, from the command to the earth and the sky to the settling of the ship and the closing word on the wrongdoers [c1][c2]. In 11:48 the blessing is on Nuh and on communities from those with him, and a warning follows for later communities [c3].
chapters.kids_md: The water went down, and the ship rested on Judi [c1][c2]. God told Nuh to come down in peace, with blessings on him and on those with him [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): In the text the account ends with peace and blessing for Nuh and those with him, and with a warning to later communities [c3]. One reading is that the passage looks past the flood to what follows it [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran names Judi as where the ship settled; it does not say where Judi is. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts identify Judi with particular mountains, one of them Ararat; none is used here.
- It does not say how long the water took to subside or how long they stayed on the ship.
- It does not say who the 'communities' of 11:48 are, or how they relate to the peoples who came later.

claims.statement_en: God saved Nuh and the people of the ship and made it a sign for the worlds; He says that He left it as a sign.
God asks whether there is anyone who will take heed, asks how His punishment and warnings were, and says that He has made the Quran easy for remembrance.
God saved Nuh and those with him in the ship, made them successors, drowned those who denied His signs, and told the hearer to look at the end of those who had been warned.
Nuh called to God, and God says how excellent are those who answer; He saved Nuh and his family from the great distress.
God made Nuh's offspring the survivors.
God left on Nuh among later generations a declaration of peace upon Nuh among the worlds; this is how He rewards those who do good, and Nuh was among His believing servants.
Then God drowned the others.
The Quran says that there is a sign in this, though most of them were not believers, that God is the Mighty, the Merciful, that there are signs in it, and that God is always testing.

chapters.summary_md: God saved Nuh and those with him, made the ship a sign, made his offspring the survivors, and left a declaration of peace upon him among later generations [c1][c3][c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
God saved Nuh and the people of the ship and made it a sign for the worlds [c1]. He asks whether there is anyone who will take heed, asks how His punishment and warnings were, and says the Quran has been made easy for remembrance [c2]. The Quran says that God made those with Nuh successors, drowned those who denied His signs, and tells the hearer to look at the end of those who had been warned [c3].

Nuh called to God, and God says how excellent are those who answer; He saved Nuh and his family from the great distress [c4]. He made Nuh's offspring the survivors [c5], and drowned the others [c7]. God left on Nuh, among later generations, a declaration of peace upon Nuh among the worlds, and the Quran says that this is how God rewards those who do good, and that Nuh was among His believing servants [c6].

The Quran says there is a sign in this, though most of them were not believers, and that God is the Mighty, the Merciful; it adds that there are signs in it, and that God is always testing [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The outcome is told in more than one way: as rescue and a sign (29:15, 54:15) [c1], as succession (10:73) [c3], as the survival of Nuh's offspring (37:77) [c5], and as lasting remembrance (37:78-79) [c6]. Some passages end by calling the account a sign [c8][c1].
chapters.kids_md: God saved Nuh and those with him and made the ship a sign [c1]. God sent peace upon Nuh, and the Quran says he was one of God's believing servants [c6]. The Quran asks whether anyone will take heed [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The account is called a sign and a reminder, and the Quran asks whether anyone will take heed [c1][c2]. One reading is that the story is offered as a reminder to take heed [c2]. The text also says that God is always testing [c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say how long Nuh lived after the flood, where he settled, or when or where he died.
- It says that Nuh's offspring were the survivors; it does not list them. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts name sons and give each a line of descent; none is used here.
- It does not say what became of the ship after it came to rest.
- The short passages 37:75-82 and 54:15-17 summarise the outcome; they add no events.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Nuh, the flood and his people. None is used in this draft.

The verses 11:35 and 11:49 are asides addressed to the one receiving the revelation, within the account; they are not used in the story texts, and a reviewer should decide whether to add a note on them.
The extent of the flood (the whole earth or the region of Nuh's people) is not stated in the verses; the draft says so and does not choose.
The sense of tannur (11:40, 23:27), of dusur (54:13) and of waqar (71:13) is left open in the texts.
The Quran gives a span of a thousand years less fifty years (29:14); the verse does not say whether it is his life or his time of calling, and the draft keeps the verse's wording.
The verse 71:25 (drowned, then made to enter a fire) is reported as written; how it is understood is left to the reviewer.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: names for Nuh's wife, sons and the mountain; the ship's dimensions. None is used in the story texts.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: Hud and the people of Ad

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that God sent to Ad their brother Hud, and that Hud told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him.
In one telling Hud added that they were only fabricating.
Ad denied the messengers, and Hud asked them whether they would not be mindful of God.
Hud said he was a trustworthy messenger to them, and told them to be mindful of God and to obey him.
Hud said he asked them for no payment for this, and that his reward lay only with his Lord, the Lord of the worlds.

Another passage tells its hearer to remember the brother of Ad, who warned his people at al-Ahqaf, when warners had passed before him and after him; he told them to worship none but God and said he feared for them the punishment of a great day.

chapters.summary_md: God sent Hud to his people, Ad, who denied the messengers [c3]. Hud told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him [c1], that he was a trustworthy messenger [c4], and that he asked them for no payment [c5].
chapters.body_md:
The Quran says that God sent to Ad their brother Hud [c1]. Hud told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him [c1]. In one telling he added that they were only fabricating [c2].

Ad denied the messengers [c3]. Hud asked them whether they would not be mindful of God [c3]. He said he was a trustworthy messenger to them, and told them to be mindful of God and to obey him [c4]. He said he asked them for no payment for this, and that his reward lay only with his Lord, the Lord of the worlds [c5].

Another passage tells its hearer to remember the brother of Ad, who warned his people at al-Ahqaf [c6]. It says that warners had passed before him and after him, that he told them to worship none but God, and that he feared for them the punishment of a great day [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The opening words of the call are the same at 7:65 and 11:50 [c1], and 11:50 adds the charge that they were only fabricating [c2]. The plural messengers at 26:123 [c3] stands beside one named man, Hud [c4]. The passage at 46:21 describes his warning as one among warnings that came before and after him [c6].
chapters.kids_md: God sent Hud to his people, the people of Ad [c1]. Hud told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him [c1]. He said he was a trustworthy messenger [c4]. He did not ask them for any payment [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that a messenger who asks for no payment shows that his message does not depend on any gain for himself [c5]. Another is that the passage presents warning as something that came to peoples again and again, since warners had passed before and after Hud [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: when Hud lived, how old he was, who his family was, or how long he called his people.
- Not established: why Ad are called his brothers (a shared descent or a shared community); the Arabic wording says only their brother.
- Not established: how many messengers were sent to Ad. The Quran uses the plural at 26:123, and speaks of warners before and after him at 46:21, and names only Hud.
- Not established: what al-Ahqaf was or where it lay; the Arabic word is generally rendered as sandy tracts, a sense for the reviewer, and the verses do not say it was the whole land of Ad.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Hud's lineage, the region of Ad's land and where Hud is buried. None is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: Hud asked his people whether they wondered that a reminder from their Lord had come upon a man from among them to warn them.
Hud told them to remember that God had made them successors after the people of Nuh and had added to them greatly in creation, and to remember God's favours so that they might prosper.

Hud told them to ask their Lord for forgiveness and to turn back to Him, and said that He would send the sky upon them in abundant rain and add strength to their strength; he told them not to turn away as guilty people.
Hud asked whether they built a landmark on every high place for amusement, and took strongholds in the hope of living forever.
Hud said that when they seized, they seized as tyrants.
Hud told them to be mindful of God and obey him, and to be mindful of the One who had supplied them with what they knew: livestock, children, gardens and springs.
Hud said he feared for them the punishment of a great day.

chapters.summary_md: Hud reminded his people that God had made them successors after the people of Nuh [c2], told them to ask forgiveness and turn back to God [c3], and told them to be mindful of the One who had supplied them with livestock, children, gardens and springs [c6].
chapters.body_md:
Hud asked his people whether they wondered that a reminder from their Lord had come upon a man from among them to warn them [c1]. He told them to remember that God had made them successors after the people of Nuh and had added to them greatly in creation, and to remember God's favours so that they might prosper [c2].

He told them to ask their Lord for forgiveness and to turn back to Him [c3]. He said that God would send the sky upon them in abundant rain and add strength to their strength, and he told them not to turn away as guilty people [c3].

In another passage Hud asked whether they built a landmark on every high place for amusement, and took strongholds in the hope of living forever [c4]. He said that when they seized, they seized as tyrants [c5]. He told them to be mindful of God and obey him, and to be mindful of the One who had supplied them with what they knew: livestock, children, gardens and springs [c6]. He said he feared for them the punishment of a great day [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passages address the same people in different ways [c1][c4]. At 7:69 the appeal is to remember favours and a succession after the people of Nuh [c2]. At 26:128-134 the appeal is a set of questions about what they built and how they used force, followed by a list of what God had supplied [c4][c5][c6]. At 11:52 the appeal is to ask forgiveness and turn back [c3]. One of them ends in a warning [c7].
chapters.kids_md: Hud told his people to remember that God had made them successors after the people of Nuh [c2]. He told them to ask God for forgiveness and to turn back to Him [c3]. He told them to be mindful of God, who had given them livestock, children, gardens and springs [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage links remembering what God has given with turning back to Him [c3][c6]. Another is that Hud's questions about building for amusement are an invitation to look at how a people use what they have [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what the landmarks and strongholds of 26:128-129 were, or where they stood; the Arabic words have more than one rendering and this draft keeps the wording general.
- Not established: the sense of the Arabic word rendered added greatly in creation (7:69); it may refer to build, strength, numbers or standing.
- Not established: whether the rain and strength promised at 11:52 are stated for any people other than the ones Hud addressed; the verse gives them as his words to his own people.
- Not established: whether the word rendered children at 26:133 means sons or children in general.

claims.statement_en: The leading group of those among his people who disbelieved said they saw him in foolishness and thought him among the liars.
Hud said there was no foolishness in him, that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, that he delivered the messages of his Lord, and that he was a trustworthy adviser to them.

They asked whether he had come so that they would worship God alone and leave what their fathers worshipped, or to turn them away from their gods, and told him to bring them what he promised if he was truthful.
They said he had brought no clear proof, that they would not leave their gods on his word, and that they did not believe in him.
They said only that some of their gods had struck him with evil; Hud said he called God to witness, and told them to be witnesses, that he was free of what they set up beside God.

Hud told them to plot against him, all of them, and give him no respite; he said he relied on God, his Lord and theirs, that there is no creature that God does not hold by its forelock, and that his Lord is on a straight path.

Hud said that if they turned away, he had still conveyed what he was sent with, that his Lord would make another people successors in their place, that they could not harm Him at all, and that his Lord is guardian over all things.
They said it was all the same to them whether he admonished them or not, that this was only the way of the earlier people, and that they would not be punished.
Hud said that the knowledge was only with God, that he conveyed what he was sent with, but that he saw them as a people who were ignorant.

chapters.summary_md: The leading group among his people said they saw foolishness in Hud [c1] and that they would not leave their gods on his word [c4]. Hud said he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds [c2], that he relied on God [c6], and that he had conveyed what he was sent with [c7].
chapters.body_md:
The leading group of those among his people who disbelieved said they saw him in foolishness and thought him among the liars [c1]. Hud said there was no foolishness in him, that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, that he delivered the messages of his Lord, and that he was a trustworthy adviser to them [c2].

They asked whether he had come so that they would worship God alone and leave what their fathers worshipped, or to turn them away from their gods, and told him to bring them what he promised if he was truthful [c3]. They said he had brought no clear proof, that they would not leave their gods on his word, and that they did not believe in him [c4]. They said only that some of their gods had struck him with evil [c5]. Hud said he called God to witness, and told them to be witnesses, that he was free of what they set up beside God [c5].

He told them to plot against him, all of them, and give him no respite [c6]. He said he relied on God, his Lord and theirs, that there is no creature that God does not hold by its forelock, and that his Lord is on a straight path [c6]. He said that if they turned away, he had still conveyed what he was sent with, that his Lord would make another people successors in their place, that they could not harm Him at all, and that his Lord is guardian over all things [c7].

They said it was all the same to them whether he admonished them or not, that this was only the way of the earlier people, and that they would not be punished [c8]. In another passage Hud said that the knowledge was only with God, that he conveyed what he was sent with, but that he saw them as a people who were ignorant [c9].
chapters.deep_md: The replies of the people are told in more than one place and are not identical [c3][c4][c8]. At 7:70 the objection is to leaving what their fathers worshipped [c3], at 11:53 it is the lack of a clear proof [c4], and at 26:137 it is that the warning is only the way of the earlier people [c8]. The draft does not say that these are one exchange [c3][c4][c8]. Hud's replies stress that he is a messenger [c2], that he relies on God [c6], and that he has conveyed his message [c7][c9].
chapters.kids_md: Some leaders of his people said Hud was foolish [c1]. They said they would not leave their gods [c4]. Hud said he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds [c2]. He said he relied on God [c6]. The people asked him to bring what he had promised [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Hud answers the charge of foolishness by saying what he is and what he has done, and by relying on God [c2][c6]. Another is that the people's replies rest on what their fathers worshipped and on the way of the earlier people [c3][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the leading group were, how many they were, or which gods the people worshipped; the verses say only our gods.
- Not established: what evil the people meant at 11:54.
- Not established: whether the replies at 7:70, 11:53, 26:136-138 and 46:22 are one exchange or more.
- Not established: the sense of the figure about holding a creature by its forelock (11:56); the Arabic is nasiya and the draft keeps the wording of the verse.
- Not established: how long Hud called them, or how many believed with him.

claims.statement_en: Hud said that rijs and anger from their Lord had fallen on them; rijs is an Arabic word for something foul or a punishment.

Hud asked whether they disputed with him about names that they and their fathers had given, for which God had sent down no authority, and told them to wait, saying he was with them among those who wait.

When they saw it as a cloud coming toward their valleys, they said it was a cloud that would bring them rain; the reply, whose speaker the verse does not name, said that it was what they had been hastening, a wind carrying a painful punishment.
The wind destroyed everything by the command of its Lord, and they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings; God says that this is how He repays the guilty people.

chapters.summary_md: Hud told his people to wait [c2]. They saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and said it would bring them rain [c3]. It was a wind that destroyed everything by the command of its Lord [c4].
chapters.body_md:
Hud said that rijs and anger from their Lord had fallen on them [c1]. He asked whether they disputed with him about names that they and their fathers had given, for which God had sent down no authority, and told them to wait, saying he was with them among those who wait [c2].

When they saw it as a cloud coming toward their valleys, they said it was a cloud that would bring them rain [c3]. The reply, whose speaker the verse does not name, said that it was what they had been hastening, a wind carrying a painful punishment [c3]. The wind destroyed everything by the command of its Lord [c4]. They became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings [c4]. God says that this is how He repays the guilty people [c4].
chapters.deep_md: Passages from different places are set side by side here by theme: Hud's statement and his word to wait at 7:71 [c1][c2], and the sight of the cloud at 46:24-25 [c3][c4]. The Quran does not link them in time [c1][c3]. The people's words about the cloud are given, and the reply is given without a named speaker [c3].
chapters.kids_md: Hud told his people to wait [c2]. They saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and said it would bring them rain [c3]. It was a wind with a painful punishment in it, and it destroyed everything by the command of its Lord [c3][c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the people took the sign for something they wanted, while the reply said it was what they had been hastening [c3]. Another is that the passage ends by saying that this is how God repays the guilty people [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how long the wind lasted, how far it reached, or how many people were in the land. This draft does not use other verses that speak of the wind.
- Not established: who gave the reply at 46:24; the verse does not name the speaker.
- Not established: which names are meant at 7:71, or exactly what the Arabic word rijs refers to.
- Not established: where the valleys of 46:24 were.

claims.statement_en: When God's command came, He saved Hud and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Him, and saved them from a harsh punishment.
God saved Hud and those with him by a mercy from Him, and cut off the root of those who denied His signs; they were not believers.
They denied Hud and God destroyed them; the Quran says there is a sign in that, and that most of them were not believers.
The Quran says that Hud's Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.
The Quran says that these were Ad: they rejected the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.
A curse followed them in this world and on the Day of Resurrection; Ad disbelieved in their Lord, and the Quran says away with Ad, the people of Hud.

God had established them in what He had not established the later hearers in, and had given them hearing, sight and hearts; but their hearing, sight and hearts availed them nothing, because they rejected the signs of God, and what they had mocked at surrounded them.

chapters.summary_md: When God's command came, He saved Hud and those who believed with him [c1]. Ad denied Hud and God destroyed them [c3]. The Quran says that Ad rejected the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers [c5].
chapters.body_md:
When God's command came, He saved Hud and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Him, and saved them from a harsh punishment [c1]. Another passage says that God saved him and those with him by a mercy from Him, and cut off the root of those who denied His signs, and that they were not believers [c2].

They denied Hud and God destroyed them [c3]. The Quran says there is a sign in that, and that most of them were not believers [c3]. It says that Hud's Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful [c4].

The Quran says that these were Ad: they rejected the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant [c5]. A curse followed them in this world and on the Day of Resurrection, and the Quran says away with Ad, the people of Hud [c6].

God had established them in what He had not established the later hearers in, and had given them hearing, sight and hearts [c7]. But their hearing, sight and hearts availed them nothing, because they rejected the signs of God, and what they had mocked at surrounded them [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The rescue is told in more than one passage, at 11:58 and at 7:72 [c1][c2]. Only the latter says that the root of those who denied was cut off [c2]. The passage at 46:26 gives the reason that their faculties did not help them: they rejected God's signs [c7]. The Quran calls Ad's disobedience a rejection of messengers in the plural at 11:59 [c5].
chapters.kids_md: When God's command came, He saved Hud and those who believed with him [c1]. The people of Ad had denied Hud, and God destroyed them [c3]. The Quran says they rejected the signs of their Lord [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage separates Hud and those who believed with him from those who denied, and speaks of a mercy for the first group [c1][c2]. Another is that having hearing, sight and hearts did not help the people of Ad when they rejected God's signs [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how many believed with Hud, where they went, or what became of them afterwards.
- Not established: what the curse of 11:60 consisted of.
- Not established: who the obstinate tyrant of 11:59 was, or whether it means one person or many.
- Not established: which period the later hearers of 46:26 belong to; the verse addresses the hearer of the Quran.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Hud. None is used in this draft.

The Ad event in the inventory also lists 41:13-16, 51:41-42, 53:50, 54:18-22, 69:4-8 and 89:6-8. They are outside the inventory range of Hud and are not used; a reviewer should decide whether to extend the range. In particular the duration of the wind is stated in an ayah that is not used here.
The speaker of the reply at 46:24 is not named in the verse; the draft says so and does not decide between Hud and the narration.

Some Arabic terms are open in sense and the draft keeps them general: rijs (7:71), basta in added greatly in creation (7:69), the landmark and strongholds of 26:128-129, the forelock wording of 11:56, and al-Ahqaf (46:21).
The Quran calls Hud their brother (akhahum) without saying whether this means kinship or shared community; the draft keeps the Arabic wording.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Hud's lineage, the place of Ad's land and of Hud's grave, and details of the cloud and the wind. None is used in the story texts.

The chapters follow a reading order (call, appeal, reply, the wind, rescue). The Quran does not give a chronology across these surahs, and the draft does not claim that the replies at 7:70, 11:53, 26:136-138 and 46:22 are one conversation.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that God sent to Thamud their brother Salih, and that Salih told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him.
Salih said that a clear proof had come to them from their Lord.
Salih said that God had produced them from the earth and made them settle in it, and told them to ask Him for forgiveness and turn back to Him, saying that his Lord is near and answers.
Thamud denied the messengers, and Salih asked them whether they would not be mindful of God.
Salih said he was a trustworthy messenger to them, told them to be mindful of God and to obey him, and said he asked them for no payment, since his reward lay only with the Lord of the worlds.

chapters.summary_md: God sent Salih to Thamud, who denied the messengers [c4]. Salih told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him [c1], that he was a trustworthy messenger [c5], and that he asked them for no payment [c5].
chapters.body_md:
The Quran says that God sent to Thamud their brother Salih [c1]. Salih told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him [c1]. He said that a clear proof had come to them from their Lord [c2].

He said that God had produced them from the earth and made them settle in it [c3]. He told them to ask God for forgiveness and turn back to Him, saying that his Lord is near and answers [c3].

In another passage Thamud denied the messengers, and Salih asked them whether they would not be mindful of God [c4]. He said he was a trustworthy messenger to them, told them to be mindful of God and to obey him, and said he asked them for no payment, since his reward lay only with the Lord of the worlds [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The call opens in the same words at 7:73 and 11:61 [c1]. Each passage then adds something of its own: the clear proof at 7:73 [c2], the reminder that God produced them from the earth at 11:61 [c3], and the questions and the claim of no payment at 26:141-145 [c4][c5]. The Quran uses the plural messengers at 26:141, beside one named man [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God sent Salih to his people, Thamud [c1]. Salih told them to worship God and said they had no god other than Him [c1]. He said he was a trustworthy messenger [c5]. He did not ask them for any payment [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Salih's call joins worship of God with asking forgiveness and turning back to Him [c1][c3]. Another is that a messenger who asks for no payment shows that his message does not depend on any gain for himself [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: when Salih lived, how old he was, who his family was, or how long he called Thamud.
- Not established: why Thamud are called his brothers (a shared descent or a shared community); the Arabic says only their brother.
- Not established: what the clear proof of 7:73 was beyond what the later verses say of the she-camel.
- Not established: where Thamud lived; these verses do not name a land.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Salih's lineage, the region of Thamud's land and where Salih is buried. None is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: Salih told them to remember that God had made them successors after Ad and settled them in the land, where they took palaces from its plains and carved houses out of the mountains; he told them to remember God's favours and not to spread corruption in the land.
Salih asked whether they would be left secure in what was there, in gardens and springs, crops and palm trees whose spathes are tender.
Salih said they carved houses from the mountains, and the Arabic word that describes how they did it is read as skilfully or as exultingly.
Salih told them to be mindful of God and obey him, and not to obey the command of the transgressors, who spread corruption in the land and do not set things right.

chapters.summary_md: Salih told his people to remember that God had made them successors after Ad and settled them in the land [c1]. He asked whether they would be left secure in gardens, springs, crops and palm trees [c2], and told them to be mindful of God and not to obey the transgressors [c4].
chapters.body_md:
Salih told them to remember that God had made them successors after Ad and settled them in the land, where they took palaces from its plains and carved houses out of the mountains [c1]. He told them to remember God's favours and not to spread corruption in the land [c1].

In another passage he asked whether they would be left secure in what was there, in gardens and springs, crops and palm trees whose spathes are tender [c2]. He said they carved houses from the mountains [c3]. He told them to be mindful of God and obey him, and not to obey the command of the transgressors, who spread corruption in the land and do not set things right [c4].
chapters.deep_md: These passages describe the land of his people with different details: palaces and carved houses at 7:74 [c1], gardens, springs, crops and palm trees at 26:146-148 [c2], and the carving of houses again at 26:149 [c3]. In both, the description comes with a warning not to spread corruption [c1][c4]. The Arabic describing the manner of carving at 26:149 has more than one reading [c3].
chapters.kids_md: Salih told his people to remember that God had made them successors after Ad [c1]. He asked whether they would be left secure in gardens and springs [c2]. He told them to be mindful of God and not to obey those who spread corruption [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Salih links what his people had been given with the call not to spread corruption [c1][c4]. Another is that his question about being left secure invites them to ask where their security comes from [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the plains, mountains and gardens of these verses were, or how long his people had lived there.
- Not established: the sense of the Arabic word at 26:149 (skilfully, or exultingly); the draft keeps both.
- Not established: who the transgressors of 26:151-152 were by name.

claims.statement_en: The leading group who were arrogant said to those they considered weak, the ones among them who believed, whether they knew that Salih was sent from his Lord; the believers said they believed in what he was sent with.
Those who were arrogant said that they disbelieved in what the others believed in.

They said to Salih that he had been among them someone hoped for before this, asked whether he forbade them to worship what their fathers worshipped, and said they were in doubt and unease about what he called them to.

Salih asked them what they thought if he was on a clear proof from his Lord and had been given mercy from Him: who would help him against God if he disobeyed Him, since they would add nothing for him but loss.
They said he was only one of the bewitched and only a human being like themselves, and told him to bring a sign if he was truthful.

They asked whether they should follow a single human being from among themselves, saying that then they would be in error and madness, and asked whether the reminder had been sent to him alone from among them; they said that he was an insolent liar.
God said that they would know tomorrow who the insolent liar was.
Thamud denied the warnings.

chapters.summary_md: Thamud denied the warnings [c8]. The leading group among them said they disbelieved in what the believers believed [c2]. They said Salih was bewitched, only a human like themselves, and an insolent liar [c5][c6]. Salih asked who would help him against God if he disobeyed Him [c4].
chapters.body_md:
The leading group who were arrogant said to those they considered weak, the ones among them who believed, whether they knew that Salih was sent from his Lord [c1]. The believers said they believed in what he was sent with [c1]. Those who were arrogant said that they disbelieved in what the others believed in [c2].

They said to Salih that he had been among them someone hoped for before this, asked whether he forbade them to worship what their fathers worshipped, and said they were in doubt and unease about what he called them to [c3]. Salih asked them what they thought if he was on a clear proof from his Lord and had been given mercy from Him: who would help him against God if he disobeyed Him, since they would add nothing for him but loss [c4].

Thamud denied the warnings [c8]. In other passages they said he was only one of the bewitched and only a human being like themselves, and told him to bring a sign if he was truthful [c5]. They asked whether they should follow a single human being from among themselves, saying that then they would be in error and madness, and asked whether the reminder had been sent to him alone from among them [c6]. They said that he was an insolent liar [c6]. God said that they would know tomorrow who the insolent liar was [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The objections of the people are told in different forms [c1][c3][c5][c6]. One is that the believers are weak and the leaders will not follow [c1][c2]. Another is that Salih had been hoped for before, yet now asks them to leave their fathers' worship [c3]. Yet another is that he is only a human being like them [c5][c6]. Salih's reply at 11:63 puts the question to them: who would help him against God [c4]. The last verse is God's word, not Salih's [c7].
chapters.kids_md: The leaders of Thamud said they did not believe in what the believers believed [c2]. They said Salih was only a human like themselves [c5]. Salih asked who would help him against God if he disobeyed Him [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the objections to Salih turn on his being a human like them and on what their fathers worshipped [c3][c5]. Another is that Salih answers by asking who could help him against God, which puts his obedience to God first [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the leading group were, how many believed, or what the weak among them were weak in.
- Not established: in what sense Salih had been hoped for before this (11:62).
- Not established: what sign they asked for at 26:154 beyond what the she-camel passages say.
- Not established: the speaker or the time of 54:26; the verse is God's word about what they will know tomorrow.

claims.statement_en: Salih said that this was the she-camel of God, a sign for them, and told them to leave her to eat in God's land and not to touch her with harm, or a painful punishment would seize them.
In another telling he said that a punishment that was near would seize them.
Salih said that the she-camel had a share of water and they had a share on a known day, and that they must not touch her with harm or the punishment of a great day would seize them.

God said that He was sending the she-camel as a trial for them, told His messenger to watch them and be patient, and told him to inform them that the water was divided among them, each share to be attended.
The messenger of God told them: the she-camel of God and her drink.

chapters.summary_md: Salih said that the she-camel was the she-camel of God and a sign for his people [c1]. He told them to leave her to eat in God's land and not to touch her with harm [c1]. The water was divided between her and them [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md:
Salih said that this was the she-camel of God, a sign for them, and told them to leave her to eat in God's land and not to touch her with harm, or a painful punishment would seize them [c1]. In another telling he said that a punishment that was near would seize them [c2].

He said that the she-camel had a share of water and they had a share on a known day, and that they must not touch her with harm or the punishment of a great day would seize them [c3].

God said that He was sending the she-camel as a trial for them, told His messenger to watch them and be patient, and told him to inform them that the water was divided among them, each share to be attended [c4]. Another passage has the messenger of God say to them: the she-camel of God and her drink [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The she-camel is called a sign at 7:73 [c1] and a trial at 54:27 [c4]. The warning attached to her differs in wording: a painful punishment at 7:73 [c1], a near one at 11:64 [c2], and the punishment of a great day at 26:156 [c3]. The ayah at 91:13 speaks of a messenger of God without naming him; this draft reads it as Salih, as the event inventory does [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Salih said that the she-camel was the she-camel of God and a sign for his people [c1]. He told them to leave her to eat in God's land and not to harm her [c1]. The water was shared out between them and her [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the she-camel is presented both as a sign and as a trial, and that the instruction concerning her is to leave her and not harm her [c1][c4]. Another is that the sharing of water gives the instruction a concrete shape [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the she-camel came from, how she appeared, or how long she was among them.
- Not established: what the known day of 26:155 was, or how the shares of water were reckoned.
- Not established: who the messenger of God is at 91:13; the verse does not name him.
- Not established: whether the water passage at 54:28 describes the same arrangement as 26:155.

claims.statement_en: They hamstrung the she-camel, defied the command of their Lord, and said: Salih, bring us what you promise us if you are among the messengers.
They hamstrung her, and Salih said they should enjoy themselves in their home for three days, which was a promise that would not be proved false.
They hamstrung her and became regretful.
They called their companion, who took up the matter and hamstrung her.
Thamud denied through their transgression, when the most wretched of them rose up.
They denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord brought ruin down upon them for their sin and levelled it.

chapters.summary_md: Thamud hamstrung the she-camel [c1]. Salih told them to enjoy themselves in their home for three days, a promise that would not be proved false [c2]. They became regretful [c3].
chapters.body_md:
They hamstrung the she-camel, defied the command of their Lord, and said: Salih, bring us what you promise us if you are among the messengers [c1]. In another passage they hamstrung her, and Salih said they should enjoy themselves in their home for three days, which was a promise that would not be proved false [c2]. They hamstrung her and became regretful [c3].

Another passage says they called their companion, who took up the matter and hamstrung her [c4]. The Quran also says that Thamud denied through their transgression, when the most wretched of them rose up [c5]. They denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord brought ruin down upon them for their sin and levelled it [c6].
chapters.deep_md: Passages from different surahs tell the hamstringing with different emphases: defiance of the command of their Lord and a challenge to Salih at 7:77 [c1], the three days at 11:65 [c2], regret at 26:157 [c3], and one who acted, called the companion of the people, at 54:29 [c4]. The passage at 91:11-12 names the cause as transgression and speaks of the most wretched of them rising up [c5]. Some passages say they hamstrung her in the plural, and the passages do not say how the act was divided [c1][c2][c3][c4].
chapters.kids_md: Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, which means they harmed her so that she could not walk [c1]. Salih told them to enjoy themselves in their home for three days [c2]. They became regretful [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage shows that a warning had been given and that the act followed it [c1][c2]. Another is that regret came after the act [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name or the family of the one called the companion of the people at 54:29, or of the most wretched of 91:12.
- Not established: whether the companion of 54:29 and the most wretched of 91:12 are the same person; the verses do not say.
- Not established: how the three days of 11:65 were counted, or what happened on each.
- Not established: the exact sense of the Arabic verb rendered levelled it at 91:14.

claims.statement_en: God sent to Thamud their brother Salih with the message to worship God, and they became a pair of parties disputing with each other.
Salih asked them why they hastened the bad before the good, and why they did not ask God for forgiveness so that they might receive mercy.
They said they took an ill omen from him and from those with him, and Salih said that their omen was with God, and that they were a people being tested.
There were in the city nine groups who spread corruption in the land and did not set things right.

They said to one another to swear by God that they would attack him and his family by night, and then say to his guardian that they had not witnessed the destruction of his family, and that they were truthful.
They devised a scheme, and God devised a scheme, and they did not perceive it.
God tells the hearer to look at the outcome of their scheme: He destroyed them and their people all together.
Their houses stand empty because of their wrongdoing, and the Quran says there is a sign in this for a people who know.
God saved those who believed and were mindful of Him.

chapters.summary_md: God sent Salih to Thamud, and they became a pair of parties disputing [c1]. There were nine groups in the city who spread corruption [c4]. They planned to attack Salih and his family by night, but God destroyed them and their people, and saved those who believed [c5][c7][c9].
chapters.body_md:
God sent to Thamud their brother Salih with the message to worship God, and they became a pair of parties disputing with each other [c1]. Salih asked them why they hastened the bad before the good, and why they did not ask God for forgiveness so that they might receive mercy [c2]. They said they took an ill omen from him and from those with him, and Salih said that their omen was with God, and that they were a people being tested [c3].

There were in the city nine groups who spread corruption in the land and did not set things right [c4]. They said to one another to swear by God that they would attack him and his family by night, and then say to his guardian that they had not witnessed the destruction of his family, and that they were truthful [c5]. They devised a scheme, and God devised a scheme, and they did not perceive it [c6].

God tells the hearer to look at the outcome of their scheme: He destroyed them and their people all together [c7]. Their houses stand empty because of their wrongdoing, and the Quran says there is a sign in this for a people who know [c8]. God saved those who believed and were mindful of Him [c9].
chapters.deep_md: This passage is not told in the order of the other chapters and does not mention the she-camel [c1][c4]. The groups in the city are described by what they did, spreading corruption, and by what they planned [c4][c5]. The Arabic word for scheme is used both for their plan and for God's [c6], a wording the reviewer should check.
chapters.kids_md: God sent Salih to Thamud [c1]. There were nine groups in the city who spread corruption [c4]. They planned to attack Salih and his family by night, but God destroyed them and saved those who believed [c5][c7][c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage places a secret plan beside God's own plan and says that the plotters did not perceive it [c5][c6]. Another is that the believers who were mindful of God are the ones the passage says were saved [c9].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what the nine groups were, whether they were families or bands, or how many people each had; the Arabic word raht is general.
- Not established: who the guardian of 27:49 was, or whether the verse means a relative or a protector.
- Not established: whether the plan of 27:49 was carried out, or in what order it stands to the she-camel passages; the Quran does not say.
- Not established: what God's scheme of 27:50 consisted of; the verse says only that they did not perceive it.

claims.statement_en: The quake seized them, and morning found them fallen in their home.
Salih turned away from them and said: my people, I conveyed the message of my Lord to you and advised you, but you do not love those who advise.
When God's command came, He saved Salih and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Him, and from the disgrace of that day; the Quran says that his Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.
The cry seized those who did wrong, and morning found them fallen in their homes, as if they had never lived there.
Thamud disbelieved in their Lord, and the Quran says away with Thamud.
The punishment seized them; there is a sign in that, and most of them were not believers; and the Quran says that Salih's Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.
God asks how His punishment and His warnings were, and says He sent against them a single cry, and they became like the dry twigs of a man who builds an enclosure.
God does not fear what follows from it.

chapters.summary_md: A quake and a cry seized Thamud, and morning found them fallen in their homes [c1][c4]. God saved Salih and those who believed with him [c3]. Salih turned away from them and said he had conveyed the message of his Lord [c2].
chapters.body_md:
The quake seized them, and morning found them fallen in their home [c1]. Salih turned away from them and said: my people, I conveyed the message of my Lord to you and advised you, but you do not love those who advise [c2].

When God's command came, He saved Salih and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Him, and from the disgrace of that day [c3]. The Quran says that his Lord is the Strong, the Mighty [c3]. The cry seized those who did wrong, and morning found them fallen in their homes, as if they had never lived there [c4]. Thamud disbelieved in their Lord, and the Quran says away with Thamud [c5].

In another passage the punishment seized them, and there is a sign in that, and most of them were not believers [c6]. The Quran says that Salih's Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful [c6]. God asks how His punishment and His warnings were, and says He sent against them a single cry, and they became like the dry twigs of a man who builds an enclosure [c7]. God does not fear what follows from it [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The end is told with different words, the quake at 7:78 [c1] and the cry at 11:67 and 54:31 [c4][c7]. The Quran does not say whether these are separate events or names for one [c1][c4]. The sequence of Salih's turning away at 7:79 and the rescue at 11:66 is not stated [c2][c3].
chapters.kids_md: A quake and a cry seized Thamud, and in the morning they were fallen in their homes [c1][c4]. God saved Salih and those who believed with him [c3]. Salih said he had conveyed the message of his Lord [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Salih's last words say that he had conveyed and advised, and that the people did not love those who advise [c2]. Another is that the passage separates Salih and those who believed with him from those who were seized [c3][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: whether the quake and the cry were one event or more, or how long they lasted.
- Not established: how many believed with Salih, where they went, or what became of them.
- Not established: whether Salih turned away before or after the quake; the verses do not give the order.
- Not established: the sense of the comparison with the dry twigs of one who builds an enclosure beyond what the verse says.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Salih and the she-camel. None is used in this draft.

The Thamud event in the inventory also lists 15:80-84, 17:59, 41:17-18, 51:43-45, 69:4-5 and 85:17-18. They are outside the inventory range of Salih and are not used; a reviewer should decide whether to extend the range.
The messenger of God at 91:13 is not named in the verse; the draft reads him as Salih, as the event inventory does, and marks it so.

The Arabic word for scheme at 27:50 is used both of the plan of the nine groups and of God; the draft keeps a single word in translation for both and a reviewer should check it. The sense of 26:149 (skilfully or exultingly), of the verb at 91:14 and of the term for the nine at 27:48 are also left open.
The draft reads the words quake (7:78) and cry (11:67, 54:31) without deciding whether they name one event or more than one.

Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Salih's lineage, the place of Thamud's land and of Salih's grave, the name of the person who struck the she-camel, and the names of the nine groups. None is used in the story texts.

The chapters follow a reading order (the call, the reminders, the answer, the she-camel, the act, the plan of the nine, the end). The Quran does not give a chronology across these surahs, and the draft does not claim that the plan of the nine came before or after the she-camel.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

chapters.title_en: Seeking and the signs in creation

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim said to his father Azar: do you take idols as gods? He said he saw him and his people in manifest error.
God showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who have certainty.
When the night covered him he saw a star and said “This is my Lord”; when it set he said “I do not love those that set.”
When he saw the moon appearing he said “This is my Lord”; when it set he said “If my Lord does not guide me, I will be among the people who are astray.”
When he saw the sun appearing he said “This is my Lord, this is greater”; when it set he said “My people, I am free of what you associate with God.”
He said he had turned his face, upright, to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, and that he was not among those who associate others with God.

His people argued with him; he asked whether they argued with him about God when God had guided him, said he did not fear what they associate with God unless his Lord willed something, and said his Lord's knowledge encompasses all things.

Ibrahim asked how he could fear what they associated with God when they did not fear associating with God that for which God sent down no authority, and asked which of the pair groups had more right to security.
Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing: for them is security and they are rightly guided.
God says this was His argument which He gave to Ibrahim against his people, and that He raises in degrees whom He wills.

chapters.summary_md: Ibrahim spoke against the idols of his father Azar and his people [c1]. God showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth [c2]. He looked at a star, the moon and the sun, said of each “This is my Lord”, and turned from each when it set [c3][c4][c5], then turned his face to the One who originated the heavens and the earth [c6].
chapters.body_md:
The passage opens with Ibrahim asking his father Azar whether he takes idols as gods, and telling him that he sees him and his people in manifest error [c1]. God says He showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth so that he would be among those who have certainty [c2].

When night covered him he saw a star and said “This is my Lord”; when it set he said “I do not love those that set” [c3]. He saw the moon appearing and said the same words, and when it set said “If my Lord does not guide me, I will be among the people who are astray” [c4]. He saw the sun appearing and said “This is my Lord, this is greater”; when it set he said “My people, I am free of what you associate with God” [c5]. He then said he had turned his face, upright, to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, and was not among those who associate [c6].

His people argued with him [c7]. He asked whether they argued with him about God when God had already guided him, said he did not fear what they associate unless his Lord willed something, and said his Lord's knowledge encompasses all things [c7]. He asked how he could fear what they associated while they did not fear associating with God that for which no authority was sent down, and which group had more right to security [c8]. The answer given is that security and guidance belong to those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing [c9]. God calls all this His argument given to Ibrahim against his people [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The same pattern is told of a star, the moon and the sun: it is seen, he says this is my Lord, it sets, and he turns from it [c3][c4][c5]. The conclusion is stated as a turning of the face to the originator of the heavens and the earth [c6], which answers the opening charge against idols [c1]. The passage closes by framing the whole sequence as God's argument given to Ibrahim [c10], with a principle about security and guidance [c9].
chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim told his father and his people that their idols were wrong [c1]. He saw a star, the moon and the sun, said of each that it was his Lord, and turned from each when it set [c3][c4][c5]. Then he said he had turned his face to the One who made the heavens and the earth [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the passage invites a reader to ask what is worthy of devotion, since the things Ibrahim turned from were things that set [c3][c4][c5]. It also shows a believer explaining his position calmly when argued with [c7][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established by the ayat: when and where this took place, Ibrahim's age, and how this scene stands in time to the scene of the idols and the fire. The words ‘this is my Lord’ are read in more than one way by interpreters, as a stage of search or as a way of arguing with his people; the ayat give the words and what followed and do not label them. The ayat say ‘his father Azar’; how this relates to other passages about his father is for scholarly notes.

claims.statement_en: God describes Ibrahim as a siddiq (one of great truthfulness) and a prophet.
Ibrahim asked his father why he worshipped what neither hears nor sees nor avails him anything.
He told his father that knowledge had come to him which had not come to his father, and asked him to follow him so that he would guide him to an even path.

He told his father not to worship Satan, who was disobedient to the Most Merciful, and said he feared that a punishment from the Most Merciful would touch his father and he would become an ally of Satan.
His father answered by asking whether Ibrahim was turning away from his gods, and said that if he did not stop he would stone him, and told him to leave him for a long time.

Ibrahim said “Peace be upon you; I will ask my Lord to forgive you; he has been gracious to me”, and said he would withdraw from them and from what they invoke besides God and would invoke his Lord, hoping not to be unfortunate in invoking his Lord.
When he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides God, God granted him Ishaq and Yaqub and made each a prophet.
God granted them of His mercy and gave them a high tongue of truth.

chapters.summary_md: God calls Ibrahim truthful and a prophet [c1]. He spoke kindly and with reasons to his father, who worshipped what cannot hear or see [c2][c3][c4].
