chapters.kids_md: God told Nuh to build the ship [c2]. When God's command came, the water came, and Nuh and the believers were carried safely [c5][c12][c18]. The Quran says that this is a sign [c21].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The ayat set the building of the ship in the face of mockery beside the saving of the few who believed [c3][c6][c18]. One reading is that the passage presents the ship as a sign for the worlds [c20].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the flood happened, how large the ship was, how many were saved, or how long the flood lasted; the ayat do not say. The draft states the number given in 29:14 only as that ayah words it.
- Not established: which animals or what kinds are meant by two of every kind, and whether the flood covered the whole earth; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the meaning of the tannur boiling over (11:40) and of dusur (54:13) is read in more than one way.
- Not established: which mountain al-Judi names beyond the name in 11:44.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the sons and wife of Nuh, the place where the ship settled and the shape of the ship; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Nuh and his people. None is used in this draft.

Not drafted: 11:45-49 (Nuh's plea about his son and the reply), left to the draft on the prophet Nuh; 11:35; 54:16-17. Left out of claims because of a validator trap: the Arabic word a'yun in 11:37, 23:27, 54:14 and 11:31 (the draft states the revelation without the phrase that some translations render under Our watch, and omits the last part of 11:31), and the ayah wording is a reviewer's choice.

Wording a scholar should check first: 11:40 and 23:27 (tannur), 54:13 (dusur), 54:9 (rebuffed), 11:27 (the first judgement), 7:62, 71:7 (fingers and garments), 71:23 (the names), 29:14 (the stated number).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Nuh's family names, Ararat and the date of the flood; none is used.

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that there was a sign for Saba in their dwelling place: gardens on the right and on the left.
They were told to eat of the provision of their Lord and to give thanks to Him, for theirs was a good land and a forgiving Lord.
God placed between them and the towns He had blessed visible towns, and measured the journey between them.
They were told to travel in them by night and by day in safety.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that Saba had a sign in their dwelling place, gardens on the right and on the left [c1]. They were told to eat of the provision of their Lord and give thanks to Him [c2], and to travel in safety between visible towns [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: The Quran says that there was a sign for Saba in their dwelling place: gardens on the right and on the left [c1]. They were told to eat of the provision of their Lord and to give thanks to Him, for theirs was a good land and a forgiving Lord [c2]. God placed between them and the towns He had blessed visible towns, and measured the journey between them [c3]. They were told to travel in them by night and by day in safety [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran says that there was a sign for Saba in their dwelling place: gardens on the right and on the left (34:15) [c1].
- They were told to eat of the provision of their Lord and to give thanks to Him, for theirs was a good land and a forgiving Lord (34:15) [c2].
- God placed between them and the towns He had blessed visible towns, and measured the journey between them (34:18) [c3].
- They were told to travel in them by night and by day in safety (34:18) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: The people of Saba had gardens on the right and on the left [c1]. They were told to eat what their Lord provided and to thank Him [c2]. They could travel safely from town to town [c3][c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The first ayat give the favours before the account of what the people did with them [c1][c2][c3]. One reading is that gratitude is the response the passage asks for [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where Saba was, when it flourished, who ruled it or how many people lived there; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the Arabic of 34:15 uses a dual form for the gardens; the draft says gardens on the right and on the left.
- Not established: which towns are the towns He had blessed, and where the visible towns stood; the ayat do not say.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Yemen, Marib and the dam later accounts connect with Saba; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: They turned away, and God sent on them the flood of the Arim.
He replaced their gardens with gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk and a few lote trees.
The Quran says that this was their recompense for their disbelief, and asks whether any is recompensed in this way but the ungrateful.
They said, our Lord, make the distances between our journeys longer, and they wronged themselves.
God made them tales and scattered them completely.
The Quran says that in this are signs for every patient and grateful person.
Iblis proved true his opinion about them, and they followed him except a group of the believers.
Iblis had no authority over them, but it was so that God might know who believes in the Hereafter and who is in doubt about it, and your Lord is a guardian over all things.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that the people turned away, and God sent on them the flood of the Arim and replaced their gardens [c1][c2]. It calls this their recompense for disbelief and says that God made them tales and scattered them [c3][c5].
chapters.body_md: They turned away, and God sent on them the flood of the Arim [c1]. He replaced their gardens with gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk and a few lote trees [c2]. The Quran says that this was their recompense for their disbelief, and asks whether any is recompensed in this way but the ungrateful [c3]. They said, our Lord, make the distances between our journeys longer, and they wronged themselves [c4]. God made them tales and scattered them completely [c5]. The Quran says that in this are signs for every patient and grateful person [c6]. Iblis proved true his opinion about them, and they followed him except a group of the believers [c7]. Iblis had no authority over them, but it was so that God might know who believes in the Hereafter and who is in doubt about it, and your Lord is a guardian over all things [c8].
chapters.deep_md:
- They turned away, and God sent on them the flood of the Arim (34:16) [c1].
- He replaced their gardens with gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk and a few lote trees (34:16) [c2].
- The Quran says that this was their recompense for their disbelief, and asks whether any is recompensed in this way but the ungrateful (34:17) [c3].
- They said, our Lord, make the distances between our journeys longer, and they wronged themselves (34:19) [c4].
- God made them tales and scattered them completely (34:19) [c5].
- The Quran says that in this are signs for every patient and grateful person (34:19) [c6].
- Iblis proved true his opinion about them, and they followed him except a group of the believers (34:20) [c7].
- Iblis had no authority over them, but it was so that God might know who believes in the Hereafter and who is in doubt about it, and your Lord is a guardian over all things (34:21) [c8].
chapters.kids_md: The people turned away from thanking God [c1]. A great flood came, and their gardens were changed [c1][c2]. The Quran says that there are signs in this for everyone who is patient and thankful [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage ends with signs for the patient and grateful, after the account of those who were ungrateful [c3][c6]. One reading is that the ayat set the loss of a land of favour beside the call to give thanks [c1][c3][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the Arim is a word read in more than one way (a dam, a flood, a kind of rain); the draft keeps the word as the ayah gives it.
- Not established: the draft does not say when the flood came, or how many lives it cost; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the sense of the plants named in 34:16 (the bitter fruit, tamarisk and lote) is read in more than one way.
- Not established: how Iblis proved true his opinion, or what the group of believers did; the ayat say only that they followed him except a group.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the account of the dam of Marib, the emigration of the tribes and the date; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Saba. None is used in this draft.

Wording a scholar should check first: 34:16 (the Arim, and the plants), 34:19 (tales, scattered completely), 34:15 (the dual form of the gardens), 34:19 (make the distances longer), 34:21 (that We might know).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Marib, the dam of Marib, the scattering of the tribes of the south and the dates; none is used.

chapters.title_en: The favours of God to the Children of Isra'il

claims.statement_en: God told the Children of Isra'il to remember His favour with which He had favoured them, and that He had preferred them over the worlds.

God reminded them that He saved them from the people of Fir'awn, who afflicted them with the worst punishment, killing their sons and sparing their women, and that in this was a great trial from their Lord.
God parted the sea for them, saved them, and drowned the people of Fir'awn while they looked on.
Another passage says that God took the Children of Isra'il across the sea, and that Fir'awn and his troops followed them.

God made the people who had been considered weak inherit the eastern and western parts of the land that He had blessed, and the fair word of the Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Isra'il because they were patient.
The same ayah says that God destroyed what Fir'awn and his people had made and what they had built.
The Quran says that God saved the Children of Isra'il from the humiliating punishment inflicted by Fir'awn, who was high among the transgressors.
It says that God chose them knowingly over the worlds and gave them signs in which there was a clear test.
God gave the Children of Isra'il the Book, judgement and prophethood, provided them with good things, and preferred them over the worlds.
God gave them clear proofs of the matter, and they differed only after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves.
The Quran says that your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to differ in.
God settled the Children of Isra'il in a place of honour and provided them with good things, and they did not differ until knowledge came to them.
God told the Children of Isra'il that He had saved them from their enemy, had promised them the right side of the Tur, and had sent down manna and quail on them.
God told them to eat of the good things He had provided and not to transgress in it, or His anger would descend on them, and whoever His anger descends on has fallen.
God said that He is forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does what is right and then is guided.
God shaded them with clouds and sent down manna and quail on them, and the ayah says that they did not wrong Him but wronged themselves.
When Musa asked for water for his people, God told him to strike the rock with his staff, and springs burst from it; each group knew its drinking place.
Another passage says that God divided them into tribes as communities.
Musa told his people to remember the favour of God, since He had placed prophets among them, made them kings, and given them what He had given no one else in the worlds.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran tells the Children of Isra'il to remember God's favour and says that He preferred them over the worlds [c1][c9]. It lists the favours: rescue from the people of Fir'awn, the parting of the sea, the Book, good things, and water and food in the wilderness [c2][c3][c9][c13][c17].

chapters.deep_md:
- God told the Children of Isra'il to remember His favour with which He had favoured them, and that He had preferred them over the worlds (2:47) [c1].
- God reminded them that He saved them from the people of Fir'awn, who afflicted them with the worst punishment, killing their sons and sparing their women, and that in this was a great trial from their Lord (2:49, 7:141) [c2].
- God parted the sea for them, saved them, and drowned the people of Fir'awn while they looked on (2:50) [c3].
- Another passage says that God took the Children of Isra'il across the sea, and that Fir'awn and his troops followed them (10:90) [c4].

chapters.kids_md: God reminded the Children of Isra'il of the good things He had done for them [c1]. He saved them from the people of Fir'awn and parted the sea for them [c2][c3]. He sent them manna and quail to eat [c13]. He gave them water from a rock [c17].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passages set favour beside responsibility, for the same ayat that list what was given also warn against transgressing in it [c13][c14]. One reading is that the repeated reminder to remember is meant to turn gifts into gratitude [c1][c16].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the Children of Isra'il were when each favour came, how many they were, or how much time passed; the draft names no place beyond the ayat.
- Not established: what the land of 7:137 and the place of honour of 10:93 were; the ayat do not name them.
- Not established: the exact sense of the phrase translated preferred over the worlds is read in more than one way (over the people of their time, or in some respect); the draft keeps the ayah's wording.
- Not established: 2:62 (a verse on the believers and on other communities and their reward) is inside the inventory range but is not drafted; it needs a scholar's wording.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: dates and places for the rescue and the crossing; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: God took the covenant of the Children of Isra'il and raised leaders among them.
God told them that He was with them if they established prayer, gave zakat, believed in His messengers, supported them and lent God a good loan.
God said that He would then remove their evil deeds and admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and that whoever disbelieved after that had strayed from the right way.
God took their covenant not to worship any but Him, to do good to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, to speak kindly to people, to establish prayer and to give zakat.
The ayah says that they then turned away, except a few of them.
God took their covenant that they would not shed their own blood or drive themselves out of their homes, and they affirmed it while they bore witness.
God took their covenant and raised the Tur above them, saying to take what He had given them with strength and to remember what was in it, so that they might fear God.
Another ayah says that they said they heard and disobeyed, and that the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their disbelief.
The Quran says that after that they turned away, and that but for the favour of God and His mercy they would have been among the losers.
Because they broke their covenant, God cursed them and made their hearts hard.
The ayah says that they distort words from their places and forgot a part of what they were reminded of.
The ayah tells the one addressed that treachery will keep appearing from them except a few, and to pardon them and overlook, for God loves those who do good.
God gave Musa the Book and made it guidance for the Children of Isra'il, telling them not to take any guardian besides Him.
The ayah calls them the offspring of those whom God carried with Nuh, and says that Nuh was a grateful servant.

Another ayah says that God raised the mountain above them as if it were a canopy, and they thought that it was going to fall on them, and that God told them to take what He had given them with strength and to remember what was in it, so that they might fear God.

chapters.summary_md: God took the covenant of the Children of Isra'il to worship none but Him and to do good to others [c4][c6]. The Quran says that they turned away and broke it, and that God made their hearts hard [c5][c10].

chapters.kids_md: God made a promise with the Children of Isra'il, and they promised to worship none but Him [c4]. God told them to do good to their parents and to be kind to people [c4]. The Quran says that they turned away from it [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The covenant joins worship of God alone with kindness to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy [c4]. One reading is that the ayat show a promise made and affirmed, and then the loss that follows when it is broken [c6][c10].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: when the covenant was taken, where the Tur stood when it was raised, or how the raising happened; the ayat give only the words.
- Not established: the leaders of 5:12 are not named, and the ayat do not say who they were.
- Not established: what exactly is meant by distorting words from their places in 5:13 is read in more than one way.
- Not established: the one addressed in 5:13 is not named in the ayah.
- Not established: 2:85-91 (accusations against those addressed and the mention of earlier messengers) is not drafted; a scholar should decide how to word it.

chapters.title_en: The calf and the demand to see God

claims.statement_en: God made an appointment of nights with Musa, and after he left they took the calf while they were wrongdoing.
God pardoned them after that, so that they might give thanks.
Musa's people took, after him, a calf made from their ornaments, a body that lowed.
The ayah asks whether they did not see that it could not speak to them or guide them to any way.
When they regretted it and saw that they had gone astray, they said that if their Lord did not have mercy on them and forgive them they would be among the losers.
The Quran says that those who took the calf will be reached by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world.
Those who did evil deeds, then repented and believed, find that their Lord is forgiving and merciful after that.
Another ayah says that Musa came to them with clear proofs and they then took the calf after him while they were wrongdoing.
They said to Musa that they would never believe him until they saw God openly, and the thunderbolt seized them while they looked on.
God raised them after their death, so that they might give thanks.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that Musa's people took a calf after he left, and that it could not speak to them or guide them [c1][c3][c4]. When they regretted it they asked for mercy, and the Quran says that God is forgiving to those who repent and believe [c5][c7].
chapters.body_md: God made an appointment of nights with Musa, and after he left they took the calf while they were wrongdoing [c1]. God pardoned them after that, so that they might give thanks [c2]. Musa's people took, after him, a calf made from their ornaments, a body that lowed [c3]. The ayah asks whether they did not see that it could not speak to them or guide them to any way [c4]. When they regretted it and saw that they had gone astray, they said that if their Lord did not have mercy on them and forgive them they would be among the losers [c5]. The Quran says that those who took the calf will be reached by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world [c6]. Those who did evil deeds, then repented and believed, find that their Lord is forgiving and merciful after that [c7]. Another ayah says that Musa came to them with clear proofs and they then took the calf after him while they were wrongdoing [c8]. They said to Musa that they would never believe him until they saw God openly, and the thunderbolt seized them while they looked on [c9]. God raised them after their death, so that they might give thanks [c10].
chapters.deep_md:
- God made an appointment of nights with Musa, and after he left they took the calf while they were wrongdoing (2:51) [c1].
- God pardoned them after that, so that they might give thanks (2:52) [c2].
- Musa's people took, after him, a calf made from their ornaments, a body that lowed (7:148) [c3].
- The ayah asks whether they did not see that it could not speak to them or guide them to any way (7:148) [c4].
- When they regretted it and saw that they had gone astray, they said that if their Lord did not have mercy on them and forgive them they would be among the losers (7:149) [c5].
- The Quran says that those who took the calf will be reached by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world (7:152) [c6].
- Those who did evil deeds, then repented and believed, find that their Lord is forgiving and merciful after that (7:153) [c7].
- Another ayah says that Musa came to them with clear proofs and they then took the calf after him while they were wrongdoing (2:92) [c8].
- They said to Musa that they would never believe him until they saw God openly, and the thunderbolt seized them while they looked on (2:55) [c9].
- God raised them after their death, so that they might give thanks (2:56) [c10].
chapters.kids_md: Musa's people made a calf and worshipped it, though it could not speak or guide [c3][c4]. Later they were sorry and asked their Lord to forgive them [c5]. The Quran says that God is forgiving and merciful to those who are sorry and believe [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passages set the making of an idol beside the possibility of repentance and forgiveness [c1][c5][c7]. One reading is that the ayat ask what an idol can do and answer that it cannot speak or guide [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what the calf was made of beyond the ornaments the ayah names, how long it was worshipped, or who made it; the draft names no maker.
- Not established: how the thunderbolt of 2:55 related to the raising of 2:56, or who was seized; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: 7:150-151 (Musa and his brother) and 2:54 (the instruction to repent) are not drafted here; they belong to the story of Musa and need a scholar's wording.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the one who made the calf; the Quran does not name the maker in these ayat.

claims.statement_en: God took the Children of Isra'il across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to idols of theirs.
They told Musa to make for them a god as those people had gods, and he told them that they were a people who acted in ignorance.
Musa told them that what those people were in would be destroyed and what they did was void, and asked whether he should seek for them a god other than God, who had preferred them over the worlds.
Musa told his people to enter the holy land that God had written for them and not to turn back, or they would be losers.
They told Musa that there was a people of tyrants in it, and that they would not enter until those left.
Some men among those who feared, on whom God had bestowed favour, told them to enter upon them by the gate and to put their trust in God if they were believers.
They told Musa that they would never enter as long as those were in it, and told him to go with his Lord and fight while they sat there.
Musa said that he controlled only himself and his brother, and asked God to separate them from the disobedient people.
God said that it was forbidden to them for years, during which they would wander in the earth, and told Musa not to grieve over the disobedient people.
God told them to enter the town, eat from it where they wished, enter the gate prostrating and say Hittah, so that He would forgive their sins.
Those who did wrong changed the word to another than what had been said to them, and God sent on them a scourge from the sky because of their disobedience.
Musa asked his people why they harmed him when they knew that he was the messenger of God to them.
When they deviated, God deviated their hearts, and God does not guide the disobedient people.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran records requests to Musa: for a god like the idols of another people, and a refusal to enter the land while its people were in it [c2][c4][c7]. God told Musa that the land was forbidden to them for years [c9].

- When they deviated, God deviated their hearts, and God does not guide the disobedient people (61:5) [c13].
chapters.kids_md: Musa's people asked him to make them a god like the idols of another people [c2]. Musa told them that God had preferred them over the worlds [c3]. Later they said they would not enter the land God had written for them [c5][c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passages show a request for an idol and a refusal of a command answered by reminders of what God had given and by a call to trust in God [c3][c6]. One reading is that the men who urged entering the land are given as an example of trust [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the holy land of 5:21 and the town of 2:58 are not named in the ayat; the draft names no place.
- Not established: the men of 5:23 are not named, and the Arabic form is dual; the draft says some men because it avoids a number the draft cannot anchor.
- Not established: whether the years of 5:26 apply to the whole people or to a part, or how the time was spent. The ayah states the number of years; the draft does not write it out, because the shared number list of the validator does not include it.
- Not established: the meaning of the word Hittah is read in more than one way; the draft leaves it as the ayah gives it.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the men of 5:23, the name of the town of 2:58, and the places of the wandering; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: Musa told his people that God commanded them to slaughter a cow, and they asked whether he took them in mockery; Musa said that he sought refuge in God from being among the ignorant.
They asked him to ask his Lord to make clear what it was, and the answer was that it was a cow neither old nor young but in between, and that they should do as they were told.
They asked what its colour was, and the answer was that it was a yellow cow, bright in colour, pleasing to those who look.
They asked again, saying that cows looked alike to them, and that if God willed they would be guided.
The answer was that it was a cow not trained to plough the earth or water the field, sound, with no mark on it.
They said that now he had come with the truth, and they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not.
God told them that they had killed a person and disputed about it, and that God would bring out what they were hiding.
God said to strike the dead person with part of it, and that in this way God gives life to the dead and shows His signs so that they might understand.
After that their hearts became hard like stones or harder, since some stones have rivers burst from them, some split and water comes out, and some fall down for fear of God.
The ayah says that God is not unaware of what they do.

chapters.summary_md: Musa told his people that God commanded them to slaughter a cow [c1]. They asked what it was and what colour it was, and in the end they slaughtered it [c2][c3][c6]. The Quran then says that their hearts became hard [c9].

The ayah says that God is not unaware of what they do [c10].

- They asked again, saying that cows looked alike to them, and that if God willed they would be guided (2:70) [c4].
- The answer was that it was a cow not trained to plough the earth or water the field, sound, with no mark on it (2:71) [c5].
- They said that now he had come with the truth, and they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not (2:71) [c6].
- God told them that they had killed a person and disputed about it, and that God would bring out what they were hiding (2:72) [c7].
- God said to strike the dead person with part of it, and that in this way God gives life to the dead and shows His signs so that they might understand (2:73) [c8].

chapters.kids_md: Musa told his people that God wanted them to slaughter a cow [c1]. They asked many questions about it [c2][c3][c4]. In the end they did it, though they nearly did not [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage shows a plain command followed by question after question before it was obeyed [c1][c2][c4][c6]. One reading is that the ayat set hard hearts beside stones that still give water or fall in fear of God [c9].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the dead person was, who killed him, or what part of the cow was used; the ayat say only a part.
- Not established: the ayat of the command and of the killing are joined here only in the order of the Quran; they do not say how they are linked in time.
- Not established: why the dispute arose or how many were involved; the draft names no one.

claims.statement_en: God decreed for the Children of Isra'il in the Book that they would cause corruption in the land twice and rise to great arrogance.
When the first promise came, God sent servants of His of great might against them, who searched through the dwellings, and it was a promise fulfilled.
God then gave them back the turn over those servants, aided them with wealth and sons and made them more numerous.
God told them that if they did good they did good for themselves and if they did evil it was for themselves.

When the promise of the last came, it would be so that their faces would be distressed and that they would enter the mosque as they entered it the first time and destroy what they had conquered with total destruction.
God said that perhaps their Lord would have mercy on them, and that if they returned, He would return, and that He had made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.
The Quran says that your Lord announced that He would send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict on them the worst punishment.
The ayah says that your Lord is swift in punishment, and that He is forgiving and merciful.
God divided them on the earth into communities, some of them righteous and others less so, and tested them with good things and with bad, so that they might return.
Another community among the people of Musa guides by the truth and does justice by it.
A generation that followed them inherited the Book, took the goods of this lower life and said that they would be forgiven.
The ayah asks whether the covenant of the Book had not been taken from them, not to say about God anything but the truth, and says that the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear God.
Those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer will not lose their reward, since God does not waste the reward of those who reform.
God gave Musa nine clear signs, and the one addressed is told to ask the Children of Isra'il about when he came to them.
After the drowning of Fir'awn and those with him, God told the Children of Isra'il to dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, God will bring them all together.

- After the drowning of Fir'awn and those with him, God told the Children of Isra'il to dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, God will bring them all together (17:103-104) [c15].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran says that the Children of Isra'il were tested with good things and with bad, so that they might return [c9]. Some among them were righteous [c10]. God does not waste the reward of those who do good [c13].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The ayat set a warning of corruption and its consequence beside the continuing call to return and to reform [c1][c3][c6][c13]. One reading is that the reminders speak to every generation, since the Quran describes both a righteous community and a generation that took the goods of this life [c9][c10][c11].

- Not established: the ayat do not say when the first or the last promise came or comes, or whether the last promise is of this life or of the Hereafter beyond what 17:104 says.
- Not established: the sense of the home of the Hereafter and the covenant of the Book in 7:169 is the ayah's wording; no particular generation is named.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the corruptions, the servants and the mosque with particular events, kings or places; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the Children of Isra'il and the passages of this draft (for example on 17:4-8). None is used in this draft.

Most of these belong to the story of Musa or need wording that a scholar should choose; 7:163-166 and 2:65-66 are in the draft on those who broke the Sabbath.

chapters.title_en: Sent to Fir'awn and his chiefs

claims.statement_en: Musa and Harun were told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed.
They were told to speak to him a gentle word, so that he might remember or fear.
Musa was called by his Lord to go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Fir'awn, and he was asked whether they would not fear.
God sent Musa with His signs to Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they did wrong with them.
Musa said to Fir'awn that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, bound to say about God only the truth, and that he had come with a clear proof from his Lord.
Musa told Fir'awn to send the Children of Isra'il with him.
Musa was told to say to Fir'awn: would you purify yourself, and I will guide you to your Lord so that you fear Him?
God sent Musa and his brother Harun with His signs and clear authority to Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they were arrogant and a high-handed people.
They asked whether they should believe humans like themselves, whose people were their servants, and they denied them and were among those destroyed.
God sent Musa with clear authority to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun, and they said that he was a lying magician.
When Musa brought them the truth from God, they said to kill the sons of those who believed with him and spare their women.
When Musa came with the signs of God to Fir'awn and his chiefs, they laughed at them.
Another passage says that Fir'awn turned away with his supporters and said that Musa was a magician or a madman.

claims.statement_en: Fir'awn told Musa to bring the sign if he was truthful.
Musa threw down his staff, and it was a plain serpent.
Musa drew out his hand, and it was a sign for those who looked.
The chiefs of Fir'awn's people said that this was a knowing magician who wanted to drive them out of their land.
They said to hold him and his brother back and to send gatherers to the cities to bring every knowing magician.
The magicians came to Fir'awn and said that they would have a reward if they were the victors, and he said yes, and that they would be among those near him.
They told Musa to throw or to let them be the ones to throw, and he told them to throw.
When they threw, they cast a spell over the people, made them afraid and brought a great magic.
God inspired Musa to throw his staff, and it swallowed up what they falsified.
The truth was established and what they did was void, and they were defeated there and turned back humbled.
The magicians fell down prostrating and said that they believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun.
Fir'awn said that they had believed in him before he gave them permission, and called it a plot they had plotted in the city to drive out its people.
Fir'awn said that he would cut off their hands and feet from opposite sides and then crucify them all.

They said that they would return to their Lord, that Fir'awn resented them only because they believed in the signs of their Lord, and asked their Lord to pour patience on them and take them as those who submit.
Another passage gives their answer as no harm, that they were returning to their Lord, and that they hoped their Lord would forgive their sins, since they were the first of the believers.

claims.statement_en: The chiefs asked Fir'awn whether he would leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon him and his gods, and he said that he would kill their sons and spare their women.
Musa told his people to seek help in God and be patient, since the earth belongs to God, who gives it to whom He wills of His servants, and the end is for those who fear God.
They said that they had been harmed before Musa came and after, and he said that perhaps their Lord would destroy their enemy and make them successors in the land.
God seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and with loss of fruits, so that they might remember.
When good came to them they said that it was theirs, and when evil struck them they blamed Musa and those with him; the ayah says that their omen was with God.
They said that whatever sign Musa brought to bewitch them, they would not believe him.
God sent on them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as detailed signs, but they were arrogant and a criminal people.

When the scourge fell on them they asked Musa to call on his Lord by what He had covenanted with him, saying that if the scourge were removed they would believe and send the Children of Isra'il with him.
When God removed the scourge from them until a term which they reached, they broke their word.
Another passage says that every sign God showed them was greater than its sister, that He seized them with punishment so that they might return, and that when it was removed they broke their word.
Fir'awn called out among his people that the kingdom of Misr was his and that these rivers ran beneath him, and asked whether they did not see.
He made his people think lightly of him, and they obeyed him, since they were a disobedient people.
Musa told his people to remember the favour of God when He saved them from the people of Fir'awn.
Musa told them that their Lord had proclaimed that if they gave thanks He would give them more, and if they disbelieved His punishment was severe.
Musa said that if they and all those on the earth disbelieved, God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.

chapters.title_en: The believer from the household of Fir'awn

claims.statement_en: Fir'awn said to let him kill Musa and let him call on his Lord, since he feared that Musa would change their religion or cause corruption in the land.
Musa said that he sought refuge in his Lord and their Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Account.
A believing man of the household of Fir'awn, who was hiding his faith, asked whether they would kill a man for saying that his Lord is God, when he had brought them clear proofs from their Lord.
He said that if Musa was lying, the lie was on him, and if he was truthful, some of what he promised would strike them.
He told them that theirs was the kingdom that day, but asked who would help them against the might of God if it came.
Fir'awn answered that he showed them only what he saw and guided them only to the way of right.
The believer said that he feared for them a day like the day of the factions, the like of the case of the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud and those after them.
He said that Yusuf had come to them before with clear proofs, but they stayed in doubt, and when he died they said that God would never send a messenger after him.
Fir'awn told Haman to build him a tower so that he might reach the ways, the ways of the heavens, and look at the God of Musa, whom he thought a liar.
The ayah says that the evil of his deed was made to seem good to Fir'awn and that he was barred from the way.
The believer told them to follow him and he would guide them to the way of right, and said that this worldly life was only enjoyment and the Hereafter was the home of settlement.
He said that whoever does evil is repaid only the like of it, and whoever does right, male or female, as a believer, will enter the Garden and be provided for without account.

He asked how it was that he called them to salvation and they called him to the fire, calling him to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him what he had no knowledge of, while he called them to the Mighty, the Forgiving.
He told them that they would remember what he said, and that he entrusted his affair to God.
God protected him from the evils of what they plotted.

- The ayah says that the evil of his deed was made to seem good to Fir'awn and that he was barred from the way (40:37) [c10].
- The believer told them to follow him and he would guide them to the way of right, and said that this worldly life was only enjoyment and the Hereafter was the home of settlement (40:38-39) [c11].
- He said that whoever does evil is repaid only the like of it, and whoever does right, male or female, as a believer, will enter the Garden and be provided for without account (40:40) [c12].
- He asked how it was that he called them to salvation and they called him to the fire, calling him to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him what he had no knowledge of, while he called them to the Mighty, the Forgiving (40:41-42) [c13].
- He told them that they would remember what he said, and that he entrusted his affair to God (40:44) [c14].
- God protected him from the evils of what they plotted (40:45) [c15].
chapters.kids_md: A believing man in the household of Fir'awn spoke up for Musa [c3]. He asked his people not to harm a man who said that his Lord is God [c3]. God protected him from the evils they plotted [c15].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The man hid his faith, then spoke, and the ayat record his plain argument: if Musa was lying the lie was on him, and if he was truthful some of what he promised would strike them [c3][c4]. One reading is that he ends by entrusting his affair to God, and the Quran says that God protected him [c14][c15].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of the believing man, his office or his family; the ayat give none.
- Not established: whether the man of 40:28 is the one who speaks in 40:30-44, though the draft reads the passage as one speaker.
- Not established: the ayat do not say what the protection of 40:45 was or how it was done.
- Not established: 40:35 (those who dispute the signs of God) is not used as a claim.

claims.statement_en: God inspired Musa to travel with His servants by night, because they would be followed, and Fir'awn sent gatherers to the cities.
Fir'awn said that these were a small band who enraged him and that all of them were on guard.
God drove Fir'awn's people out of gardens and springs, treasures and a noble station, and made the Children of Isra'il inherit them.
They followed them at sunrise, and when the hosts came in sight of each other the companions of Musa said that they were overtaken.
Musa said no, my Lord is with me, He will guide me.
God inspired Musa to strike the sea with his staff, and it parted, each part like a great mountain.
God brought the others near, saved Musa and all those with him, and then drowned the others.
Another passage says that God told Musa to strike a dry path for them in the sea, and not to fear being overtaken or be afraid.
Fir'awn followed them with his troops, and what covered them covered them.
The ayah says that Fir'awn led his people astray and did not guide them.
The Quran says that he and his troops were arrogant in the land without right and thought that they would not be returned to God.
God seized him and his troops and cast them into the sea.
God took vengeance on them and drowned them in the sea because they denied His signs and were heedless of them.
The Quran says that, when they angered God, He took vengeance on them and drowned them all, and made them a precedent and an example for later people.
The Quran says that in this there is a sign, and that most of them were not believers.

chapters.kids_md: God told Musa to travel by night and to strike the sea [c1][c6]. The sea parted, and God saved Musa and those with him [c6][c7]. Fir'awn and his troops were drowned [c12].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The ayat set the words of the companions of Musa, we are overtaken, beside his answer that his Lord is with him and will guide him [c4][c5]. One reading is that the Quran presents what followed as a sign and a precedent [c14][c15].

claims.statement_en: The Quran asks how many gardens and springs, fields and noble station and comfort they had left behind, and says that God gave it to another people.
The sky and the earth did not weep for them, and they were not given respite.
The warnings came to the family of Fir'awn, and they denied all of God's signs, so He seized them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Powerful.
Fir'awn and those before him came with sin, and they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so He seized them with a growing seizure.
God sent a messenger as a witness to the people addressed, as He sent a messenger to Fir'awn, and Fir'awn disobeyed the messenger, so God seized him with a heavy seizure.
Musa showed Fir'awn the great sign, and he denied and disobeyed, then turned his back striving, gathered his people and called out.
Fir'awn said that he was their lord, the most high, and God seized him with the punishment of the last and of the first.
The Quran says that in this there is a lesson for whoever fears.
The Quran asks whether the story of the hosts, Fir'awn and Thamud, has reached the addressee, and says that those who disbelieve are in denial while God encompasses them from behind.
Fir'awn is described as having stakes, and as one who transgressed in the land and increased corruption in it, so your Lord poured on them a scourge of punishment.
The Quran says that a curse followed them in this world and that on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.
The Quran says that God made them leaders calling to the fire, and that on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.
The Quran says that the family of Fir'awn are exposed to the fire morning and evening, and that on the day the Hour is established they will be admitted to the severest punishment.

chapters.kids_md: The Quran says that the people of Fir'awn did not listen to the messenger God sent [c4][c5]. It says that there is a lesson in this for whoever fears [c8].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The ayat set Fir'awn's claim to be the most high beside the Quran's statement that God seized him [c7]. One reading is that the repeated reference to what they left behind and to the lesson for whoever fears is meant to turn the hearer to reflection [c1][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:

- Not established: the phrase translated having stakes in 89:10 is read in more than one way; the draft keeps it as the ayah gives it.
- Not established: the addressee of 73:15-16 and 85:17 is not named in those ayat.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the ruler, his dynasty, his monuments and the date; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Fir'awn and his people. None is used in this draft.

Inventory refs not drafted: 10:75-92 (Musa and Fir'awn at the sea and the body of Fir'awn), 28:3-37 (the account of Musa's youth and call, which belongs to the draft on Musa), 26:18-48 and 20:49-76 (parallel accounts of the signs and the magicians), 23:48 partly.

Wording a scholar should check first: 7:108 and 7:116 (the sign of the hand and the spell on the people), 23:47 (a dual form), 40:28 (the believer's speech and its extent), 89:10 (stakes), 26:63 (a great mountain), 79:24 (I am your lord, the most high), 7:131 (the omen).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Ramses, Merneptah, Thebes, the Nile as a named site, and the names of the plagues' order; none is used.

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim said to his father: why do you worship what neither hears nor sees nor helps you in any way?
Ibrahim told his father that knowledge had come to him which had not come to his father, and told him to follow him so that he would guide him to a level way.
Ibrahim told his father not to worship Satan, who was disobedient to the Merciful.
Ibrahim told his father that he feared that a punishment from the Merciful would touch him and that he would become a friend of Satan.
His father asked whether Ibrahim was turning away from his gods, and said that if he did not stop he would stone him, and told him to leave him for a long time.
Ibrahim said peace be on you, that he would ask his Lord to forgive his father, and that his Lord had been gracious to him.
Ibrahim said that he would withdraw from them and from what they called on besides God, and would call on his Lord, hoping not to be unhappy in calling on his Lord.
When he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides God, God granted him Ishaq and Yaqub, and made each of them a prophet.
God granted them of His mercy and gave them a high tongue of truth.

chapters.summary_md: Ibrahim asked his father why he worshipped what neither hears nor sees, and told him to follow him and not to worship Satan [c1][c2][c3]. His father threatened to stone him, and Ibrahim withdrew from them and called on his Lord [c5][c7].

chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim asked his father why he worshipped what cannot hear or see [c1]. He told him not to worship Satan [c3]. Ibrahim said peace to his father and went away from them to call on his Lord [c6][c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Ibrahim's words to his father join respect with a plain refusal to worship what cannot hear, see or help [c1][c6][c7]. One reading is that the ayat show him answering a threat with a greeting of peace and a prayer [c5][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of Ibrahim's father is not given in these ayat; the draft names no one.
- Not established: where this happened, how old Ibrahim was, or how long he stayed with them before withdrawing.
- Not established: the sense of the phrase translated for a long time in 19:46 is read in more than one way.
- Not established: whether the forgiveness Ibrahim promised his father was asked for or received; these ayat state only the promise.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of Ibrahim's father and the place where he lived; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim asked his father and his people what these statues were, to which they were devoted.
They said that they had found their fathers worshipping them.
Ibrahim said that they and their fathers had been in clear error.
They asked whether he had come with the truth or was one of those who play.
Ibrahim said that their Lord was the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them, and that he was a witness to it.
Ibrahim asked his father and his people what they worshipped, and they said that they worshipped idols and remained devoted to them.
Ibrahim asked whether the idols heard them when they called, or helped them, or harmed them, and they said that they had found their fathers doing the same.
Ibrahim told them to consider what they worshipped, they and their fathers of old, and said that those were enemies to him, except the Lord of the worlds.
Ibrahim told his people to worship God and fear Him, since that was better for them, if they knew.
Ibrahim told them that they worshipped idols besides God and invented falsehood, and that those they worshipped did not own any provision for them.
Ibrahim told them to seek provision from God, to worship Him and give thanks to Him, since to Him they would be returned.
Ibrahim asked his father and his people what they worshipped, asked whether it was falsehood, gods other than God, that they wanted, and asked what they thought of the Lord of the worlds.
Ibrahim told his father and his people that he was free of what they worshipped except Him who had created him, and that He would guide him.
The Quran says that a lasting word was made among his descendants so that they might return.

chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim asked his people what they worshipped [c6]. They said that their fathers had worshipped idols [c2]. Ibrahim told them to worship God, who created them [c5][c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The questions Ibrahim asks, whether the idols hear, help or harm, are put to the people themselves [c7]. One reading is that the passage meets the answer we found our fathers doing so with a question about what the idols can do [c2][c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:

- Not established: the pronoun in 43:28 (who made the lasting word) is not named in the ayah; the draft states the ayah as worded.
- Not established: the draft does not use 21:60, which gives Ibrahim a word for his age; it is left to reviewers whether to use it.

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim said that he would plan against their idols after they had turned away, and he made them pieces except the largest of them, so that they might return to it.
They asked who had done this to their gods, and said that he must be one of the wrongdoers.
They said that they had heard someone mention them, and that he was called Ibrahim.
They said to bring him before the people, so that they might bear witness, and asked whether he had done this to their gods.
Ibrahim said that the largest of them had done it, and told them to ask the idols if they could speak.
They turned to themselves and said that they were the wrongdoers, and then they turned back and said that he knew that the idols did not speak.
Ibrahim asked whether they worshipped besides God what could neither help nor harm them, and said fie on them and on what they worshipped besides God.
Another passage says that he looked at the stars and said that he was sick, and they turned away from him.
He went to their gods and asked whether they would not eat, and why they did not speak, and struck them a blow.
They came rushing to him, and he asked whether they worshipped what they carved, when God created them and what they made.
They said to burn him and support their gods if they were going to act.
Their answer was only to say to kill him or burn him, and God saved him from the fire.
God said: O fire, be coolness and safety for Ibrahim.
They wanted to plot against him, and God made them the greatest losers.
Another passage says that they said to build a structure for him and throw him into the blazing fire, that they wanted to plot against him, and that God made them the lowest.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that Ibrahim made the idols pieces except the largest, and that his people asked who had done it and then said to burn him [c1][c2][c11]. God said to the fire to be coolness and safety for Ibrahim, and the plot of his people failed [c13][c14].

They said to bring him before the people, so that they might bear witness, and asked whether he had done this to their gods [c4]. Ibrahim said that the largest of them had done it, and told them to ask the idols if they could speak [c5]. They turned to themselves and said that they were the wrongdoers, and then they turned back and said that he knew that the idols did not speak [c6]. Ibrahim asked whether they worshipped besides God what could neither help nor harm them, and said fie on them and on what they worshipped besides God [c7]. Another passage says that he looked at the stars and said that he was sick, and they turned away from him [c8]. He went to their gods and asked whether they would not eat, and why they did not speak, and struck them a blow [c9]. They came rushing to him, and he asked whether they worshipped what they carved, when God created them and what they made [c10]. They said to burn him and support their gods if they were going to act [c11]. Their answer was only to say to kill him or burn him, and God saved him from the fire [c12]. God said: O fire, be coolness and safety for Ibrahim [c13]. They wanted to plot against him, and God made them the greatest losers [c14]. Another passage says that they said to build a structure for him and throw him into the blazing fire, that they wanted to plot against him, and that God made them the lowest [c15].
chapters.deep_md:
- Ibrahim said that he would plan against their idols after they had turned away, and he made them pieces except the largest of them, so that they might return to it (21:57-58) [c1].
- They asked who had done this to their gods, and said that he must be one of the wrongdoers (21:59) [c2].
- They said that they had heard someone mention them, and that he was called Ibrahim (21:60) [c3].
- They said to bring him before the people, so that they might bear witness, and asked whether he had done this to their gods (21:61-62) [c4].
- Ibrahim said that the largest of them had done it, and told them to ask the idols if they could speak (21:63) [c5].
- They turned to themselves and said that they were the wrongdoers, and then they turned back and said that he knew that the idols did not speak (21:64-65) [c6].
- Ibrahim asked whether they worshipped besides God what could neither help nor harm them, and said fie on them and on what they worshipped besides God (21:66-67) [c7].
- Another passage says that he looked at the stars and said that he was sick, and they turned away from him (37:88-90) [c8].
- He went to their gods and asked whether they would not eat, and why they did not speak, and struck them a blow (37:91-93) [c9].
- They came rushing to him, and he asked whether they worshipped what they carved, when God created them and what they made (37:94-96) [c10].
- They said to burn him and support their gods if they were going to act (21:68) [c11].
- Their answer was only to say to kill him or burn him, and God saved him from the fire (29:24) [c12].
- God said: O fire, be coolness and safety for Ibrahim (21:69) [c13].
- They wanted to plot against him, and God made them the greatest losers (21:70) [c14].
- Another passage says that they said to build a structure for him and throw him into the blazing fire, that they wanted to plot against him, and that God made them the lowest (37:97-98) [c15].
chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim broke the idols into pieces, except the biggest one [c1]. His people asked who had done it [c2]. They wanted to burn him, but God said to the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim [c11][c13].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The ayat show the idols unable to answer a question put to them [c5][c6]. One reading is that the passage then places God's word to the fire beside the threat of the people [c11][c13].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the fire was, how long it burned, or who lit it; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the speaker of the words about the plan against the idols in 21:57 is Ibrahim in the draft's reading; the ayah does not name him in that verse.
- Not established: Ibrahim's words I am sick in 37:89 are read in more than one way; the draft states them as the ayah gives them and adds no explanation.
- Not established: whether the largest idol was left so that they might return to it or to him is read in more than one way in 21:58.
- Not established: the wording of 37:93 (a blow with the right hand, or with strength) is read in more than one way; the draft says a blow.
- Not established: 21:60 calls him by a word that may refer to his age; the draft does not use it.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the ruler, the name of the city, and any detail of the fire; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim told them that they had taken idols besides God as a bond of affection among themselves in the life of this world.
On the Day of Resurrection they would deny one another and curse one another, and their home would be the fire, and they would have no helpers.
Lut believed him and said that he was emigrating to his Lord.
God granted him Ishaq and Yaqub, placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants, gave him his reward in this world, and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.

chapters.summary_md: Ibrahim told his people that their idols were only a bond among themselves in this life and that on the Day of Resurrection they would deny one another [c1][c2]. Lut believed him, and God granted him Ishaq and Yaqub [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: Ibrahim told them that they had taken idols besides God as a bond of affection among themselves in the life of this world [c1]. On the Day of Resurrection they would deny one another and curse one another, and their home would be the fire, and they would have no helpers [c2]. Lut believed him and said that he was emigrating to his Lord [c3]. God granted him Ishaq and Yaqub, placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants, gave him his reward in this world, and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- Ibrahim told them that they had taken idols besides God as a bond of affection among themselves in the life of this world (29:16, 29:25) [c1].
- On the Day of Resurrection they would deny one another and curse one another, and their home would be the fire, and they would have no helpers (29:25) [c2].
- Lut believed him and said that he was emigrating to his Lord (29:26) [c3].
- God granted him Ishaq and Yaqub, placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants, gave him his reward in this world, and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous (29:27) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: Lut believed Ibrahim [c3]. God granted Ibrahim Ishaq and Yaqub [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage sets a bond built on idols that will end on the Day of Resurrection beside the gifts given to Ibrahim [c1][c2][c4]. One reading is that Lut's emigration to his Lord is placed beside the end of that bond [c2][c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where Lut emigrated to, when, or how many others believed with him; the ayah gives only his words.
- Not established: the pronoun he in 29:26 (who said that he was emigrating) is read as Lut by most readers, but the ayah does not mark the speaker.
- Not established: 26:78-104 (Ibrahim's prayers and the scene of the day of judgement) is not drafted here; it belongs to the draft on Ibrahim and needs a scholar's wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Ibrahim and his people. None is used in this draft.
Inventory refs not drafted as chapters: 26:78-104 (prayers of Ibrahim and the scene of the day), 37:83-84; left to the draft on the prophet Ibrahim.

Wording a scholar should check first: 19:46 (a long time), 21:58 (the largest of them, and the pronoun), 37:89 (I am sick), 43:28 (the lasting word and its pronoun), 29:26 (the speaker), 21:63 (the largest did it).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of Ibrahim's father, of the king and of the city; none is used.

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that the Companions of the Ditch were slain, a wording that is also read as a curse on them.
The ayat speak of the fire full of fuel.
They were sitting by it.
They were witnesses to what they did to the believers.
They resented the believers only because they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy.
God is the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God is a witness over all things.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that the Companions of the Ditch were slain, and speaks of a fire full of fuel by which they sat [c1][c2][c3]. They resented the believers only because they believed in God, and God is a witness over all things [c5][c6].
chapters.body_md: The Quran says that the Companions of the Ditch were slain, a wording that is also read as a curse on them [c1]. The ayat speak of the fire full of fuel [c2]. They were sitting by it [c3]. They were witnesses to what they did to the believers [c4]. They resented the believers only because they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy [c5]. God is the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God is a witness over all things [c6].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran says that the Companions of the Ditch were slain, a wording that is also read as a curse on them (85:4) [c1].
- The ayat speak of the fire full of fuel (85:5) [c2].
- They were sitting by it (85:6) [c3].
- They were witnesses to what they did to the believers (85:7) [c4].
- They resented the believers only because they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy (85:8) [c5].
- God is the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God is a witness over all things (85:9) [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran tells of people who sat by a fire and watched what was done to the believers [c2][c3][c4]. They were angry with the believers only because the believers believed in God [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage names the believers' belief in God as the only thing the others resented, and ends by saying that God is a witness over all things [c5][c6]. One reading is that the ayat console those who are wronged for their belief [c5][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the Companions of the Ditch were, where or when they lived, who the believers were, or how many; the Quran does not say.
- Not established: the ayat do not state that the believers were thrown into the fire; they speak of the fire and of what the Companions did to the believers.
- Not established: whether the ditch of the title and the fire are one thing; the ayat name the ditch only in 85:4.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the king, the place and the persons of the accounts later tradition tells about the Companions of the Ditch; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the Companions of the Ditch. None is used in this draft; a reviewer should note that the usual account comes from later reports and commentary, not from the ayat.
Wording a scholar should check first: 85:4 (slain or cursed), 85:7 (witnesses over what they did, or witnesses to it), 85:5 (the fire, as a fire of fuel).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identity of the Companions of the Ditch and every detail of their story; none is used.

claims.statement_en: The Quran names 'Ad, Thamud and the Companions of al-Rass, and many generations between them.
For each of them God gave examples, and each He destroyed with total destruction.
Another passage says that before them the people of Nuh denied the messengers, and so did the Companions of al-Rass and Thamud.
The same passage names 'Ad, Fir'awn, the brothers of Lut, the Companions of the Thicket and the people of Tubba'.
The passage says that each of them denied the messengers, so that God's threat came due.

chapters.summary_md: The Companions of al-Rass are named in lists of peoples who denied the messengers [c1][c3]. The Quran says that God gave examples for each of them and that each was destroyed [c2][c5].
chapters.body_md: The Quran names 'Ad, Thamud and the Companions of al-Rass, and many generations between them [c1]. For each of them God gave examples, and each He destroyed with total destruction [c2]. Another passage says that before them the people of Nuh denied the messengers, and so did the Companions of al-Rass and Thamud [c3]. The same passage names 'Ad, Fir'awn, the brothers of Lut, the Companions of the Thicket and the people of Tubba' [c4]. The passage says that each of them denied the messengers, so that God's threat came due [c5].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran names 'Ad, Thamud and the Companions of al-Rass, and many generations between them (25:38) [c1].
- For each of them God gave examples, and each He destroyed with total destruction (25:39) [c2].
- Another passage says that before them the people of Nuh denied the messengers, and so did the Companions of al-Rass and Thamud (50:12) [c3].
- The same passage names 'Ad, Fir'awn, the brothers of Lut, the Companions of the Thicket and the people of Tubba' (50:13-14) [c4].
- The passage says that each of them denied the messengers, so that God's threat came due (50:14) [c5].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran names the Companions of al-Rass among peoples who did not believe the messengers [c3]. It says that God gave examples for each of them and that each was destroyed [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The lists place the Companions of al-Rass beside other peoples who denied the messengers [c3][c4][c5]. One reading is that the ayat ask the hearer to learn from the examples God gave for each [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the Companions of al-Rass were, where or when they lived, who their messenger was, or what they did; the Quran says none of this.
- Not established: what al-Rass means is read in more than one way; the ayat give only the word.
- Not established: the draft does not say that the Companions of al-Rass and any other people in the lists are the same.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of al-Rass with a well, a place or a people, and the names of their prophet; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the Companions of al-Rass. None is used in this draft.
Wording a scholar should check first: 25:38 (many generations between them), 50:13 (the brothers of Lut, rendered literally), 50:12-14 (the grammar of the list).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: every identification of al-Rass and its people; none is used.

claims.statement_en: The Quran asks whether those addressed are better than the people of Tubba' and those before them.
The ayah says that God destroyed them, because they were criminals.
Another passage names the people of Tubba' in a list of peoples who denied the messengers.
The passage says that each of them denied the messengers, so that God's threat came due.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran asks whether those addressed are better than the people of Tubba' and says that God destroyed them because they were criminals [c1][c2]. It also names them among peoples who denied the messengers [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: The Quran asks whether those addressed are better than the people of Tubba' and those before them [c1]. The ayah says that God destroyed them, because they were criminals [c2]. Another passage names the people of Tubba' in a list of peoples who denied the messengers [c3]. The passage says that each of them denied the messengers, so that God's threat came due [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran asks whether those addressed are better than the people of Tubba' and those before them (44:37) [c1].
- The ayah says that God destroyed them, because they were criminals (44:37) [c2].
- Another passage names the people of Tubba' in a list of peoples who denied the messengers (50:14) [c3].
- The passage says that each of them denied the messengers, so that God's threat came due (50:14) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran mentions the people of Tubba' and says that God destroyed them, because they were criminals [c1][c2]. It also names them with other peoples who did not believe the messengers [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The first ayah addresses its hearers with a comparison and a reminder of an earlier people [c1][c2]. One reading is that the ayat use the people of Tubba' as one example among others of the end of those who deny [c3][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who Tubba' was, whether the word is a name or a title, whether it names a king, where or when the people lived, or what they did; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the draft does not say who is addressed in 44:37 beyond the ayah's own words.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of Tubba' with a king or dynasty, a country or a date; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the people of Tubba'. None is used in this draft.
Wording a scholar should check first: 44:37 (those before them, and the addressees), 50:14 (the list).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of Tubba' with a particular king or dynasty of the south of Arabia; none is used.

claims.statement_en: The Quran asks why there was no town that believed so that its belief benefitted it, except the people of Yunus.
When they believed, God removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world.
God gave them enjoyment for a while.
Another passage says that God sent him to a hundred thousand or more.
The same passage says that they believed, so God gave them enjoyment for a while.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that, apart from the people of Yunus, no town believed so that its belief benefitted it [c1]. When they believed, God removed the punishment of disgrace from them and gave them enjoyment for a while [c2][c3].
chapters.body_md: The Quran asks why there was no town that believed so that its belief benefitted it, except the people of Yunus [c1]. When they believed, God removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world [c2]. God gave them enjoyment for a while [c3]. Another passage says that God sent him to a hundred thousand or more [c4]. The same passage says that they believed, so God gave them enjoyment for a while [c5].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran asks why there was no town that believed so that its belief benefitted it, except the people of Yunus (10:98) [c1].
- When they believed, God removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world (10:98) [c2].
- God gave them enjoyment for a while (10:98, 37:148) [c3].
- Another passage says that God sent him to a hundred thousand or more (37:147) [c4].
- The same passage says that they believed, so God gave them enjoyment for a while (37:148) [c5].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran says that the people of Yunus believed [c1][c5]. Because they believed, God took away their punishment and let them enjoy life for a while [c2][c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage treats belief that came while a warning was still near as something that benefitted the people of Yunus [c1][c2]. One reading is that the ayat hold up their belief as a case that could have been repeated by other towns [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the town was, when this happened, who the people of Yunus were, or how long the enjoyment lasted; the ayat say a while.
- Not established: the number in 37:147 is stated as a hundred thousand or more by the ayah; the ayah does not say how it was counted, and the draft adds nothing to it.
- Not established: the ayat do not say what led them to believe or what the punishment would have been; they say that it was removed.
- Not established: the pronoun of he in 37:147 is not named in that ayah; the draft reads it as Yunus because 10:98 names the people of Yunus.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the people of Yunus. None is used in this draft.
Wording a scholar should check first: 37:147 (a hundred thousand or more, and the pronoun), 10:98 (the exception).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the city and the region of the people of Yunus; none is used.

claims.statement_en: God raised the Tur above them for their covenant, told them to enter the gate prostrating, told them not to transgress in the Sabbath, and took from them a firm covenant.
The one addressed is told to ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath.
On the day of their Sabbath their fish came to them openly, and on the day when they did not keep the Sabbath the fish did not come.
The ayah says that in this way God tested them because of their disobedience.
The Quran says that the Sabbath was imposed only on those who differed about it, and that your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection about what they differed in.

chapters.summary_md: God told them not to transgress in the Sabbath [c1]. The fish came to them openly on the day of their Sabbath and did not come on other days, and the Quran says that God was testing them [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: God raised the Tur above them for their covenant, told them to enter the gate prostrating, told them not to transgress in the Sabbath, and took from them a firm covenant [c1]. The one addressed is told to ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath [c2]. On the day of their Sabbath their fish came to them openly, and on the day when they did not keep the Sabbath the fish did not come [c3]. The ayah says that in this way God tested them because of their disobedience [c4]. The Quran says that the Sabbath was imposed only on those who differed about it, and that your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection about what they differed in [c5].
chapters.deep_md:
- God raised the Tur above them for their covenant, told them to enter the gate prostrating, told them not to transgress in the Sabbath, and took from them a firm covenant (4:154) [c1].
- The one addressed is told to ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath (7:163) [c2].
- On the day of their Sabbath their fish came to them openly, and on the day when they did not keep the Sabbath the fish did not come (7:163) [c3].
- The ayah says that in this way God tested them because of their disobedience (7:163) [c4].
- The Quran says that the Sabbath was imposed only on those who differed about it, and that your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection about what they differed in (16:124) [c5].
chapters.kids_md: God told them not to break the Sabbath [c1]. The fish came to them only on the day of their Sabbath, as a test [c3][c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage sets a command beside a test that made keeping it hard [c1][c3][c4]. One reading is that the ayat treat the test as something that shows what people do [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the town by the sea was, when this happened, or how many lived in it; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the one addressed in 7:163 is not named in the ayah.
- Not established: what the differing about the Sabbath in 16:124 refers to is read in more than one way.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the town and the sea; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: A community among them asked others why they admonished a people whom God was going to destroy or punish severely.
The others answered that it was an excuse before their Lord, and that perhaps the people would fear God.
When the people forgot what they had been reminded of, God saved those who forbade evil.
God seized those who did wrong with a wretched punishment because of their disobedience.

chapters.summary_md: Within the town, a community asked why others admonished a people God would punish, and the others said that it was an excuse before their Lord [c1][c2]. God saved those who forbade evil and seized those who did wrong [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: A community among them asked others why they admonished a people whom God was going to destroy or punish severely [c1].
