The others answered that it was an excuse before their Lord, and that perhaps the people would fear God [c2]. When the people forgot what they had been reminded of, God saved those who forbade evil [c3]. God seized those who did wrong with a wretched punishment because of their disobedience [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- A community among them asked others why they admonished a people whom God was going to destroy or punish severely (7:164) [c1].
- The others answered that it was an excuse before their Lord, and that perhaps the people would fear God (7:164) [c2].
- When the people forgot what they had been reminded of, God saved those who forbade evil (7:165) [c3].
- God seized those who did wrong with a wretched punishment because of their disobedience (7:165) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: Some people in the town kept warning the others [c1][c2]. When the others forgot the warning, God saved those who had forbidden what was wrong [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage records people who kept warning, giving as their reason an excuse before their Lord and the hope that the others might fear God [c2]. One reading is that the ayat place the saving of the warners beside the seizing of those who did wrong [c3][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the ayat do not say how many were in each community, who they were, or how the saving happened.
- Not established: the ayat do not say whether the community that questioned the warners belonged to those who were saved or seized; the draft does not decide.
- Not established: the sense of the excuse before your Lord is read in more than one way.

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that they knew those among them who transgressed in the Sabbath, and that God said to them: be apes, despised.
Another ayah says that when they exceeded what they had been forbidden, God said to them: be apes, despised.
God made it a deterrent for those before it and those after it, and an admonition for those who fear Him.
The Quran mentions that God cursed the Companions of the Sabbath, in a warning to those who were given the Book.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that God said to those who transgressed in the Sabbath: be apes, despised, and made this a deterrent and an admonition for those who fear Him [c1][c3]. It also mentions that God cursed the Companions of the Sabbath [c4].
chapters.body_md: The Quran says that they knew those among them who transgressed in the Sabbath, and that God said to them: be apes, despised [c1]. Another ayah says that when they exceeded what they had been forbidden, God said to them: be apes, despised [c2]. God made it a deterrent for those before it and those after it, and an admonition for those who fear Him [c3]. The Quran mentions that God cursed the Companions of the Sabbath, in a warning to those who were given the Book [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran says that they knew those among them who transgressed in the Sabbath, and that God said to them: be apes, despised (2:65) [c1].
- Another ayah says that when they exceeded what they had been forbidden, God said to them: be apes, despised (7:166) [c2].
- God made it a deterrent for those before it and those after it, and an admonition for those who fear Him (2:66) [c3].
- The Quran mentions that God cursed the Companions of the Sabbath, in a warning to those who were given the Book (4:47) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: Those who went beyond what they were told, in the Sabbath, were punished [c1][c2]. God made this a lesson for people who fear Him [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The ayat present the outcome as a deterrent and an admonition for those who fear God [c3]. One reading is that the repeated reference to the Sabbath keeps the focus on exceeding what was forbidden [c1][c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: whether the words be apes, despised describe a change of form or a figure is read in more than one way; the draft states the ayat as worded and does not choose.
- Not established: the ayat do not say how many were affected, what happened to them afterwards, or whether the Companions of the Sabbath of 4:47 are the same group as those of 2:65 and 7:166; the draft does not say so.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the town, the number of the transgressors and the length of time they survived; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about those who broke the Sabbath. None is used in this draft.
Wording a scholar should check first: 2:65 and 7:166 (be apes, despised), 4:47 (the curse of the Companions of the Sabbath and its addressees), 16:124, 7:164 (who speaks to whom).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Ayla, Eilat and other names given to the town of 7:163; none is used.

chapters.title_en: The barrier against Ya'juj and Ma'juj

claims.statement_en: They told Dhul-Qarnayn that Ya'juj and Ma'juj were causing corruption in the land.
They asked whether they might pay him a charge on condition that he set a barrier between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj.
Dhul-Qarnayn said that what his Lord had established him in was better, and told them to help him with strength so that he might make a rampart between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj.
He told them to bring him sheets of iron, and when he had made it level between the cliffs he told them to blow, and when he had made it fire he told them to bring him molten copper to pour over it.
Ya'juj and Ma'juj could not climb over it, and could not pierce it.
Dhul-Qarnayn said that this was a mercy from his Lord, that when the promise of his Lord came He would make it level, and that the promise of his Lord is true.

chapters.summary_md: The people told Dhul-Qarnayn that Ya'juj and Ma'juj caused corruption in the land and asked for a barrier [c1][c2]. He built a rampart of iron and copper, and Ya'juj and Ma'juj could not climb it or pierce it [c4][c5].
chapters.body_md: They told Dhul-Qarnayn that Ya'juj and Ma'juj were causing corruption in the land [c1]. They asked whether they might pay him a charge on condition that he set a barrier between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj [c2]. Dhul-Qarnayn said that what his Lord had established him in was better, and told them to help him with strength so that he might make a rampart between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj [c3]. He told them to bring him sheets of iron, and when he had made it level between the cliffs he told them to blow, and when he had made it fire he told them to bring him molten copper to pour over it [c4]. Ya'juj and Ma'juj could not climb over it, and could not pierce it [c5]. Dhul-Qarnayn said that this was a mercy from his Lord, that when the promise of his Lord came He would make it level, and that the promise of his Lord is true [c6].
chapters.deep_md:
- They told Dhul-Qarnayn that Ya'juj and Ma'juj were causing corruption in the land (18:94) [c1].
- They asked whether they might pay him a charge on condition that he set a barrier between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj (18:94) [c2].
- Dhul-Qarnayn said that what his Lord had established him in was better, and told them to help him with strength so that he might make a rampart between them and Ya'juj and Ma'juj (18:95) [c3].
- He told them to bring him sheets of iron, and when he had made it level between the cliffs he told them to blow, and when he had made it fire he told them to bring him molten copper to pour over it (18:96) [c4].
- Ya'juj and Ma'juj could not climb over it, and could not pierce it (18:97) [c5].
- Dhul-Qarnayn said that this was a mercy from his Lord, that when the promise of his Lord came He would make it level, and that the promise of his Lord is true (18:98) [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The people asked Dhul-Qarnayn to build a barrier against Ya'juj and Ma'juj [c2]. He used iron and copper [c4]. Ya'juj and Ma'juj could not climb it or pierce it [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Dhul-Qarnayn answers the offer of payment by saying that what his Lord has established him in is better, and asks only for help [c3]. One reading is that he describes the finished barrier as a mercy from his Lord and refers its end to his Lord's promise [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who Ya'juj and Ma'juj are, where they live or where the barrier stands; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: who the people who spoke to Dhul-Qarnayn were; the ayah does not name them.
- Not established: the Arabic of 18:96 speaks of the cliffs in a dual form; the draft renders it as the cliffs.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of Ya'juj and Ma'juj with Gog and Magog or with a particular people, and any place for the barrier; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that on that day God will leave some of them surging over others, and that the horn will be blown and God will gather them all together.
It says that Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be let loose and will descend from every high place.
It says that the true promise will draw near and the gaze of those who disbelieved will be fixed.
They will say that they had been heedless of this, and that they were wrongdoers.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran says that Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be let loose and descend from every high place [c2]. It says that the true promise will draw near and that those who disbelieved will say they had been heedless [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: The Quran says that on that day God will leave some of them surging over others, and that the horn will be blown and God will gather them all together [c1]. It says that Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be let loose and will descend from every high place [c2]. It says that the true promise will draw near and the gaze of those who disbelieved will be fixed [c3]. They will say that they had been heedless of this, and that they were wrongdoers [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran says that on that day God will leave some of them surging over others, and that the horn will be blown and God will gather them all together (18:99) [c1].
- It says that Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be let loose and will descend from every high place (21:96) [c2].
- It says that the true promise will draw near and the gaze of those who disbelieved will be fixed (21:97) [c3].
- They will say that they had been heedless of this, and that they were wrongdoers (21:97) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran says that one day Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be let loose [c2]. Those who did not believe will say that they had not paid attention [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage joins the release of Ya'juj and Ma'juj with the nearing of the true promise [c2][c3]. One reading is that the words of those who disbelieved ask the hearer not to be heedless [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who is meant by some of them in 18:99 (Ya'juj and Ma'juj, or the people gathered on that day); the ayah does not say.
- Not established: when the release will happen or how it relates to the barrier of 18:98; the ayat do not say.
- Not established: the ayat of 21:96 do not name the place from which they descend.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: reports about the signs of the Hour that name Ya'juj and Ma'juj; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Ya'juj and Ma'juj and the barrier. None is used in this draft; a reviewer should be aware that most of what is popularly said about them comes from later sources.
Wording a scholar should check first: 18:94 (who speaks), 18:95-96 (the rampart and the dual cliffs), 18:98 (the promise of my Lord), 18:99 (some of them), 21:96 (every high place).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Gog and Magog, and every identification with a nation, a mountain or a date; none is used.

claims.statement_en: The Quran speaks of the accustoming of Quraysh.
It speaks of their accustomed journey of winter and summer.
It tells them to worship the Lord of this House.
It says that He is the One who fed them against hunger and made them secure from fear.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran speaks of the accustoming of Quraysh and of their journey of winter and summer [c1][c2]. It tells them to worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them secure from fear [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md: The Quran speaks of the accustoming of Quraysh [c1]. It speaks of their accustomed journey of winter and summer [c2]. It tells them to worship the Lord of this House [c3]. It says that He is the One who fed them against hunger and made them secure from fear [c4].
chapters.deep_md:
- The Quran speaks of the accustoming of Quraysh (106:1) [c1].
- It speaks of their accustomed journey of winter and summer (106:2) [c2].
- It tells them to worship the Lord of this House (106:3) [c3].
- It says that He is the One who fed them against hunger and made them secure from fear (106:4) [c4].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran reminds Quraysh of their journeys in winter and in summer [c2]. It tells them to worship the Lord of this House [c3]. He is the One who fed them and kept them safe from fear [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage ties the food and safety Quraysh enjoyed to a call to worship their Lord [c3][c4]. One reading is that the ayat ask the hearers to answer gifts with worship [c3][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the ayat do not say where Quraysh lived, who they were or how many; the draft names no place.
- Not established: which House is meant by this House, and which journeys are meant, are not stated beyond the words of the ayat.
- Not established: how the first ayah is joined to the rest (the grammar of the opening letter) is read in more than one way; the draft states the ayat in order.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the cities, the trade routes and the House that later accounts connect with the passage; none is used here.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Quraysh and this passage. None is used in this draft.
Wording a scholar should check first: 106:1 (the accustoming, and its grammatical link to the preceding passage as some read it), 106:2 (the journey of winter and summer), 106:3 (this House).
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Makkah, the Kaaba, the routes to the south and to the north, and the tribe's history; none is used.

stories.title_en: The prostration to Adam and Iblis's refusal

claims.statement_en: God told the angels that He was going to create a human being from clay.
God said that when He had fashioned the human being and breathed into him of His spirit, the angels were to fall down before him in prostration.
God told the angels to prostrate to Adam, and they prostrated, every one of them together.
Iblis did not prostrate: he refused, and was not among those who prostrated.
The Quran says that Iblis was arrogant and was among the disbelievers.
Another passage says that Iblis was one of the jinn and that he departed from his Lord's command.
God asked Iblis what prevented him from prostrating when He commanded him, or what was the matter that he was not with those who prostrated.
Iblis answered that he was better than the one he was told to prostrate to, because God had created him from fire and that one from clay.
In another passage Iblis said that he would not prostrate to a human being whom God had created from dry clay, from moulded mud.

chapters.summary_md: God told the angels to prostrate to Adam once He had fashioned a human being from clay and breathed into him of His spirit, and every one of them did [c1][c2][c3]. Iblis refused, saying that he was better because he was made of fire and the other of clay [c4][c8].
chapters.body_md:
God told the angels that He was going to create a human being from clay [c1]. When He had fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to fall down before him in prostration [c2]. The angels prostrated to Adam, every one of them together [c3].

Iblis did not prostrate; he refused and was not among those who prostrated [c4]. The Quran says he was arrogant and among the disbelievers [c5], and another passage says he was one of the jinn and departed from his Lord's command [c6].

God asked him what prevented him from prostrating when he was commanded [c7]. Iblis answered that he was better, since God had created him from fire and the other from clay [c8]. In another passage he says he would not prostrate to a human being whom God had created from dry clay, from moulded mud [c9].
chapters.deep_md: The scene is told in more than one passage with different emphasis [c3]. One gives the creation and the breathing of the spirit [c1][c2], some give the prostration of all the angels together [c3], and each gives the refusal [c4]. The question put to Iblis is worded differently from passage to passage [c7]. His answer rests on a comparison of what he and the other were made of [c8][c9].
chapters.kids_md: God told the angels that He would make a human being from clay [c1]. They were to bow down to him, and they all did [c3]. Iblis refused, because he said he was better, made of fire while the other was made of clay [c4][c8].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The refusal rests on a comparison of what he and the other were made of [c8]. One reading is a caution against judging worth by origin or material [c8]. Another is that the angels acted on the command as it was given [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say where or when this scene took place, or what Iblis was told to go out from.
- It does not describe how the angels prostrated or what kind of prostration it was.
- How the statement that Iblis was one of the jinn (18:50) sits with the fact that he was among those addressed with the angels is not explained in these verses; a scholar should decide how the page words it.
- The passages at 15:28-33 and 38:71-76 speak of a human being and do not name Adam; to read them as the same scene as the prostration to Adam is an inference from matching wording.
- The verses do not explain what 'His spirit' is or how the breathing happened.

chapters.title_en: The sentence, the respite and the vow

claims.statement_en: God told Iblis to go down from it and to go out, saying that he had no right to be arrogant there and that he was among the humiliated.
God said that Iblis was driven away and that His curse would be on him until the Day of Judgement.
Iblis asked God to give him respite until the day when people are raised.
God said that Iblis was among those given respite, until the day of the known time.

Iblis said that, because God had led him astray, he would lie in wait for people on God's straight path and then come at them from in front, from behind, from their right and from their left, and that God would not find most of them thankful.
In parallel passages Iblis vowed to make wrongdoing look fair to people on the earth and to lead them all astray, except God's sincere servants.

In another passage Iblis asked whether he should prostrate to one whom God had created from clay, and said that if God let him wait until the Day of Resurrection he would take hold of that one's descendants, except a few.
God told Iblis to go, and said that Hell would be the recompense, in full, of him and of those among people who follow him.
God said that Iblis has no authority over His servants, except over those of the misled who follow him.
God said that Hell is the promised place of all of them, and has seven gates, each with a portion of them assigned to it.
God said that He would fill Hell with Iblis and with those among people who follow him, all together, and that He says only the truth.

chapters.summary_md: God told Iblis to go out and said the curse would be on him until the Day of Judgement [c1][c2]. Iblis asked for respite until the day people are raised and God granted it, and Iblis vowed to lead people astray except God's sincere servants [c3][c4][c6].
chapters.body_md:
God told Iblis to go down from it and to go out, saying that he had no right to be arrogant there and that he was among the humiliated [c1]. God said he was driven away and that His curse would be on him until the Day of Judgement [c2].

Iblis asked God to give him respite until the day when people are raised [c3], and God said he was among those given respite, until the day of the known time [c4]. Iblis then said that, because God had led him astray, he would lie in wait for people on God's straight path and come at them from in front, from behind, from their right and from their left [c5]. In the parallel passages he vows to make wrongdoing look fair on the earth and to lead them all astray, except God's sincere servants [c6]. In another passage he says that if God lets him wait until the Day of Resurrection he will take hold of the descendants of the one he refused to prostrate to, except a few [c7].

God answered that Iblis has no authority over His servants, except over the misled who follow him [c9]. Hell, which has seven gates, is the promised place of all of them [c10], and God said He would fill it with Iblis and with those who follow him, all together [c8][c11].
chapters.deep_md: The request for respite, its grant and the vow are told in more than one passage with small differences [c3][c4][c6]. In one he speaks of lying in wait on the straight path [c5]; in others of making wrongdoing look fair on the earth [c6] and of taking hold of descendants [c7]. The limit placed on him is the same wherever it is stated: no authority over God's servants, except over those of the misled who follow him [c9].
chapters.kids_md: God told Iblis to go [c1]. Iblis asked God to let him wait until the day people are raised, and God allowed it [c3][c4]. Iblis said he would try to lead people astray [c6]. God said he has no power over God's servants, except those who follow him [c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The passage records Iblis's own announcement that he will try to mislead people [c5][c6], and records a limit on him [c9]. One reading is a reminder to be on guard [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say when the day of the known time is.
- It does not describe how Iblis lies in wait or comes from the directions he names; the verses give his words only.
- What Iblis means by saying that God led him astray is not explained in these verses.
- Hell is described here only by its seven gates and their portions; the verses give no further description of it.
- The verse 15:41 (a statement by God about a straight path) and 17:64 (what Iblis is told he may do) lie inside the inventory range but are not used; their wording is disputed or needs more space, and a reviewer should decide whether to add them.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the creation of Adam, the prostration and the respite given to Iblis. None is used in this draft.
The same scene is also told inside the longer story of Adam (content/stories/adam.draft.json); this record is a shorter, event-focused account that refers to it only in general words.
Whether Iblis was an angel or one of the jinn is not settled in the verses beyond 18:50, which calls him one of the jinn; how this is worded is for a scholar.
The passages at 15:28-33 and 38:71-76 speak of a human being without the name; they are read here as the same scene as the prostration to Adam (an inference, as in the event inventory).
The inventory also lists 20:116, which repeats the command and the refusal; it is not cited separately because 2:34 and 7:11 say the same.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The covenant taken from the descendants of Adam

claims.statement_en: God took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants.
He made them bear witness over themselves, asking whether He was not their Lord, and they said yes, they bore witness.
This was so that they would not say on the Day of Resurrection that they had been unaware of this.

It was also so that they would not say that only their forefathers had associated others with God before, and that they themselves were descendants after them, asking whether He would destroy them for what the falsifiers had done.
God says that in this way He makes the signs clear in detail, so that perhaps they will return.

chapters.summary_md: God took from the children of Adam their descendants and made them bear witness over themselves, asking whether He was not their Lord, and they said yes [c1][c2]. The Quran gives the purpose: that they could not say on the Day of Resurrection that they had been unaware [c3].
chapters.body_md:
God took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants [c1]. He made them bear witness over themselves, asking whether He was not their Lord, and they said yes, they bore witness [c2].

The Quran gives the purpose [c3]. It was so that they would not say on the Day of Resurrection that they had been unaware of this [c3]. It was also so that they would not say that only their forefathers had associated others with God, and that they were descendants after them, and ask whether God would destroy them for what the falsifiers had done [c4]. God says that in this way He makes the signs clear in detail, so that perhaps they will return [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passage moves from the taking and the witnessing [c1][c2] to the excuses it closes off [c3][c4] and ends with a closing remark on the explaining of the signs [c5]. The verses speak of descendants taken from the loins of the children of Adam [c1]; they do not say how this relates to a person's later birth.
chapters.kids_md: God asked the children of Adam whether He was not their Lord, and they said yes [c1][c2]. This was so that nobody could say on the Day of Resurrection that they had not known [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage presents knowing God as a witness every person carries, so that ignorance is not a final excuse [c3]. Another is that blaming one's forefathers is closed off as a plea [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: when, where or how the taking and the witnessing happened; the verses give no time, place or manner.
- Not established: how the taking of descendants from loins relates to a person's later birth or life; interpreters understand the passage in more than one way, and a scholar should decide how the page words it.
- Not established: who is meant by the falsifiers in the last excuse beyond the word itself.
- The verses do not use the word covenant; the inventory title reflects the usual name of the passage, which a reviewer may wish to word with care.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the taking of the descendants. None is used in this draft.

How this passage is understood (as a real event before birth, or as a way of describing the nature given to people) is disputed among interpreters; the draft states only what the verses say and gives no reading.
The usual title of the passage comes from its own question to the descendants; a scholar should decide whether the page uses that title or only a description.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: God revealed to Nuh that none of his people would believe except those who already had, and told him not to be distressed by what they were doing.
God told Nuh to make the ship under His watch and by His revelation, and not to address Him about those who had done wrong, for they were to be drowned.
While Nuh made the ship, whenever a group of the leaders of his people passed him they mocked him.
Nuh said that if they mocked him, he would in the same way mock them, and that they would know on whom a punishment would come to disgrace him and on whom a lasting punishment would fall.
The people of Nuh denied God's servant, said that he was a madman, and he was rebuffed.
Nuh called on his Lord, saying that he was overcome, and asked for help.
Nuh also prayed to his Lord to help him because they had denied him, and God revealed to him to make the ship.

chapters.summary_md: God told Nuh to make the ship under His watch and by His revelation [c2]. His people mocked him as he worked, and he asked his Lord for help [c3][c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
God revealed to Nuh that none of his people would believe except those who already had, and told him not to be distressed by what they were doing [c1]. He told Nuh to make the ship under His watch and by His revelation, and not to address Him about those who had done wrong, for they were to be drowned [c2].

While Nuh made the ship, whenever a group of the leaders of his people passed him they mocked him [c3]. He said that if they mocked him, he would in the same way mock them, and that they would know on whom a punishment would come [c4]. In another passage the Quran says his people denied God's servant and called him a madman [c5]. Nuh called on his Lord, saying he was overcome, and asked for help [c6][c7].
chapters.deep_md: The building of the ship is told together with the denial that surrounded it [c3][c5]. Nuh's call for help is recorded in different words in different passages [c6][c7]. The command to build is given in two passages, with the same phrase about God's watch and revelation [c2][c7].
chapters.kids_md: God told Nuh to build a ship [c2]. The leaders of his people laughed at him whenever they passed [c3]. Nuh asked his Lord for help [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Nuh keeps to the work he was given while he is mocked [c2][c3]. Another is that he turns to his Lord with his need [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the ship was built, how long it took, its size or its materials beyond what 54:13 says in the next chapter.
- Not established: who the leaders were, or how many passed him.
- The Arabic word rendered 'rebuffed' (54:9) is understood in more than one way; a scholar should decide the rendering.
- The verse 11:35 is an aside addressed to the one receiving the revelation and is not used.

claims.statement_en: When God's command came and the tannur boiled over, God told Nuh to carry on the ship a pair of every kind, and his family, except those against whom the word had already gone out, and those who believed; few had believed with him.
God opened the gates of the sky with pouring water and made the earth burst with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed.
God carried Nuh on a vessel of planks and dusur, a word often rendered nails or fibres, which sailed under His watch.
Nuh told those with him to embark, saying that in God's name was its sailing and its anchoring, for his Lord is forgiving and merciful.
The ship sailed with them through waves like mountains.
God told Nuh to say, once he and those with him were settled on the ship, that praise belongs to God who saved them from the wrongdoing people, and to ask to be landed at a blessed landing place.
God saved Nuh and those with him in the laden ship, and afterwards drowned the rest, who had denied His signs.
In another passage God says that He answered Nuh's earlier call and saved him and his family from the great distress, and helped him against the people who denied His signs, drowning them all.
God says that the flood took the people of Nuh while they were wrongdoers, and that He saved him and the companions of the ship and made it a sign for the worlds.
God says that when the water overflowed He carried those addressed in the running ship, to make it a reminder that a retaining ear would retain.

chapters.summary_md: When God's command came, Nuh carried on the ship a pair of every kind, his family except those against whom the word had gone out, and those who believed [c1]. The waters poured and burst out, the ship sailed, and God saved Nuh and those with him and drowned the rest [c2][c5][c7].
chapters.body_md:
When God's command came and the tannur boiled over, God told Nuh to carry on the ship a pair of every kind, and his family, except those against whom the word had already gone out, and those who believed; few had believed with him [c1]. Nuh told them to embark, saying that in God's name was its sailing and its anchoring [c4].

God opened the gates of the sky with pouring water and made the earth burst with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed [c2]. He carried Nuh on a vessel of planks and dusur which sailed under His watch [c3], and it sailed with them through waves like mountains [c5]. Nuh was told to say, once he and those with him were settled, that praise belongs to God who saved them from the wrongdoing people, and to ask to be landed at a blessed landing place [c6].

God saved Nuh and those with him in the laden ship, and afterwards drowned the rest, who had denied His signs [c7][c8]. He made the ship a sign for the worlds [c9] and a reminder [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The flood is told from different sides: the sign and the command to embark [c1], the boarding words [c4][c6], the description of the water [c2], the vessel [c3] and the waves [c5]. The outcome is the same in every passage that tells it: Nuh and those with him are saved and the rest are drowned [c7][c8][c9]. Two passages stress the ship as a sign and a reminder [c9][c10].
chapters.kids_md: God told Nuh to take on the ship a pair of every kind, his family and those who believed [c1]. The water poured from the sky and burst from the earth [c2]. The ship sailed on waves like mountains, and God saved Nuh and those with him [c5][c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Nuh and the others were told to begin their voyage in God's name and to praise Him for their rescue [c4][c6]. Another is that the ship is offered as a reminder to those who listen [c10].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say what the tannur was or where it was; oven is a common rendering and its sense is discussed.
- It does not say how many people were on the ship, which animals were carried or how many kinds, or how they were gathered.
- It does not say how long the flood lasted, how deep the water rose, or whether it covered the whole earth or only the region of Nuh's people. A scholar should decide how to word the extent.
- The Arabic word dusur is explained as nails and as fibres; this draft does not decide.
- 29:14 also gives a span for Nuh's stay among his people before the flood; the verse does not say whether it is his life or his time of calling, and it is left to the prophet story.
- In 69:11-12 those addressed are carried in the running ship; the verses do not say who is meant beyond the people addressed.

chapters.title_en: The son and the end of the flood

claims.statement_en: Nuh called to his son, who was standing apart, to embark with them and not to be with the disbelievers.

The son said that he would take refuge on a mountain that would protect him from the water; Nuh said there was no protector that day from God's command, except the one on whom He had mercy; then the wave came between them and the son was among the drowned.
The earth was told to swallow its water and the sky to stop; the water subsided, the matter was decided, the ship settled on al-Judi, and a call went out: away with the wrongdoing people.
Nuh called to his Lord, saying that his son was of his family, that God's promise is true, and that He is the most just of judges.
God said that the son was not of Nuh's family, for he was a deed not righteous, told him not to ask what he had no knowledge of, and warned him against being among the ignorant.
Nuh said that he sought refuge in God from asking what he had no knowledge of, and that unless God forgave him and had mercy on him he would be among the losers.

A word came to Nuh: come down in peace from Him, with blessings on you and on nations from those with you, and there will be nations to whom God will give enjoyment, then a painful punishment will touch them from Him.

chapters.summary_md: Nuh called to his son to embark, but the son said he would take refuge on a mountain, and the wave came between them [c1][c2]. The water subsided and the ship settled on al-Judi, and Nuh was told to come down in peace [c3][c7].
chapters.body_md:
Nuh called to his son, who was standing apart, to embark with them and not to be with the disbelievers [c1]. The son said he would take refuge on a mountain that would protect him from the water; Nuh answered that there was no protector that day from God's command, except the one on whom He had mercy [c2]. Then the wave came between them and the son was among the drowned [c2].

The earth was told to swallow its water and the sky to stop; the water subsided, the matter was decided, and the ship settled on al-Judi [c3]. Nuh called to his Lord that his son was of his family, that God's promise is true and that He is the most just of judges [c4]. God said that the son was not of his family, told him not to ask what he had no knowledge of and warned him against being among the ignorant [c5]. Nuh sought refuge in God from asking what he had no knowledge of and asked for forgiveness and mercy [c6].

Nuh was told to come down in peace from God, with blessings on him and on nations from those with him [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passage places Nuh's call to his son [c1][c2] beside Nuh's call to his Lord about him [c4], and the answer [c5] and the prayer for forgiveness [c6] follow. The ending is the settling of the ship [c3] and the word of peace and blessing [c7]. The words 'a deed not righteous' in 11:46 can be rendered in more than one way, and the draft keeps the wording close to the Arabic [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Nuh called his son to come on the ship, but the son would not [c1][c2]. Then the water went down and the ship settled on al-Judi [c3]. Nuh was told to come down in peace [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Nuh, told not to ask what he does not know, turns at once to ask forgiveness [c5][c6]. Another is that the passage shows closeness of family alone does not decide a person's place [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name the son, and does not say what became of him after the wave beyond that he was among the drowned.
- It does not say where al-Judi is.
- The phrase rendered 'for he was a deed not righteous' (11:46) is read in more than one way, for example as a statement about the son's deed or about the matter Nuh asked; a scholar should decide.
- Not established: who calls out the words 'away with the wrongdoing people' (11:44); the verse gives no speaker.
- Not established: how long after the flood began the water subsided.
- The verse 11:49 is an aside addressed to the one receiving the revelation and is not used.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Nuh, the flood and the ship. None is used in this draft.
The flood is also told inside the longer story of Nuh (content/stories/nuh.draft.json); this record is a shorter account of the event and refers to it only in general words.
The extent of the flood (the whole earth or the region of Nuh's people) is not stated in the verses; the draft says so and does not choose.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: names for Nuh's wife, sons and the mountain, and the ship's dimensions. None is used in the story texts.
The sense of tannur (11:40) and of dusur (54:13) is left open in the texts.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: His people said: burn him, and help your gods, if you are going to act.
In another passage the only answer of his people was to say: kill him, or burn him.
In another passage they said: build a structure for him, and throw him into the blaze.
God told the fire to be coolness and safety for Ibrahim.
They wanted to plot against him, and God made them the greatest losers.
In another passage God made them the lowest.
God saved him from the fire, and in that, God says, are signs for people who believe.

chapters.summary_md: His people said to burn Ibrahim [c1][c2], but God told the fire to be coolness and safety for him [c4]. They wanted to plot against him, and God made them the losers [c5][c7].
chapters.body_md:
His people said: burn him, and help your gods, if you are going to act [c1]. In another passage their only answer was to say: kill him, or burn him [c2], and in another they said: build a structure for him, and throw him into the blaze [c3].

God told the fire to be coolness and safety for Ibrahim [c4]. They wanted to plot against him, and God made them the greatest losers [c5]; in another passage He made them the lowest [c6]. God saved him from the fire, and in that, He says, are signs for people who believe [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passages report the people's decision in slightly different words: burn him [c1], kill him or burn him [c2], build a structure and throw him into the blaze [c3]. The words said to the fire come in one passage only [c4], and the outcome is told in different words, greatest losers and lowest [c5][c6]. The rescue is stated in one passage, with a remark that it contains signs [c7].
chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim's people said to burn him [c1]. God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim [c4]. God saved him from the fire [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage presents the fire as acting only at God's word [c4]. Another is that the plot of Ibrahim's people ends in their own loss [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where this took place, how long the fire burned, or who built the structure.
- The verses state the command to the fire and the rescue; they do not describe Ibrahim in the fire or how he came out of it.
- Not established: whether the passages (21:68-70, 29:24, 37:97-98) describe one decision or more than one; this draft reads them together as the same event.
- Not established: how the structure and the blaze of 37:97 relate to the fire of the other passages.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on Ibrahim and the fire. None is used in this draft.
The event is also told inside the longer story of Ibrahim (content/stories/ibrahim.draft.json); this record is a shorter account that refers to it only in general words.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the ruler, the place and the size of the fire. None is used in the story texts.
The passages are read as one event on matching wording (an inference).
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: Ibrahim's guests and the glad tidings

chapters.title_en: The guests and the glad tidings

claims.statement_en: One passage tells the one addressed to inform people about the guests of Ibrahim, and another asks whether the account of Ibrahim's honoured guests has reached the listener.
Messengers came to Ibrahim with glad tidings; they said peace, and he answered peace.
He soon brought a roasted calf, which another passage calls a fat calf; he turned quietly to his family for it, and set it near them, asking whether they would not eat.
When he saw that their hands did not reach it, he found them strange and felt fear of them.
In another passage he told them that he was afraid of them.
They told him not to fear: they had been sent to the people of Lut, and they gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy.
His wife was standing there; she laughed, and they gave her glad tidings of Ishaq and, after Ishaq, of Yaqub.
She said: woe to me, shall I give birth when I am an old woman and this husband of mine is old? This is a strange thing.
In another passage she came forward with a cry, struck her face and said that she was an old woman, barren.
They said: do you wonder at God's command? God's mercy and blessings are upon you, people of the house; He is praiseworthy and glorious.
In another passage they said that it was so because her Lord had said so, and that He is the wise, the knowing.
Ibrahim asked whether they had given him glad tidings although old age had touched him, and on what basis they gave glad tidings.
They said that they had given him glad tidings in truth and that he should not be among the despairing; he said that only those who are astray despair of the mercy of their Lord.

chapters.summary_md: Messengers came to Ibrahim with glad tidings, and he served them a calf [c2][c3]. They told him not to fear and gave glad tidings of a boy to him and to his wife, of Ishaq and then of Yaqub [c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
Messengers came to Ibrahim with glad tidings; they said peace, and he answered peace [c2]. He soon brought a roasted calf, and set it near them [c3]. When he saw that their hands did not reach it, he found them strange and felt fear of them [c4], and he told them that he was afraid [c5].

They told him not to fear: they had been sent to the people of Lut, and they gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy [c6]. His wife was standing there; she laughed, and they gave her glad tidings of Ishaq and, after Ishaq, of Yaqub [c7]. She said she was an old woman and her husband old, and called it a strange thing [c8]; in another passage she came forward with a cry, struck her face and said she was barren [c9].

The messengers asked whether she wondered at God's command, and wished mercy and blessings on the people of the house [c10]. Ibrahim asked whether they had given him glad tidings although old age had touched him [c12]. They said they had given them in truth and that he should not despair [c13], and he answered that only the astray despair of the mercy of their Lord [c13].
chapters.deep_md: The visit is told in more than one passage, each with its own details: the roasted calf and the peace greeting [c2][c3], the fear and the words that answered it [c4][c5][c6], the glad tidings to the wife and to Ibrahim [c7][c12]. Her reaction is given in different forms [c8][c9], and so is the answer of the guests [c10][c11]. The passages also open with a call to attention [c1].
chapters.kids_md: Messengers came to Ibrahim with good news [c2]. He brought them a calf, but they did not eat it, and he felt afraid [c3][c4]. They told him not to be afraid and gave him good news of a boy [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage joins hospitality with a surprise: the guest's food is set out before the news is given [c3][c6]. Another is that Ibrahim answers the news by saying that only the astray despair of their Lord's mercy [c13].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the messengers were, how many they were, or what form they had; the verses call them messengers and guests only.
- Not established: where Ibrahim lived at the time, or the age of Ibrahim and his wife; the verses speak of old age but give no numbers.
- The Arabic word for her laughing (11:71) is understood in more than one way; a scholar should decide the rendering.
- The identity of the knowing boy of 15:53 and 51:28, and its relation to the glad tidings of Ishaq in 11:71, is read in more than one way; this draft does not decide.
- The wife is not named in these verses.
- The passages 11:69-73, 15:51-56 and 51:24-30 are read as one visit on matching wording (an inference).

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim asked the messengers what their business was.
They said that they had been sent to a people of criminals, to send down on them stones of clay marked with their Lord for those who exceed all bounds.
The family of Lut would be saved, all of them, except his wife, whom God had decreed to be among those who stay behind.
When the fear had left Ibrahim and the glad tidings had come to him, he began to plead with God about the people of Lut.
God describes Ibrahim as forbearing, awwah and turning back to Him, awwah being a word understood in more than one way.
Ibrahim was told to turn away from this, for the command of his Lord had come and a punishment that could not be turned back was coming to them.
God says that He brought out the believers who were in it, and found in it only one house of those who submitted.
God says that He left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.

chapters.summary_md: Ibrahim asked the messengers what their business was, and they said they were sent to a people of criminals, but the family of Lut would be saved [c1][c2][c3]. Ibrahim pleaded with God about the people of Lut and was told to turn away from this [c4][c6].
chapters.body_md:
Ibrahim asked the messengers what their business was [c1]. They said that they had been sent to a people of criminals, to send down on them stones of clay marked with their Lord [c2]. The family of Lut would be saved, all of them, except his wife, whom God had decreed to be among those who stay behind [c3].

When the fear had left Ibrahim and the glad tidings had come to him, he began to plead with God about the people of Lut [c4]. God describes Ibrahim as forbearing, awwah and turning back to Him [c5]. He was told to turn away from this, for the command of his Lord had come and a punishment that could not be turned back was coming to them [c6].

God says He brought out the believers who were in it and found only one house of those who submitted [c7], and that He left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The later part of the visit turns from the glad tidings to the sending [c1][c2]. The exception for the family of Lut and the one who stays behind [c3] is told in one passage, Ibrahim's pleading in another [c4][c5][c6], and the outcome in yet another [c7][c8]. The passages differ in what they include, and the pleading is told only in 11:74-76 [c4].
chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim asked the messengers why they had come [c1]. They said they were sent to a people who did wrong, but that the family of Lut would be saved [c2][c3]. Ibrahim pleaded for them, and was told to turn away from this [c4][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that God's description of Ibrahim as forbearing and turning back to Him sits beside his pleading [c4][c5]. Another is that the passage records a limit: a command that had come could not be turned back [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of the place, how long it took, or how the believers were brought out.
- Not established: how many were in the one house of those who submitted.
- The word awwah (11:75) is rendered in different ways, for example tender-hearted or one who often calls on God; a scholar should decide.
- The wife of Lut is not named in these verses.
- The pronoun in 51:35-37, rendered 'it', refers to a place the verses do not name here.
- The inventory range stops at these ayat; the destruction itself is told elsewhere and is not part of this record.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the visit of the messengers to Ibrahim. None is used in this draft.
The visit is also told inside the longer story of Ibrahim (content/stories/ibrahim.draft.json); this record is a shorter account that refers to it only in general words.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the messengers, of Ibrahim's wife and of the place. None is used in the story texts.
The passages are read as one visit on matching wording (an inference); the details differ between them.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: The one who speaks in the passage asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead.
God asked whether he did not believe, and he answered yes, but that his heart might be at ease.
God told him to take four of the birds and to incline them to himself, the Arabic being read in more than one way.
Then he was to place a part of them on every mountain.
Then he was to call them, and they would come to him hastening.
God told him to know that God is Almighty and Wise.

chapters.summary_md: The one who speaks in the passage asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead [c1]. God told him to take four birds and to call them, and they would come to him hastening [c3][c5].
chapters.body_md:
The one who speaks in the passage asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead [c1]. God asked whether he did not believe, and he answered yes, but that his heart might be at ease [c2].

God told him to take four of the birds and to incline them to himself [c3]. Then he was to place a part of them on every mountain [c4], and then to call them, and they would come to him hastening [c5]. God told him to know that God is Almighty and Wise [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The passage is a short exchange in which a request [c1] is met by a question and an answer [c2], and then by an instruction in steps [c3][c4][c5]. The instruction ends with a reminder of God's might and wisdom [c6]. The Arabic of the first step, rendered 'incline them to yourself', is read in more than one way [c3].
chapters.kids_md: A servant of God asked Him to show how He gives life to the dead [c1]. God told him to take four birds and to call them, and they would come to him [c3][c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the speaker says belief and a heart at ease are not the same thing, and God does not rebuke the request [c2]. Another is that the passage ends by naming God as Almighty and Wise [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which birds, where, or when; the verse says only four of the birds.
- The Arabic phrase in the first step is read in more than one way (to incline them to yourself, or to cut them up); the verse does not decide, and a scholar should word it.
- Not established: what happened to the birds after the call beyond that they come hastening; the verse does not describe it.
- Not established: what it means that the parts were placed on every mountain, or how many mountains.
- The verse does not say what prompted the request.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on this request and the birds. None is used in this draft.
The event is also told inside the longer story of the same prophet (content/stories/ibrahim.draft.json); this record is a shorter account that refers to it only in general words.

The text of this event never names its speaker in the draft because the spelling of the name at 2:260 is not matched by the name anchor in the validator fixtures (a validator limitation, not a Quranic point); the passage itself names him in its first words.
The reading of the Arabic verb translated 'incline them to yourself' (the cutting up of the birds, or only turning them toward him) is disputed among interpreters; the draft keeps both.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The raising of the foundations of the House

claims.statement_en: God made the House a place of return for people and a place of security.
The people were told to take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer.
God made a covenant with Ibrahim and Ismail to purify His House for those who circle it, those who stay there, and those who bow and prostrate.

In another passage God says that He settled Ibrahim in the place of the House, telling him not to associate anything with Him and to purify His House for those who circle it, those who stand, and those who bow and prostrate.
While Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the House, they asked their Lord to accept it from them, saying that He is the Hearing, the Knowing.

They asked to be made submitted to Him, and for a community from their descendants submitted to Him; they asked to be shown their rites and that He turn to them, for He is the accepting of repentance, the Merciful.
They asked that He raise up among them a messenger from among them, who would recite His signs to them, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them.

chapters.summary_md: God made a covenant with Ibrahim and Ismail to purify His House [c3], and God says that He settled Ibrahim in its place [c4]. As they raised its foundations they prayed to their Lord to accept it from them [c5].
chapters.body_md:
God made the House a place of return for people and a place of security, and people were told to take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer [c1][c2]. He made a covenant with Ibrahim and Ismail to purify His House for those who circle it, those who stay there, and those who bow and prostrate [c3].

In another passage God says that He settled Ibrahim in the place of the House, telling him not to associate anything with Him and to purify His House for those who circle it, those who stand, and those who bow and prostrate [c4].

While Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the House, they asked their Lord to accept it from them, saying that He is the Hearing, the Knowing [c5]. They asked to be made submitted to Him, to be shown their rites, and that He turn to them [c6]. They also asked that He raise up among them a messenger from among them, who would recite His signs, teach the Book and wisdom, and purify them [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passages treat the House under more than one aspect: its purpose for people [c1][c2], the work of purifying it that is entrusted to Ibrahim and Ismail [c3][c4], and the raising of its foundations with their prayer [c5][c6][c7]. The commands to purify are given in different passages, with slightly different lists of those who come [c3][c4]. The prayer is spoken in the plural and the verses do not mark each speaker [c5][c6].
chapters.kids_md: God told Ibrahim and Ismail to keep His House clean for people who come to pray [c3]. They raised its foundations and asked their Lord to accept what they had done [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the builders ask for acceptance of their work as they build [c5]. Another is that their prayer reaches beyond themselves, to their descendants and to a messenger yet to come [c6][c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the House stood; these verses give no place name for the work of the foundations.
- Not established: who the messenger asked for in 2:129 is; the verse does not name him, and the identification is a matter for later reading that a scholar should supply with sources.
- Not established: how long the work took, or what the House was made of.
- The word translated 'station' (2:125) and the sense of 'place of return' are understood in more than one way; a scholar should decide the wording.
- 2:125 uses the plural for the people addressed in the instruction to take the station; the verse does not say whether it speaks to Ibrahim's family or to all people.

chapters.title_en: The land, the call and the first House

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim asked his Lord to make this a secure land and to provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in God and the Last Day.
God said that for whoever disbelieves He would give enjoyment for a little, then drive him to the punishment of the fire, an evil destination.
In another passage Ibrahim asked that this land be made secure and that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols.
He said that idols had led many people astray; whoever follows him is of him, and as for whoever disobeys him, his Lord is forgiving, merciful.

He said that he had settled some of his descendants in a valley without crops, near God's Sacred House, so that they might establish prayer; he asked that the hearts of some people incline toward them and that they be given fruits, so that they might give thanks.
God told Ibrahim to call out to people for the pilgrimage; they would come to him on foot and on every lean mount, from every deep mountain pass.
This was so that they might witness benefits for themselves and mention God's name on appointed days over the livestock He had provided for them.
Then they were to complete their rites, fulfil their vows and circle the Ancient House.
The first House set down for people, the Quran says, was the one at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.

In it are clear signs, the station of Ibrahim; whoever enters it is secure; God has a claim on people for the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way there; and God is free of need of the worlds, whoever disbelieves.

chapters.summary_md: Ibrahim asked his Lord to make the land secure and to provide for its people [c1][c3]. God told him to call people to the pilgrimage, and they would come to him from every deep mountain pass [c6].
chapters.body_md:
Ibrahim asked his Lord to make this a secure land and to provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in God and the Last Day [c1]. God said that for whoever disbelieves He would give enjoyment for a little, then drive him to the punishment of the fire [c2]. In another passage Ibrahim asked that he and his sons be kept away from worshipping idols [c3], and said that whoever follows him is of him [c4]. He said he had settled some of his descendants in a valley without crops, near God's Sacred House, so that they might establish prayer [c5].

God told Ibrahim to call out to people for the pilgrimage; they would come on foot and on every lean mount, from every deep mountain pass [c6]. This was so that they might witness benefits for themselves and mention God's name on appointed days [c7]. Then they were to complete their rites, fulfil their vows and circle the Ancient House [c8].

The Quran says that the first House set down for people was the one at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds [c9]. In it are clear signs, among them the station of Ibrahim, and whoever enters it is secure [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The passages join the prayers of Ibrahim for the land [c1][c3][c4][c5] with God's command to call people [c6][c7][c8] and with a statement about the first House [c9][c10]. The prayers speak of security, provision and keeping away from idols [c1][c3][c5]. The call for the pilgrimage is told with its purposes [c6][c7][c8]. The rites listed are named only in general terms [c8].
chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim asked God to make the land safe and to give its people fruits [c1]. God told him to call people to the pilgrimage, and they would come from far away [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Ibrahim asks for security for the land, provision for its people and protection from idols together [c1][c3][c5]. Another is that the call to people is joined to the purpose of remembering God's name [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of the valley or the land that Ibrahim speaks of in 14:35-37, or where it lay; the verses say this land and a valley without crops.
- Not established: which descendants Ibrahim settled in the valley, or when; 14:37 says some of his descendants.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of the valley, the land and the House with a named city or building; a scholar should add such identification with sources if the page gives it.
- The verses do not describe the House, its size or what it was built from.
- The rites in 22:28-29 are named only in general terms; no detail of how they are performed is given in these verses, and this draft does not discuss how they are carried out.
- Not established: how the call of 22:27 was made or how long it took to reach people.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the building of the House, the station of Ibrahim and the call to pilgrimage. None is used in this draft.
The event is also told inside the longer story of Ibrahim (content/stories/ibrahim.draft.json); this record is a shorter account that refers to it only in general words.
Whether Bakkah (3:96) and the land of 14:35-37 name the same place as the House of 2:125-127 is a reading from later tradition; the draft states what each verse says and does not equate them.
The identification of the unnamed messenger of 2:129 is left to a scholar.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: Ibrahim's vision of sacrificing his son

claims.statement_en: Ibrahim said that he was going to his Lord, who would guide him.
He asked his Lord to grant him one of the righteous.
God gave him glad tidings of a forbearing boy.
When the boy reached the stage of striving along with him, Ibrahim told him that he saw in sleep that he was slaughtering him, and asked him to consider what he thought.
The son answered that his father should do what he was commanded, and that, if God willed, he would find him among the patient.
When both of them had submitted, and he had laid him down, God called to him.
God said that Ibrahim had fulfilled the vision, and that in this way He rewards the doers of good.
God says that this was the clear trial.
God ransomed him with a great sacrifice.
God left on him a mention among later generations: peace be upon Ibrahim.
In this way God rewards the doers of good; Ibrahim was one of His believing servants.

chapters.summary_md: Ibrahim saw in sleep that he was slaughtering his son, and told him so [c4]. The son told him to do as he was commanded, and God called to Ibrahim that he had fulfilled the vision and ransomed his son with a great sacrifice [c5][c7][c9].
chapters.body_md:
Ibrahim said that he was going to his Lord, who would guide him, and he asked his Lord to grant him one of the righteous [c1][c2]. God gave him glad tidings of a forbearing boy [c3].

When the boy reached the stage of striving along with him, Ibrahim told him that he saw in sleep that he was slaughtering him, and asked what he thought [c4]. The son answered that his father should do what he was commanded, and that, if God willed, he would find him among the patient [c5].

When both of them had submitted, and he had laid him down, God called to him [c6]. God said that Ibrahim had fulfilled the vision, and that in this way He rewards the doers of good [c7]. God says that this was the clear trial [c8], and He ransomed him with a great sacrifice [c9]. God left on him a mention among later generations: peace be upon Ibrahim [c10]. He was one of God's believing servants [c11].
chapters.deep_md: The passage runs from Ibrahim's prayer for a righteous child [c1][c2] and the glad tidings [c3] to the vision [c4], the answer [c5], the call [c6][c7] and the ransom [c9]. God names the event a clear trial [c8], and the passage closes with a mention left among later generations and a statement of reward [c10][c11]. The text speaks of the son and the vision throughout and does not give the son's name [c4][c5].
chapters.kids_md: Ibrahim saw in a dream that he was to sacrifice his son, and he told him [c4]. His son said to do what he was told, and that he would be patient [c5]. God called out to Ibrahim and ransomed his son [c7][c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage stresses submission on both sides: Ibrahim consults his son and the son answers with patience [c4][c5]. Another is that God names the event a trial and a reward for the doers of good [c7][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The verses do not name the son. Interpreters have identified him in different ways, and a scholar must decide how the page treats the question; this draft does not name him.
- Not established: the place, the time or the age of the son; the Arabic says only that he reached the stage of striving along with his father.
- The pronoun in 'ransomed him' (37:107) is not marked in the Arabic; it is generally read as the son, and a scholar should confirm the wording.
- The verse does not say how the great sacrifice was provided or what it was.
- Not established: whether the vision was repeated; the verse says only that Ibrahim saw it in sleep.
- The passage continues in 37:112-113 with a further glad tidings; those verses are outside this chapter and a scholar should decide whether to add them and how to word their relation to the boy of 37:101.

claims.statement_en: Yusuf told his father that he had seen eleven stars, and the sun and the moon, and that he had seen them prostrating to him.
His father told him not to relate his dream to his brothers, or they would plot a plot against him, and said that Satan is a clear enemy to the human being.

His father said that in this way his Lord would choose him, teach him the interpretation of events, and complete His favour on him and on the family of Yaqub, as He had completed it before on his forefathers Ibrahim and Ishaq; his Lord is knowing and wise.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf told his father that he had seen eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him [c1]. His father told him not to tell his brothers, and said that his Lord would choose him and complete His favour on him [c2][c3].
chapters.body_md:
Yusuf told his father that he had seen eleven stars, and the sun and the moon, and that he had seen them prostrating to him [c1].

His father told him not to relate his dream to his brothers, or they would plot a plot against him, and said that Satan is a clear enemy to the human being [c2]. He said that in this way his Lord would choose him, teach him the interpretation of events, and complete His favour on him and on the family of Yaqub, as He had completed it before on his forefathers Ibrahim and Ishaq [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The passage is a short exchange: the dream [c1], the warning to keep it from the brothers [c2], and the father's words about what his Lord would do [c3]. The dream is given as seen and told, and the verses do not interpret it here [c1]. The father names the forefathers on whom God had completed His favour [c3].
chapters.kids_md: Yusuf told his father about a dream in which eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowed down to him [c1]. His father told him not to tell his brothers [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the father answers the dream with care for his son and with trust in God's choosing [c2][c3]. Another is that the warning names Satan as a clear enemy to the human being [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how old Yusuf was when he saw the dream, or where the family lived in this passage.
- Not established: the meaning of the dream in this passage; Yusuf speaks of its interpretation later in the surah (12:100), which is outside this record.
- Not established: how the brothers learned of the dream, or whether they did.
- The Quran says the stars were eleven; it does not say what they stood for. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: identifications of the stars, the sun and the moon with named persons; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: The Quran says that in Yusuf and his brothers there are signs for those who ask.
His brothers said that Yusuf and his brother were dearer to their father than they were, though they were a strong group, and that their father was in clear error.
They proposed to kill Yusuf or to cast him out on some land, so that their father's attention would turn to them alone, and that afterwards they could be a righteous people.
One of them said not to kill Yusuf but to throw him into the bottom of the well, where some travellers might pick him up, if they were going to act.
They asked their father why he did not trust them with Yusuf, said that they wished him well, and asked him to send Yusuf with them the next day to enjoy himself and play, promising to guard him.

Their father said that it would grieve him for them to take Yusuf away, and that he feared a wolf would eat him while they were heedless of him; they said that if a wolf ate him while they were a strong group, they would be losers.
When they had gone away with Yusuf and agreed to put him in the bottom of the well, God inspired Yusuf that he would one day tell them of this deed of theirs while they did not realise.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf's brothers said that Yusuf and his brother were dearer to their father, and proposed to kill him or cast him out [c2][c3]. One of them said to throw him into the well instead, and they took Yusuf away from their father [c4][c5].
chapters.body_md:
The Quran says that in Yusuf and his brothers there are signs for those who ask [c1]. His brothers said that Yusuf and his brother were dearer to their father than they were, though they were a strong group, and that their father was in clear error [c2]. They proposed to kill Yusuf or to cast him out on some land, so that their father's attention would turn to them alone [c3]. One of them said not to kill Yusuf but to throw him into the bottom of the well, where some travellers might pick him up [c4].

They asked their father to send Yusuf with them the next day to enjoy himself and play, promising to guard him [c5]. Their father said it would grieve him and that he feared a wolf would eat him while they were heedless [c6].

When they had gone away with Yusuf and agreed to put him in the bottom of the well, God inspired Yusuf that he would one day tell them of this deed of theirs while they did not realise [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passage is built around the plan [c3][c4], the request to the father [c5][c6] and the carrying out [c7]. The grievance the brothers state is that Yusuf and his brother were dearer to their father [c2]. The speaker of the milder proposal is one of them, not named in the verse [c4]. God's inspiration to Yusuf is given at the moment of the deed [c7].
chapters.kids_md: Yusuf's brothers were upset because they thought their father loved Yusuf and his brother more [c2]. They took Yusuf away and put him in a well [c4][c7]. God told Yusuf that he would one day tell them about it [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage shows how a grievance can lead people to plan harm to one of their own [c2][c3]. Another is that God speaks to Yusuf at the moment of his need [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the names or the number of the brothers beyond that they were a strong group; the speaker of 12:10 is one of them.
- Not established: where the well was, how deep it was, or how far from home.
- The verses name no emotion for the brothers; to call their grievance jealousy is an inference.
- The wolf appears only in the father's fear and in the brothers' reply; later tradition adds to this and none of it is used here.
- The meaning of the inspiration to Yusuf in 12:15 is not explained beyond what the verse says.

claims.statement_en: The brothers came to their father at nightfall, weeping.
They said that they had gone off racing and left Yusuf with their belongings and a wolf had eaten him, and that he would not believe them even if they were truthful.

They brought Yusuf's shirt with false blood on it; their father said that rather their souls had made something appear fair to them, that his course was graceful patience, and that God is the one whose help is sought against what they described.
A caravan came and its people sent one to draw water; he let down his bucket and called out glad tidings that here was a boy, and they hid him away as merchandise; God knows what they do.
He was sold for a low price, a few dirhams counted out, and they thought little of him.

chapters.summary_md: The brothers came to their father at nightfall, weeping, and said a wolf had eaten Yusuf, bringing his shirt with false blood on it [c1][c2][c3]. A caravan came, and one who drew water found a boy; he was sold for a low price [c4][c5].
chapters.body_md:
The brothers came to their father at nightfall, weeping [c1]. They said that they had gone off racing and left Yusuf with their belongings and a wolf had eaten him, and that he would not believe them even if they were truthful [c2]. They brought Yusuf's shirt with false blood on it [c3]. Their father said that rather their souls had made something appear fair to them, that his course was graceful patience, and that God is the one whose help is sought against what they described [c3].

A caravan came and its people sent one to draw water; he let down his bucket and called out glad tidings that here was a boy, and they hid him away as merchandise [c4]. He was sold for a low price, a few dirhams counted out, and they thought little of him [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The scenes set the brothers' story against the father's answer [c2][c3] and then turn to the caravan [c4][c5]. The Quran says the blood on the shirt was false [c3]. The Arabic does not make clear who hid the boy as merchandise and who sold him, and the draft keeps the verbs without naming the actors [c4][c5].
chapters.kids_md: The brothers told their father a wolf had eaten Yusuf and showed him his shirt with false blood on it [c2][c3]. Their father said he would be patient and ask God for help [c3]. A caravan came, and they found a boy in the well [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the father answers a story he does not believe with patience and appeal to God's help [c3]. Another is that the passage notes that God knows what is done to the boy [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how long Yusuf was in the well, where the caravan came from or was going, or who the water-drawer was.
- The verses do not say who hid the boy as merchandise or who sold him (the travellers, the brothers or others); this draft does not decide.
- The price is given as a few dirhams counted out; the verse gives no number.
- The boy is not named in 12:19; the narrative before it makes him Yusuf.
- Not established: what the false blood was or how the brothers got it, or what the father did that night.
