stories.title_en: Yusuf in the house of the Aziz

chapters.title_en: Into the household and the trial

claims.statement_en: The man in Egypt who bought him told his wife to give him an honourable place to stay, saying that he might benefit them or they might take him as a son.
God says that in this way He established Yusuf in the land so that He might teach him the interpretation of events; God prevails over His affair, but most people do not know.
When Yusuf reached his full strength, God gave him judgement and knowledge.

The woman in whose house Yusuf was staying tried to seduce him; she closed the doors and called him to her; Yusuf said that he sought refuge in God, that his lord had made his stay good, and that the wrongdoers do not succeed.

The verse says that she was set on him, and that he would have inclined toward her had he not seen a proof from his Lord; in this way God turned evil and indecency away from him, for he was among His sincere servants.

They raced to the door and she tore his shirt from behind; they met her master at the door, and she said that the penalty for one who wanted evil for his family should be prison or a painful punishment.

Yusuf said that she had tried to seduce him; a witness from her household said that if his shirt was torn from the front she spoke truly, and if it was torn from behind she had lied and he was truthful.

When he saw that the shirt was torn from behind, he said that this was from their plotting, and that their plotting was great; he told Yusuf to turn away from this, and told her to ask forgiveness for her sin, for she was among the wrongdoers.

chapters.summary_md: A man in Egypt bought Yusuf and told his wife to give him an honourable place, and God says He established Yusuf in the land [c1][c2]. The woman of the house tried to seduce him, and a witness from her household spoke about his torn shirt [c4][c7].
chapters.body_md:
The man in Egypt who bought him told his wife to give him an honourable place to stay, saying that he might benefit them or they might take him as a son [c1]. God says that in this way He established Yusuf in the land so that He might teach him the interpretation of events [c2]. When Yusuf reached his full strength, God gave him judgement and knowledge [c3].

The woman in whose house Yusuf was staying tried to seduce him; she closed the doors and called him to her [c4]. Yusuf said that he sought refuge in God and that the wrongdoers do not succeed [c4]. The verse says that she was set on him, and that he would have inclined toward her had he not seen a proof from his Lord; in this way God turned evil and indecency away from him, for he was among His sincere servants [c5].

They raced to the door and she tore his shirt from behind [c6]. A witness from her household said that if his shirt was torn from the front she spoke truly, and if it was torn from behind she had lied and he was truthful [c7]. When he saw that the shirt was torn from behind, he said that this was from their plotting, and told Yusuf to turn away from this and her to ask forgiveness for her sin [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The passage joins God's establishing of Yusuf in the land [c1][c2][c3] with the trial in the household [c4][c5][c6]. The word rendered 'lord' in 12:23 can mean his master or his Lord, and the draft keeps both [c4]. The verse about what each was set on (12:24) is read in more than one way, and this draft states only the verse's condition and the statement that God turned evil away from him [c5]. The testimony turns on the shirt torn from behind [c7][c8].
chapters.kids_md: A man in Egypt bought Yusuf and told his wife to treat him well [c1]. When she tried to make him do wrong, Yusuf said he sought refuge in God [c4]. The torn shirt showed who was telling the truth [c7][c8].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Yusuf's first answer is to seek refuge in God [c4]. Another is that the verse says God turned evil and indecency away from him because he was among His sincere servants [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name the buyer, his wife, his position or the household in this passage. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: personal names for the buyer and his wife; none is used here.
- Not established: how old Yusuf was when he was bought, when he reached his full strength, or how long he was in the household.
- The Arabic of 12:24 about Yusuf's part is read in more than one way; this draft states the verse's condition and decides nothing more, and a reviewer must check the wording against the classical readings.
- The verse does not say what the proof from his Lord was.
- The verses do not say whether the witness was a man or a woman or how related to her; the speaker of 12:28-29 is not named in the verses and the draft reads it as her master.
- The Arabic word rendered 'lord' in 12:23 can mean his master or his Lord; this draft keeps both.

claims.statement_en: Women in the city said that the wife of the Aziz was seducing her young manservant, that love for him had gripped her, and that they saw her in clear error.
When she heard of their scheming she sent for them and prepared a place for them to recline; she gave each of them a knife and told him to come out before them.
When they saw him they were amazed at him and cut their hands, and said, glorifying God, that this was no human being but a noble angel.

She told them that this was the one they had blamed her for, that she had tried to seduce him and he had held back, and that if he did not do what she ordered him he would be imprisoned and be among the humiliated.
The young man said to his Lord that prison was dearer to him than what they called him to, and that unless God turned their plotting away from him he might incline to them and be among the ignorant.
His Lord answered him and turned their plotting away from him; He hears and knows.

chapters.summary_md: Women in the city blamed the wife of the Aziz, and she gave them a gathering at which they saw her young manservant and were amazed [c1][c2][c3]. The young man said to his Lord that prison was dearer to him, and God turned their plotting away from him [c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
Women in the city said that the wife of the Aziz was seducing her young manservant and that they saw her in clear error [c1]. When she heard of their scheming she sent for them and prepared a place for them to recline; she gave each of them a knife and told him to come out before them [c2]. When they saw him they were amazed at him and cut their hands, and said, glorifying God, that this was no human being but a noble angel [c3].

She told them that this was the one they had blamed her for, and that if he did not do what she ordered him he would be imprisoned [c4]. The young man said to his Lord that prison was dearer to him than what they called him to, and that unless God turned their plotting away from him he might incline to them [c5]. His Lord answered him and turned their plotting away from him [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The scene moves from the talk of the women [c1] to the gathering [c2][c3], the woman's warning [c4] and the young man's prayer [c5], and ends with God's answer [c6]. The verses record what the women did and said and do not describe the young man [c3]. Aziz is a title; the verses do not say what office it names [c1].
chapters.kids_md: Some women in the city talked about the wife of the Aziz [c1]. She invited them and they were amazed at the young man [c2][c3]. The young man asked his Lord for help, and God turned their plotting away from him [c5][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the young man asks his Lord for help against plotting and puts his trust in Him [c5]. Another is that the passage ends with God's answer to the prayer [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the women were or how many, or what the knives were for beyond each being given one; the verses say they cut their hands and give no further detail.
- The verses do not describe the young man or say what the women saw beyond their amazement and their words.
- Not established: how long after the earlier events this was.
- Aziz is a title; the Quran does not say what office it names. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: personal names for the Aziz and his wife; none is used here.

chapters.title_en: The two companions and the forgotten request

claims.statement_en: After they had seen the signs, it occurred to them to imprison the young man of the story for a time.

Two young men entered the prison with him; one said he saw himself pressing wine, and the other that he saw himself carrying bread on his head, from which birds were eating; they asked him to tell them the interpretation, for they saw him as one of those who do good.

He said that no food provided for them would come before he had informed them of its interpretation; this, he said, was from what his Lord had taught him; and he had left the way of a people who do not believe in God and who deny the Hereafter.

He said that he followed the way of his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub, that it was not for them to associate anything with God, and that this was from God's favour on them and on people, though most people are not thankful.

Speaking to his companions in prison, he asked whether scattered lords were better, or God, the One who prevails; he said that what they worshipped besides Him were only names that they and their fathers had given, for which God had sent down no authority, and that judgement belongs to God alone.
He gave the interpretation: one of them would serve wine to his lord, and the other would be crucified and the birds would eat from his head; the matter about which they asked was decided.
He said to the one he thought would be saved that he should mention him to his lord; Satan caused a forgetting of the mention of his lord, and he remained in prison for several years.

chapters.summary_md: The young man of the story was imprisoned for a time, and two young men entered the prison with him and told him their dreams [c1][c2]. He gave them the interpretation, and asked the one he thought would be saved to mention him, but Satan caused a forgetting, and he stayed in prison for several years [c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
After they had seen the signs, it occurred to them to imprison the young man of the story for a time [c1]. Two young men entered the prison with him; one said he saw himself pressing wine, and the other that he saw himself carrying bread on his head, from which birds were eating, and they asked him to tell them the interpretation [c2].

He said that no food provided for them would come before he had informed them of its interpretation, and that this was from what his Lord had taught him [c3]. He said he followed the way of his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub, and that it was not for them to associate anything with God [c4]. He asked his companions whether scattered lords were better, or God, the One who prevails, and said that judgement belongs to God alone [c5].

He gave the interpretation: one of them would serve wine to his lord, and the other would be crucified and the birds would eat from his head [c6]. He said to the one he thought would be saved that he should mention him to his lord; Satan caused a forgetting of the mention of his lord, and he remained in prison for several years [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The prison scene has several movements: the dreams of the companions [c2], his speech about what his Lord taught him and about God alone [c3][c4][c5], and the interpretation with its sequel [c6][c7]. The reference of 'his lord' in 12:42 can be read in two ways, as the freed man's master or as the speaker's own Lord, and the draft keeps both [c7]. The length of the stay is given only as several years [c7].
chapters.kids_md: Two young men came into the prison with him and told him their dreams [c2]. He told them what the dreams meant [c6]. He asked the one who would be saved to mention him, but that man forgot, and he stayed in prison for several years [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that he speaks to his companions of God alone before he gives the interpretation [c3][c5]. Another is that the request to be mentioned is followed by a long wait [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The verses in this event do not name the young man; the story that surrounds them does, and this record does not name him because these verses do not.
- The Quran does not name the two young men or say what they had done; it does not say who his lord is in 12:41.
- Not established: how long a time (12:35) was, how old he was when he was imprisoned, what the signs were that they had seen, or who they are who decided on the prison.
- The Arabic for several years does not give an exact number of years.
- The reference of his lord in 12:42 can be read in two ways, as noted in the text; the verse does not settle it.

stories.title_en: The king's dream and Yusuf's rise

claims.statement_en: The king said that he saw seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and other dry ones; he asked his chiefs to explain his vision if they could interpret visions.
They said that it was a confusion of dreams and that they had no knowledge of the interpretation of such dreams.
The one who had been saved remembered after a period, said that he would inform them of its interpretation and asked to be sent.
He came to Yusuf, addressed him as the truthful one, and asked for the interpretation of the cows and the ears, so that he might return to the people and they might know.
Yusuf said that they would sow for seven years continuously, and that what they harvested they should leave in its ear, except a little for eating.
Yusuf said that after that would come seven hard years that would eat what they had stored for them, except a little of what they preserved.
Yusuf said that after that would come a year in which people would be given relief and in which they would press.

chapters.summary_md: The king saw seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones and seven green ears and seven dry ones, and his chiefs could not interpret it [c1][c2]. The man who had been saved came to Yusuf, and Yusuf gave the interpretation of seven years, then seven hard years, then a year of relief [c4][c5][c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
The king said that he saw seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and other dry ones, and asked his chiefs to explain his vision if they could interpret visions [c1]. They said that it was a confusion of dreams and that they had no knowledge of the interpretation of such dreams [c2].

The one who had been saved remembered after a period, said that he would inform them of its interpretation and asked to be sent [c3]. He came to Yusuf, addressed him as the truthful one, and asked for the interpretation, so that he might return to the people and they might know [c4].

Yusuf said that they would sow for seven years continuously, and that what they harvested they should leave in its ear, except a little for eating [c5]. After that would come seven hard years that would eat what they had stored, except a little of what they preserved [c6]. After that would come a year in which people would be given relief and in which they would press [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The vision is given once and the interpretation follows it in steps [c1][c5][c6][c7]. The chiefs decline [c2], and the man who had been saved is the link to Yusuf [c3][c4]. The Arabic for what the people would press does not say what was pressed [c7].
chapters.kids_md: The king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones [c1]. Yusuf said there would be seven years of sowing, then seven hard years, then a year of relief [c5][c6][c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the interpretation comes with instructions to keep a store through the years of plenty [c5][c6]. Another is that the one who forgot Yusuf earlier remembers him when the chiefs cannot answer [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name the king or the land he ruled; it uses the word king for the ruler in this account. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: names for the king, his dynasty and his title; none is used here.
- Not established: who the chiefs were or how long the period of 12:45 was.
- The Arabic for press does not say what was pressed (grapes, olives or something else).
- Not established: how long after the prison scene this came.

claims.statement_en: The king ordered that Yusuf be brought to him; when the messenger came, Yusuf told him to return to his lord and ask about the women who had cut their hands, for his Lord knows their plotting.

The king asked the women what their affair was when they tried to seduce Yusuf; they said that they knew no evil against him; and the wife of the Aziz said that now the truth had become clear: she had tried to seduce him and he was among the truthful.

A speaker, not named in the verses, says that this was so that the master would know that he had not betrayed him in his absence, and that God does not guide the plotting of the betrayers; and that he does not declare himself innocent, for the self commands evil except where his Lord has mercy.
The king said to bring Yusuf to him, that he would take him for himself; and when he had spoken with him, the king said that he was that day established with them and trusted.
Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land, saying that he was a knowing guardian.
God says that in this way He established Yusuf in the land, where he could settle wherever he wished; He reaches with His mercy whomever He wills and does not waste the reward of those who do good.
The reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God.

chapters.summary_md: The king sent for Yusuf, and Yusuf asked him to look into the matter of the women who had cut their hands [c1]. The women and the wife of the Aziz spoke, and the king then gave Yusuf his trust, and Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land [c2][c4][c5].
chapters.body_md:
The king ordered that Yusuf be brought to him; when the messenger came, Yusuf told him to return to his lord and ask about the women who had cut their hands [c1]. The king asked the women what their affair was; they said that they knew no evil against him, and the wife of the Aziz said that now the truth had become clear: she had tried to seduce him and he was among the truthful [c2].

A speaker, not named in the verses, says that this was so that the master would know that he had not betrayed him in his absence, and that he does not declare himself innocent, for the self commands evil except where his Lord has mercy [c3].

The king said to bring Yusuf to him, and when he had spoken with him, said that he was that day established with them and trusted [c4]. Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land, saying he was a knowing guardian [c5]. God says that in this way He established Yusuf in the land [c6], and that the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter has the investigation of the women [c1][c2], a speech whose speaker the verses do not name [c3], the king's trust [c4], Yusuf's request [c5] and God's comment on it [c6][c7]. The draft does not decide who speaks 12:52-53 and says so [c3]. The Quran does not narrate the moment of Yusuf's release from prison [c1].
chapters.kids_md: The king sent for Yusuf, and the women said they knew no evil against him [c1][c2]. The king trusted him, and Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land [c4][c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Yusuf asks that the matter of the women be cleared before he comes out [c1][c2]. Another is that the passage ends by saying the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how long after the king's dream these events came, or the title and rank of the post Yusuf asked for; the verse says the storehouses of the land.
- The verses do not say who speaks 12:52-53. Some read it as Yusuf and some as the wife of the Aziz; a reviewer must confirm, because the verses do not name the speaker.
- The Quran does not narrate the moment of Yusuf's release; he says later (12:100) that God brought him out of the prison, which is outside this record.
- The Quran does not say in so many words that the king granted the post; 12:56 says God established Yusuf in the land.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Yusuf and the king. None is used in this draft.
The event is also told inside the longer story of Yusuf (content/stories/yusuf.draft.json); this record is a shorter, event-focused account that refers to it only in general words.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: personal names for Yusuf's brothers, mother, the Aziz, his wife and the king, and the name and story of the wolf. None is used in the story texts.
The speaker of 12:52-53 is not named in the verses; the draft marks it as unnamed and does not choose.
The numbers in this event (seven cows, ears and years) are those stated in 12:43-49; no other number is used.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: Yusuf's brothers came and entered where he was; he recognised them, but they did not recognise him.

When Yusuf had supplied them with their provisions, he told them to bring him a brother of theirs from their father, and asked whether they did not see that he gave full measure; if they did not bring him, there would be no measure for them from him and they should not come near him.
Yusuf told his servants to put the brothers' goods back in their saddlebags, so that they would recognise them when they returned to their family and might come back.

When they went back to their father they said that the measure had been withheld from them, and asked him to send their brother with them so that they could have their measure, promising to guard him.

When they opened their goods and found their merchandise returned, they said that they wanted nothing more; their father said that he would not send him with them until they gave him a pledge by God that they would bring him back unless they were surrounded; when they gave their pledge, he said that God was guardian over what they said.

He told them not to enter by one gate but by different gates, though he could avail them nothing against God, for judgement belongs to God alone and in Him he put his trust; when they entered as their father had ordered, it availed them nothing against God, but it met a need in Yaqub's soul which he fulfilled; he had knowledge because God had taught him, though most people do not know.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf's brothers came and he recognised them, but they did not recognise him [c1]. He told them to bring a brother of theirs, returned their goods to their saddlebags, and their father agreed to send the brother only after they gave a pledge by God [c2][c3][c5].
chapters.body_md:
Yusuf's brothers came and entered where he was; he recognised them, but they did not recognise him [c1]. When he had supplied them with their provisions, he told them to bring him a brother of theirs from their father, saying that otherwise there would be no measure for them from him [c2]. He told his servants to put the brothers' goods back in their saddlebags [c3].

When they went back to their father they said that the measure had been withheld, and asked him to send their brother with them [c4]. Their father said he would not send him until they gave a pledge by God that they would bring him back unless they were surrounded, and when they gave it he said that God was guardian over what they said [c5].

He told them to enter by different gates; when they did so as he had ordered, it availed them nothing against God, but it met a need in Yaqub's soul which he fulfilled [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The first journey is told through its steps: the meeting without recognition [c1], the demand to bring a brother [c2], the returned goods [c3], the father's pledge [c5] and his instruction about the gates [c6]. The verses give no reason why the brothers did not recognise Yusuf, only that they did not [c1]. The father's words about the gates and the need in his soul are not explained further in the verses [c6].
chapters.kids_md: Yusuf's brothers came to him, and he knew them, but they did not know him [c1]. He told them to bring their other brother [c2]. Their father agreed only after they gave a promise by God [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the father asks for a pledge by God before he sends his son [c5]. Another is that the father tells his sons to take care and still says that judgement belongs to God alone [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: when the brothers came, how many years had passed since they parted from Yusuf, or how many came.
- Not established: how Yusuf knew of the brother or why he asked for him.
- The Quran gives no reason why the brothers did not recognise Yusuf.
- Not established: why the father told them to enter by different gates, or what the need in Yaqub's soul was.
- The brother is not named. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: a name for Yusuf's full brother; none is used here.
- The verses 12:61 and 12:64 are in the inventory range but not used in this shorter chapter.

claims.statement_en: When the brothers came in to Yusuf, he took his brother aside and told him that he was his brother, so he should not grieve over what the others had been doing.
Yusuf placed the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag, and then a caller cried out that the caravan were thieves.

The brothers turned and asked what they were missing; they were told that the king's measuring cup was missing, that whoever brought it would have a camel's load, and that the speaker was responsible for it.

They asked what the penalty would be if they were found to be liars; the answer was that the penalty would be the one in whose saddlebag it was found, who himself would be the penalty, for that is how they penalise wrongdoers.

Yusuf began with their bags before his brother's bag, and then brought the cup out of his brother's bag; God says that in this way He devised for Yusuf, who could not have taken his brother under the king's law unless God willed.

The brothers said that if he had stolen, a brother of his had stolen before; Yusuf kept this in himself and did not reveal it to them, and said that they were in a worse position and that God knew best what they described.

When they despaired of him they withdrew to confer privately; the eldest of them reminded the rest that their father had taken a pledge from them before God, and that they had failed regarding Yusuf before; he said that he would not leave the land until his father permitted him or God judged for him.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf told his brother that he was his brother, and a cup was found in that brother's saddlebag [c1][c2][c5]. The brothers withdrew to confer, and the eldest reminded them of their father's pledge [c7].
chapters.body_md:
When the brothers came in to Yusuf, he took his brother aside and told him that he was his brother, so he should not grieve over what the others had been doing [c1]. Yusuf placed the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag, and then a caller cried out that the caravan were thieves [c2]. The brothers asked what they were missing and were told that the king's measuring cup was missing [c3]. They asked what the penalty would be, and were told that it would be the one in whose saddlebag it was found [c4].

Yusuf began with their bags before his brother's bag, and then brought the cup out of his brother's bag; God says that in this way He devised for Yusuf [c5]. The brothers said that if he had stolen, a brother of his had stolen before; Yusuf kept this in himself and did not reveal it to them [c6].

When they despaired of him they withdrew to confer privately; the eldest reminded the rest that their father had taken a pledge from them before God, and said that he would not leave the land until his father permitted him or God judged for him [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter tells of the cup in steps: Yusuf's word to his brother [c1], the placing of the cup [c2], the search [c3][c4][c5], the brothers' remark [c6] and their withdrawal [c7]. God's comment that He devised for Yusuf is given at the point of the search [c5]. The verses do not discuss the placing of the cup beyond that comment, and this draft gives no verdict on it [c2][c5].
chapters.kids_md: Yusuf told his brother that he was his brother [c1]. A cup was found in that brother's bag [c2][c5]. The brothers talked privately, and the eldest reminded them of their promise to their father [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the eldest recalls the pledge their father took from them before God [c7]. Another is that God's devising for Yusuf is stated in the passage, and the verse says Yusuf could not have acted as he did unless God willed [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the caller was, or whether Yusuf's brother knew of the plan beforehand; the verse says only that Yusuf told him who he was.
- The Quran does not describe the cup beyond giving it different names, or say what it was made of.
- Not established: what the earlier theft by a brother of his (12:77) was. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: stories told to explain this remark; none is used here.
- Not established: which brother is the eldest or how the decision to confer was reached.
- How Yusuf's placing of the cup (12:70-76) is to be assessed is not discussed in the verses beyond saying it was God's device; this draft gives no verdict on it and leaves the matter to the scholarly reviewer.
- How the king's law of 12:76 worked is not described.

chapters.title_en: The father's patience and Yusuf makes himself known

claims.statement_en: Their father said that rather their souls had enticed them to something, that his course was graceful patience, and that perhaps God would bring them all to him.
He turned away from them and said how great was his sorrow over Yusuf; his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing it.
He said that he complained of his distress and sorrow only to God, and that he knew from God what they did not know.
He told his sons to go and inquire about Yusuf and his brother, and not to despair of God's mercy, for none despairs of God's mercy except the disbelieving people.

The brothers entered on Yusuf, addressed him as the Aziz and said that hardship had touched them and their family; they had brought poor merchandise, and asked him to give them full measure and be charitable to them.

Yusuf asked whether they knew what they had done with Yusuf and his brother when they were ignorant; they asked whether he was indeed Yusuf, and he said that he was Yusuf and that this was his brother, that God had been gracious to them, and that God does not waste the reward of those who do good.

They said that God had preferred him over them and that they had been sinners; he said that there was no blame on them that day and that God forgives them, for He is the most merciful of the merciful.
Yusuf told them to take his shirt and throw it over his father's face, and he would come seeing; and to bring all their family to him.

chapters.summary_md: Their father said that his course was graceful patience, and turned to God in his sorrow over Yusuf [c1][c3]. The brothers then came to Yusuf and learned who he was, and he told them there was no blame on them that day and to cast his shirt over his father's face [c5][c6][c7][c8].
chapters.body_md:
Their father said that rather their souls had enticed them to something, that his course was graceful patience, and that perhaps God would bring them all to him [c1]. He turned away and said how great was his sorrow over Yusuf; his eyes turned white from grief [c2]. He said that he complained of his distress only to God [c3], and told his sons to go and inquire about Yusuf and his brother and not to despair of God's mercy [c4].

The brothers entered on Yusuf, addressed him as the Aziz and said that hardship had touched them, and asked him for full measure and charity [c5]. Yusuf asked whether they knew what they had done with Yusuf and his brother when they were ignorant; they asked whether he was indeed Yusuf, and he said that he was Yusuf and that this was his brother [c6]. They said that God had preferred him and that they had been sinners, and he said there was no blame on them that day [c7]. He told them to take his shirt and throw it over his father's face, and he would come seeing, and to bring all their family [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter pairs the father's patience [c1][c2][c3][c4] with the meeting of the brothers and Yusuf [c5][c6][c7][c8]. The verses say that the father's eyes turned white from grief [c2]; they do not say whether he lost his sight, and a later verse outside this record speaks of his returning seeing. The father's first words repeat the words he used when the shirt with false blood was brought [c1].
chapters.kids_md: Their father was very sad about Yusuf, but he turned to God and told his sons to look for him [c2][c3][c4]. The brothers came to Yusuf and learned who he was [c6]. He told them there was no blame on them that day [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the father tells his sons not to despair of God's mercy while he complains only to God [c3][c4]. Another is that Yusuf answers the confession of his brothers with forgiveness and a prayer for their pardon [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how long it had been since Yusuf was lost, how many years had passed since the first visit, or where the meeting took place beyond before him.
- The verse says his eyes turned white from grief; it does not say whether he lost his sight.
- Not established: what led the brothers to ask whether he was Yusuf, or what the father knew from God (12:86).
- The Quran does not say whether the shirt of 12:93 is the same as the earlier shirt, or that it had any property beyond Yusuf's instruction.
- The verses 12:85 and 12:81-82 (the sons' reply and the eldest's instructions) are in the inventory range but not used in this shorter chapter.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the brothers' journeys. None is used in this draft.
The event is also told inside the longer story of Yusuf (content/stories/yusuf.draft.json); this record is a shorter, event-focused account that refers to it only in general words.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: personal names for Yusuf's brothers, mother, the Aziz, his wife and the king, and the name and story of the wolf. None is used in the story texts.
How Yusuf's placing of the cup (12:70-76) is to be assessed is not given in the verses beyond calling it God's device; the draft gives no verdict and a scholar should look at it.

The inventory range 12:58-93 is only partly covered: the chapters keep to the verses the claims cite and leave 12:61, 12:64, 12:73, 12:78-79, 12:81-82 and 12:85 out. A reviewer should decide whether to add them.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The reunion of Yaqub and Yusuf

chapters.title_en: The scent, the shirt and the reunion

claims.statement_en: When the caravan set out, their father said that he found the scent of Yusuf, unless they thought him weak-minded.
Others said that, by God, he was in his old error.
When the bearer of good news came, he cast the shirt on the father's face, and the father returned seeing; he said, did he not tell them that he knew from God what they did not know.
His sons asked their father to ask forgiveness for their sins, since they had been sinners, and he said he would ask forgiveness for them from his Lord, who is forgiving and merciful.
When they entered on Yusuf, he took his parents to himself and told them to enter Egypt, if God willed, in safety.
Yusuf raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration; he said that this was the interpretation of his dream of before, which his Lord had made true.

Yusuf said that his Lord had been good to him in bringing him out of the prison and in bringing them from the desert, after Satan had stirred up enmity between him and his brothers; his Lord is subtle in what He wills, the knowing, the wise.

Yusuf prayed that God, who had given him of the kingdom and taught him the interpretation of events, and who is the creator of the heavens and the earth, would take him as one who submits and join him with the righteous.

chapters.summary_md: Their father said he found the scent of Yusuf, and when the shirt was cast on his face he returned seeing [c1][c3]. Yusuf took his parents to himself, and they fell down before him in prostration, and he said this was the interpretation of his dream of before [c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
When the caravan set out, their father said that he found the scent of Yusuf, unless they thought him weak-minded [c1]. Others said that, by God, he was in his old error [c2]. When the bearer of good news came, he cast the shirt on the father's face, and the father returned seeing [c3]. His sons asked him to ask forgiveness for their sins, and he said he would ask forgiveness for them from his Lord [c4].

When they entered on Yusuf, he took his parents to himself and told them to enter Egypt, if God willed, in safety [c5]. He raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration; he said that this was the interpretation of his dream of before, which his Lord had made true [c6]. He said that his Lord had been good to him in bringing him out of the prison and bringing them from the desert, after Satan had stirred up enmity between him and his brothers [c7].

Yusuf prayed that God would take him as one who submits and join him with the righteous [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter joins movements: the scent and the shirt [c1][c2][c3], the forgiveness asked from the father [c4] and the meeting with its prostration, with Yusuf's words about the dream [c5][c6][c7]. It ends with his prayer [c8]. The verses do not say who the parents are, and the sense of the Arabic verb in the prayer, the one used for taking a soul, is read in more than one way [c8].
chapters.kids_md: Their father said he could smell Yusuf [c1]. When the shirt was put on his face, he could see again [c3]. Yusuf's parents bowed before him, and he said this was the meaning of his old dream [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Yusuf names the fulfilled dream as his Lord's doing and speaks of Satan's part in the enmity [c6][c7]. Another is that the chapter ends with a prayer to be taken as one who submits [c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how much time passed between the first dream and the reunion; Yusuf calls the dream one of before.
- The verses do not say who the others are in 12:95.
- The verses do not say who the parents of 12:99-100 are; later accounts differ and none is used here.
- The father is not named in these verses.
- The Quran does not say what the prostration was, whether greeting, honour or something else.
- The Arabic verb in Yusuf's prayer (12:101) is the one used for taking a soul; how to render it is left to the reviewer.
- Not established: what became of the brothers, or Yusuf's death.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about the reunion of Yusuf and his family. None is used in this draft.
The event is also told inside the longer story of Yusuf (content/stories/yusuf.draft.json); this record is a shorter, event-focused account that refers to it only in general words.
The dream of Yusuf is told in 12:4-6 (see the event record on his dream); the draft does not equate the prostration of 12:100 with the dream beyond Yusuf's own words in 12:100.
Who the parents of 12:99-100 are is not stated; the draft does not decide.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: personal names for Yusuf's brothers, mother, the Aziz, his wife and the king, and the name and story of the wolf. None is used in the story texts.
The chapters group repeated passages by theme. The Quran does not give a chronology across the surahs, so the order of the chapters is a reading order only.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The birth of Musa and the river

claims.statement_en: God recites to the listener the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe.
Fir'awn exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing one group of them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive; he was among the corrupters.

God says He wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the land, make them leaders and inheritors, establish them in the land, and show Fir'awn, Haman and their soldiers what they feared from them.
God inspired the mother of Musa to nurse him, and, when she feared for him, to cast him into the river, and not to fear or grieve, for He would return him to her and make him one of the messengers.

In another passage God reminds Musa that He had favoured him another time, when He inspired his mother with what was inspired: to put him in the chest and cast it into the river, so that the river would throw it on the bank, where an enemy of God and of Musa would take him.
God says He cast love from Himself upon Musa, so that he would be brought up under His watch.

chapters.summary_md: God inspired the mother of Musa to nurse him and, when she feared for him, to cast him into the river, promising to return him to her and make him one of the messengers [c4]. This came while Fir'awn was slaughtering the sons of one group and keeping their women alive [c2].
chapters.body_md:
God recites the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe [c1]. Fir'awn exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing one group of them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive [c2]. God says He wished to show favour to those who were oppressed, make them leaders and inheritors, and show Fir'awn, Haman and their soldiers what they feared from them [c3].

God inspired the mother of Musa to nurse him, and, when she feared for him, to cast him into the river, and not to fear or grieve, for He would return him to her and make him one of the messengers [c4]. Another passage tells the same inspiration to Musa: to put him in the chest and cast it into the river, so that the river would throw it on the bank, where an enemy of God and of Musa would take him [c5]. God says He cast love from Himself upon Musa, so that he would be brought up under His watch [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The passages give the inspiration to his mother from different sides: the first sets it beside Fir'awn's oppression and God's wish to favour the oppressed [c2][c3][c4], and a later one recalls it to Musa himself as a favour [c5][c6]. The command to cast the child into the river comes with a promise to return him [c4]. The chest is named only in the passage that recalls it to Musa [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Fir'awn was harsh to a group of people [c2]. God told the mother of Musa to nurse him and, when she was afraid, to put him in the river, and promised to give him back to her [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the command to cast the child away comes joined to a promise, not to fear or grieve [c4]. Another is that God says He cast love upon Musa [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of the mother, the name of the river (the Arabic says yamm, the river or the sea), the date, the years of the oppression, or the name or dynasty of Fir'awn.
- Not established: how the child came to the bank, or how long the chest travelled.
- The verses give no detail on Haman beyond naming him with Fir'awn.
- The enemy of God and of Musa who would take him (20:39) is not named.

chapters.title_en: In the household and back to his mother

claims.statement_en: The household of Fir'awn picked him up so that he would become to them an enemy and a grief; Fir'awn, Haman and their soldiers were sinners.
The wife of Fir'awn said that he was a comfort for her and for him, and told them not to kill him, for perhaps he would benefit them or they might take him as a son; and they did not perceive.
The heart of the mother of Musa became empty; she was about to disclose it, had God not strengthened her heart so that she would be among the believers.
She told his sister to follow him; the sister watched him from a distance while they did not perceive.
God had forbidden wet-nurses to him beforehand; and she asked whether she should direct them to a household who would take care of him for them and be sincere to him.
God returned him to his mother so that she would be comforted and not grieve, and so that she would know that God's promise is true, though most of them do not know.

In another passage God reminds Musa that his sister walked and asked whether she should direct them to someone who would take care of him, and that God returned him to his mother so that she would be comforted and not grieve.

chapters.summary_md: The household of Fir'awn picked up the child, and the wife of Fir'awn said they should not kill him [c1][c2]. His sister followed him, and God returned him to his mother so that she would be comforted [c4][c6].
chapters.body_md:
The household of Fir'awn picked him up so that he would become to them an enemy and a grief [c1]. The wife of Fir'awn said that he was a comfort for her and for him, and told them not to kill him, for perhaps he would benefit them or they might take him as a son [c2].

The heart of the mother of Musa became empty; she was about to disclose it, had God not strengthened her heart [c3]. She told his sister to follow him, and the sister watched him from a distance [c4]. God had forbidden wet-nurses to him beforehand, and his sister asked whether she should direct them to a household who would take care of him for them [c5].

God returned him to his mother so that she would be comforted and not grieve, and so that she would know that God's promise is true [c6]. Another passage recalls this to Musa [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter follows the child from the household of Fir'awn [c1][c2] to the mother's heart [c3], the sister [c4][c5] and the return [c6]. The first passage says it was done so that she would know God's promise is true [c6]; the other recalls it to Musa as a favour [c7]. The Arabic idiom for being comforted is rendered here without the literal image [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The household of Fir'awn picked up the baby, and the wife of Fir'awn said not to kill him [c1][c2]. His sister watched, and God gave him back to his mother so that she would not grieve [c4][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that God strengthened the mother's heart so that she would be among the believers [c3]. Another is that the return is described as a sign that God's promise is true [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the names of the wife of Fir'awn, of Musa's sister, and of the household that took care of him.
- Not established: where in the household of Fir'awn he lived; the verses describe no building.
- Not established: how long he was with his mother before he returned to the household, or how old he was.
- The verse 28:9 does not say whom the wife of Fir'awn addressed beyond the words, and the pronouns are read in more than one way; the draft keeps them close to the Arabic.

stories.title_en: Musa kills a man and flees

chapters.title_en: The man in the city and the flight

claims.statement_en: When Musa reached his full strength and was established, God gave him judgement and knowledge.

He entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people and found a pair of men fighting, one from his party and one from his enemy; the one from his party asked him for help against the one from his enemy; Musa struck him, and ended his life.
He said that this was of the work of Satan, a clear misleading enemy.
He said that he had wronged himself and asked his Lord to forgive him, and He forgave him; He is the forgiving, the merciful.
He said that, for the favour his Lord had shown him, he would never be a supporter of the criminals.
In the morning he was in the city, fearful and watching; the one who had asked for his help the day before cried out to him again, and Musa told him he was clearly misguided.

When he wished to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, a speaker asked whether he wanted to kill him as he had killed a person the day before, and said that he only wanted to be a tyrant in the land and not to be among the reformers.
A man came running from the far end of the city and said that the chiefs were conspiring about him to kill him, and told him to leave, for he was one of the sincere advisers.
Musa left the city fearful and watching, and asked his Lord to save him from the wrongdoing people.

chapters.summary_md: Musa entered the city and found a pair of men fighting; he struck one, who died, and said it was of the work of Satan [c2][c3]. He asked his Lord to forgive him and was forgiven, and when a man warned him that the chiefs were conspiring, he left the city fearful and asked to be saved from the wrongdoing people [c4][c8][c9].
chapters.body_md:
When Musa reached his full strength and was established, God gave him judgement and knowledge [c1]. He entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people and found a pair of men fighting, one from his party and one from his enemy; the one from his party asked him for help, and Musa struck the other, and ended his life [c2]. He said that this was of the work of Satan, a clear misleading enemy [c3]. He asked his Lord to forgive him, and He forgave him [c4], and said that he would never be a supporter of the criminals [c5].

In the morning he was in the city, fearful and watching; the one who had asked for his help the day before cried out to him again, and Musa told him he was clearly misguided [c6]. When he wished to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, a speaker asked whether he wanted to kill him as he had killed a person the day before [c7].

A man came running from the far end of the city and said that the chiefs were conspiring to kill him, and told him to leave [c8]. Musa left the city fearful and watching, and asked his Lord to save him from the wrongdoing people [c9].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter has the deed [c2][c3], the prayer for forgiveness and the resolve [c4][c5], and the flight [c6][c7][c8][c9]. The verses do not say who the speaker of 28:19 is; the word of the speaker is read as that of the enemy or of the one he had helped [c7]. The man who warns him is not named [c8].
chapters.kids_md: Musa went into the city and a man died after Musa struck him [c2]. Musa asked his Lord to forgive him, and God forgave him [c4]. Then a man warned him that the chiefs were planning to hurt him, and Musa left [c8][c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Musa turns to his Lord at once and asks forgiveness, and is forgiven [c4]. Another is that the passage records his wish never to support the criminals after the favour he had been shown [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of the city, how Musa struck the man, or how long the interval was between the days.
- Not established: who spoke in 28:19; interpreters differ and the draft keeps the speaker unnamed.
- Not established: the name of the man who warned him.
- The verses call the pair of men one from his party and one from his enemy; the draft does not name their peoples.
- The verses give Musa's own words about the deed (28:15-16); this draft gives no further verdict on it.

stories.title_en: The call to Musa at the mountain

claims.statement_en: One passage asks the listener whether the account of Musa has reached him, and another asks the same and says his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa.

When Musa had completed the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire on the side of the mountain and told his family to stay, saying that perhaps he would bring them news or a burning brand from it, so that they might warm themselves, or find guidance at the fire.
When he came to it he was called by name: God is his Lord, and he was in the sacred valley of Tuwa, so he was to take off his sandals.
In another passage he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: God is the Lord of the worlds.
In another passage the call says that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, glory be to God, Lord of the worlds, and that God is the Almighty, the Wise.
God told him that He had chosen him, so he should listen to what was revealed; that He is God, there is no god but He, so he should worship Him and establish prayer for His remembrance.

God told him that the Hour is coming, which He almost keeps hidden, so that every soul is recompensed for its striving, and that one who does not believe in it and follows his desire must not turn him from it.
Another passage says of Musa that he was chosen, a messenger and a prophet, and that God called him from the right side of the mountain and brought him near in private converse.

chapters.summary_md: Musa perceived a fire on the side of the mountain, told his family to stay, and went to it [c2]. He was called by name, told that he was in the sacred valley of Tuwa, and told that God had chosen him [c3][c6].
chapters.body_md:
A passage asks the listener whether the account of Musa has reached him [c1]. When Musa had completed the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire on the side of the mountain and told his family to stay, saying that perhaps he would bring them news or a burning brand from it [c2].

When he came to it he was called by name: God is his Lord, and he was in the sacred valley of Tuwa, so he was to take off his sandals [c3]. In another passage he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: God is the Lord of the worlds [c4]. The call in a further passage says that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and that God is the Almighty, the Wise [c5].

God told him that He had chosen him, so he should listen to what was revealed, that He is God, and that he should worship Him and establish prayer [c6]. He told him that the Hour is coming, which He almost keeps hidden [c7]. Another passage says of Musa that he was chosen, a messenger and a prophet, and that God brought him near in private converse [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The call is told in more than one passage with different emphases [c3]. One gives the sandals and the valley of Tuwa [c3], one the tree and the blessed spot [c4], one the blessing on those in and around the fire [c5]. The content of the call is the declaration of who is calling [c3][c4][c5], the choosing of Musa [c6] and the coming of the Hour [c7]. A passage elsewhere sums up his standing [c8].
chapters.kids_md: Musa saw a fire on the side of the mountain and went toward it [c2]. A voice called him by name and said that God had chosen him [c3][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the call first states who is calling and only then gives instructions [c3][c6]. Another is that the passage joins the choosing of Musa with a reminder that every soul is recompensed [c6][c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the exact place or the date, what the fire was, what the tree was, which night, or the names of those with him; the verses say his family and do not list them.
- The caller's voice is described only as a call, and the verses give no further description.
- Whether the words about whoever is in the fire name a particular being is read differently by interpreters; the draft makes no claim.
- The word rendered chosen in 19:51 is read in more than one way (the Arabic differs by a vowel in the variant readings); the page should state which reading it follows.
- Not established: how the different calls relate in time to one another.

claims.statement_en: God asked what was in his right hand, and he said that it was his staff, that he leans on it, beats down leaves with it for his sheep, and has other uses for it.
He was told to throw it, and it became a moving snake; he was told to take it and not to fear, for God would return it to its first state.

In other passages, when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned in flight and did not look back; he was told to come forward and not to fear, that he was secure, and that the messengers do not fear in God's presence.

He was told to put his hand to his side, or into his bosom, and it would come out white without harm, as another sign; these are a pair of proofs from his Lord to Fir'awn and his chiefs, among nine signs; they were a defiantly disobedient people.
He was told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed.

In another passage Musa said that he had killed a person among them and feared they would kill him, and that his brother Harun was more fluent than he in speech, so he asked that he be sent with him as support.
God said that He would strengthen his arm with his brother and give them authority so that they could not reach them; with God's signs, they and those who followed them would be the victors.
Another passage says that out of His mercy God gave him his brother Harun as a prophet.

chapters.summary_md: God asked what was in Musa's right hand, told him to throw it, and it became a moving snake [c1][c2]. He was given another sign and told to go to Fir'awn, and he asked that his brother Harun be sent to help him [c4][c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
God asked what was in his right hand, and Musa said that it was his staff, which he leans on and uses for his sheep [c1]. He was told to throw it, and it became a moving snake; he was told to take it and not to fear [c2]. In other passages he turned in flight when he saw it move, and was told to come forward and not to fear [c3].

He was told to put his hand to his side, or into his bosom, and it would come out white without harm, as another sign; these are a pair of proofs to Fir'awn and his chiefs, among nine signs [c4]. He was told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed [c5].

In another passage Musa said he had killed a person among them and feared they would kill him, and that Harun was more fluent in speech [c6]. God said He would strengthen his arm with his brother and give them authority [c7]. Another passage says God gave him Harun as a prophet [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The signs are given in more than one passage: the staff [c1][c2][c3] and the hand [c4]. The mission to Fir'awn is stated in the same breath [c5]. The request for help is told in one passage [c6], and the answer is given in the next verse [c7]. A further passage names Harun as given a prophet's rank by God's mercy [c8]. The hand comes out white as a sign, and the draft says nothing more about it [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God asked Musa what was in his hand, and he said it was his staff [c1]. When he threw it, it became a moving snake [c2]. God told him to go to Fir'awn, and Musa asked that his brother Harun help him [c5][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Musa is told not to fear before he is sent, and asks for help for his task [c3][c6]. Another is that God answers by giving him his brother as support [c7][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what the nine signs are; the plagues are listed elsewhere and are not assumed to be the nine.
- Not established: what Musa's difficulty in speech was; the verses record only his words about Harun in this chapter.
- Not established: the age of Harun relative to Musa, or where Harun was when he was sent for.
- The verse 27:11 (an exception to the reassurance at 27:10) is in the inventory range but is not used; its grammar and reference are discussed by interpreters and a scholar should decide how to word it. The long prayer of Musa at 20:25-36 lies outside the event's inventory refs and is left to the prophet story.
- The verse 28:32 speaks of drawing the arm to the side as a gesture of fear; the draft keeps the wording general.

stories.title_en: Musa before Fir'awn and the magicians

claims.statement_en: God told Musa and his brother to go with His signs and not to slacken in remembering Him, to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed, and to speak to him a gentle word, so that perhaps he would remember or fear.
They said that they feared he would hasten against them or transgress; God said they were not to fear, for He was with them both, hearing and seeing.
In another passage God called Musa to go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Fir'awn, asking whether they would not be mindful.

Musa said that he feared they would deny him, that his chest would be straitened and his tongue not free, and asked God to send to Harun; he said they also had a charge against him, so he feared they would kill him.

God said no, and told them both to go with His signs, for He was with them, listening; they were to say that they were the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and to ask that he send the Children of Israel with them.

They were to say that they were the messengers of his Lord, that he should send the Children of Israel with them and not torment them, that they had come with a sign from his Lord, and that peace is on the one who follows the guidance; it had been revealed to them that the punishment is for one who denies and turns away.
Fir'awn asked who the Lord of them both was; Musa said that their Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided.
Fir'awn asked about the earlier generations, and Musa said that knowledge of them is with his Lord in a record; his Lord neither errs nor forgets.

In another passage Fir'awn asked what the Lord of the worlds is, and Musa answered that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Lord of their forefathers, and the Lord of the east and the west and what is between them.
Fir'awn said to those around him that their messenger who had been sent to them was mad, and told Musa that if he took a god other than him, he would make him one of the imprisoned.
Another passage says that Musa was told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed, and to ask whether he would purify himself, and that Musa would guide him to his Lord so that he would fear.

chapters.summary_md: God told Musa and his brother to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed, and speak to him a gentle word, and said He was with them, hearing and seeing [c1][c2]. Fir'awn asked who their Lord was, and Musa answered that He gave everything its form and then guided [c7].
chapters.body_md:
God told Musa and his brother to go with His signs and not to slacken in remembering Him, to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed, and to speak to him a gentle word, so that perhaps he would remember or fear [c1]. They said that they feared he would hasten against them or transgress; God said they were not to fear, for He was with them both, hearing and seeing [c2].

In another passage God called Musa to go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Fir'awn [c3]. Musa said that he feared they would deny him and asked God to send to Harun [c4]. God said no, and told them both to go with His signs, for He was with them, listening [c5]. They were to say that they had come with a sign from his Lord and that he should send the Children of Israel with them and not torment them [c6].

Fir'awn asked who the Lord of them both was; Musa said that their Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided [c7]. Fir'awn asked about the earlier generations, and Musa said that knowledge of them is with his Lord in a record [c8]. In another passage Fir'awn asked what the Lord of the worlds is, and Musa answered that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them [c9]. Fir'awn said their messenger was mad, and threatened Musa with prison if he took a god other than him [c10]. Another passage tells Musa to go to Fir'awn and ask whether he would purify himself [c11].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter follows the sending [c1][c2][c3][c4][c5][c11], the words they were to say [c6] and the exchange with Fir'awn [c7][c8][c9][c10]. The sending is told in different passages with different emphasis, one on gentle speech [c1] and one on Musa's fears [c4]. The exchange is told in different forms, with questions about the Lord of them both [c7] and about the Lord of the worlds [c9]. The Arabic of 20:50, rendered here gave everything its form, has more than one possible rendering for scholarly review [c7].
chapters.kids_md: God told Musa and his brother to go to Fir'awn and to speak gently to him [c1]. God said He was with them, hearing and seeing [c2]. Fir'awn asked who their Lord was, and Musa answered [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the sending begins with a command to speak gently, even to one who has transgressed [c1]. Another is that Musa's fear is met with a promise that God is with them [c2][c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the meeting took place, how many times it happened, or which passage describes the first meeting.
- Not established: the personal name or period of this Fir'awn. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification with a named ruler of Egypt.
- The wording of 20:50 (everything its form) has more than one possible rendering.
- The passages 20:42-52 and 26:10-29 are read as one sending on matching wording (an inference); the details differ.
- Some passages in the inventory range (7:103-126, 10:75-82) are not used in this shorter record; a reviewer should decide whether to add them.

claims.statement_en: Musa asked whether Fir'awn would still not listen if he brought something clear; Fir'awn said to bring it, if he was of the truthful.
Musa threw his staff and it was a clear serpent; he drew out his hand and it was white to those looking.

Fir'awn told the chiefs around him that this was a learned magician who wanted to drive them from their land with his magic, and asked what they commanded; they said to delay him and his brother and to send gatherers into the cities to bring every learned magician.

In another passage Fir'awn asked whether he had come to drive them out of their land with his magic, said that they would bring magic like it, and asked for an appointment; Musa said the appointment was the day of the festival, and that the people were to be gathered at forenoon.

The magicians were gathered for the appointed time of a known day; the people were asked whether they would gather, so that they might follow the magicians if they were the victors; the magicians asked Fir'awn whether they would have a reward if they were the victors, and he said yes, and that they would be among those brought near.
In another passage Fir'awn turned away, gathered his plan and came; Musa told them not to invent a lie against God, lest He destroy them with a punishment, for whoever invents has failed.
Musa told them to throw what they were going to throw; they threw their ropes and staffs and said that by the might of Fir'awn they were the victors.
In another passage they asked whether he would throw or they would be the first; he said they should throw, and their ropes and staffs seemed to him, from their magic, to be moving.

Musa felt fear within himself; God said that he should not fear, that he was the uppermost, and that he should throw what was in his right hand and it would swallow what they had made, for it was only the trick of a magician.
Musa threw his staff and it swallowed what they fabricated.
The magicians were cast down in prostration; they said that they believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun.

Fir'awn said that they had believed him before he gave them permission, that he was their chief who had taught them magic, and threatened to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and to crucify them.
They said that there was no harm, for they would return to their Lord; they hoped He would forgive their faults because they were the first of the believers.

In another passage they said that they would never prefer him over the clear proofs that had come to them and over Him who created them, and that he could decree what he decreed, for he decreed only for this worldly life; they had believed so that their Lord would forgive their faults and the magic to which he had compelled them, for God is better and more lasting.

chapters.summary_md: Musa threw his staff and it was a clear serpent, and Fir'awn called him a learned magician and gathered the magicians [c2][c3][c5]. When Musa threw his staff it swallowed what they had made, and the magicians were cast down in prostration, saying that they believed in the Lord of Musa and Harun [c10][c11].
chapters.body_md:
Musa asked whether Fir'awn would still not listen if he brought something clear, and Fir'awn said to bring it [c1]. Musa threw his staff and it was a clear serpent; he drew out his hand and it was white to those looking [c2]. Fir'awn told the chiefs that this was a learned magician who wanted to drive them from their land, and they said to send gatherers into the cities to bring every learned magician [c3].

The magicians were gathered for the appointed time of a known day [c5]. In another passage Musa named the day of the festival for the appointment [c4], and Fir'awn gathered his plan and came [c6]. Musa told them to throw what they were going to throw, and they threw their ropes and staffs and said that by the might of Fir'awn they were the victors [c7]. Musa felt fear within himself, and God said that he should not fear, for he was the uppermost [c9]. Musa threw his staff and it swallowed what they fabricated [c10].

The magicians were cast down in prostration; they said that they believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun [c11]. Fir'awn said that they had believed him before he gave them permission, and threatened to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and to crucify them [c12]. They said that there was no harm, for they would return to their Lord [c13], and in another passage that they would never prefer him over the clear proofs and over Him who created them [c14].
chapters.deep_md: The contest is told in passages that overlap and differ: the appointment and the day of the festival [c4][c5], the throwing [c7][c8], the fear of Musa [c9] and the swallowing of what they had made [c10]. The magicians' belief [c11], Fir'awn's threat [c12] and their reply [c13][c14] close it. The verses do not narrate what became of the magicians after the threat [c12][c13]. One passage records God's word to Musa at his fear [c9].
chapters.kids_md: Musa threw his staff and it became a snake [c2]. Fir'awn gathered the magicians, and they threw their ropes and staffs [c5][c7]. Musa's staff swallowed what they had made, and the magicians bowed down and said they believed in the Lord of Musa and Harun [c10][c11].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that Musa's fear is met with a word from God, not to fear [c9]. Another is that the magicians answer the threat by saying that they will return to their Lord and hope for forgiveness [c13].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how many magicians there were, the place and date of the festival, or the nature of their ropes and staffs beyond that they seemed to move.
- Not established: whether the descriptions of the throwing in 26:43-45 and 20:65-69 describe separate moments.
- The fate of the magicians after the threat is not narrated.
- Not established: how the white hand of 26:33 relates to the other signs; the draft says nothing more about it.
- The verses 20:62-64 (the magicians' private talk) are in the inventory range but not used in this shorter chapter.

stories.title_en: The signs sent upon the people of Fir'awn

chapters.title_en: The signs sent upon the people of Fir'awn

claims.statement_en: God seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and a shortage of fruits, so that they might remember.
When good came to them they said it was theirs, and if evil struck them they took Musa and those with him as an omen; God says that their omen is with Him, but most of them do not know.
They said that whatever sign he brought to bewitch them, they would not believe him.
God sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as signs in detail; they were arrogant and a criminal people.

When the plague fell upon them they said to Musa that he should call upon his Lord by the covenant He had made with him; if he removed the plague they would believe him and send the Children of Israel with him.
When God removed the plague from them for a term which they were to reach, they broke their word.
God says that He gave Musa nine clear signs, and that Fir'awn said to him that he thought him bewitched.
Musa was told to put his hand into his bosom and it would come out white without harm, among nine signs to Fir'awn and his people, who were a defiantly disobedient people.

chapters.summary_md: God seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and a shortage of fruits, and then sent the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as signs [c1][c4]. When the plague fell on them they asked Musa to call upon his Lord, but broke their word once it was removed [c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
God seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and a shortage of fruits, so that they might remember [c1]. When good came to them they said it was theirs, and if evil struck them they took Musa and those with him as an omen; God says their omen is with Him [c2]. They said that whatever sign he brought, they would not believe him [c3].

God sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as signs in detail; they were arrogant and a criminal people [c4]. When the plague fell upon them they said to Musa that he should call upon his Lord, and that if he removed it they would believe and send the Children of Israel with him [c5]. When God removed it for a term which they were to reach, they broke their word [c6].

God says that He gave Musa nine clear signs [c7], and that among nine signs Musa was told to put his hand into his bosom and it would come out white without harm [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The chapter has the first seizing [c1][c2][c3], the signs in detail [c4], the people's promise and the breaking of it [c5][c6], and verses that name nine signs [c7][c8]. The Quran lists signs by name here [c4] and speaks of nine elsewhere [c7][c8]; it does not say that the listed signs are among the nine or that they are the nine. The omen is placed with God and not with Musa [c2].
chapters.kids_md: God sent hard times and signs on the people of Fir'awn so that they might remember [c1][c4]. They asked Musa to pray to his Lord, but when the trouble went away they broke their word [c5][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the people credited good to themselves and blamed Musa for harm [c2]. Another is that a promise made in trouble was broken when the trouble was lifted [c5][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the order, length and number of the plagues beyond those named in 7:133, or how many years of drought are meant.
- The Arabic words for the flood (tufan) and the lice (qummal) are understood in more than one way; a scholar should decide the renderings.
- Not established: what the nine signs are; the signs named here are not assumed to be among them.
- Not established: how long the term was after which the people broke their word.
- The verses do not say how Musa's prayer was made or in what words.
