chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat show Satan's words changing once the human being obeyed [c2]. Another is that the ayat describe the end of the wrongdoers as the Fire [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who those shortly before them were, or what they did; the ayah says they tasted the evil result of their conduct.
- Not established: which human being is meant in the comparison with Satan; the ayah speaks of the human being in general.
- Not established: when or where the words of Satan were spoken.
- The ayat do not say how this comparison is tied to the particular events of the expulsion.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the expulsion, the party involved and the sequence of events. None is used in this draft.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the party, Nadir, and the place and date of the expulsion; the inventory title itself says the identification is from later tradition.
59:7 (the allocation of what was returned) is not drafted because it is legal in kind.
The link of the hypocrites' promise (59:11-14) to the same event comes from the event inventory; the ayat do not name the event.

claims.statement_en: God has helped the believers in many places and on the day of Hunayn, when their great number pleased them but did not avail them at all; the earth, for all its breadth, closed in on them, and then they turned back, retreating.
Then God sent down His tranquillity on His Messenger and on the believers, sent down forces they did not see and punished those who disbelieved; that is the recompense of the disbelievers.
Then, after that, God turns in mercy to whom He wills; God is Forgiving, Merciful.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat say that on the day of Hunayn the great number of the believers did not avail them, and they turned back [c1]. God then sent down His tranquillity on His Messenger and on the believers, sent down forces they did not see, and turns in mercy to whom He wills [c2][c3].
chapters.body_md:
God has helped the believers in many places and on the day of Hunayn, when their great number pleased them but did not avail them at all [c1]. The earth, for all its breadth, closed in on them, and then they turned back, retreating [c1].

Then God sent down His tranquillity on His Messenger and on the believers, sent down forces they did not see and punished those who disbelieved; that is the recompense of the disbelievers [c2]. Then, after that, God turns in mercy to whom He wills; God is Forgiving, Merciful [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat make a contrast between the number that pleased the believers and the help that came from God [c1][c2]. They name what followed the retreat: tranquillity, forces that were not seen, and punishment of those who disbelieved [c2]. The last ayah turns to God's mercy for whom He wills [c3].
chapters.kids_md: On the day of Hunayn the believers were pleased with how many they were, but that did not help them [c1]. God sent calm and forces they could not see, and He is Forgiving, Merciful [c2][c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat set pride in great numbers beside the help that came from God [c1][c2]. Another is that the passage ends with God's mercy to whom He wills [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how many the believers were, how many their opponents, where the valley or the place was, or the date; the ayat name only the day.
- Not established: who retreated and for how long, or how the forces they did not see acted.
- Not established: what the punishment of those who disbelieved was, or who they were.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the opponents, the places and the commanders. The detailed accounts rest on biographical and historical sources (sira) and on later reports that the repository does not yet hold.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the day of Hunayn, the retreat and what followed. None is used in this draft.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Hawazin, Thaqif and Taif, and the names of the commanders and the place.
The ayat give no casualties, no dates and no numbers; none are given in this draft.
The chapter on this day in the prophet drafts (content/stories) is separate; this event draft stays inside its own refs.

stories.title_en: The hardship and the call to go out

claims.statement_en: The believers were asked what was wrong with them that when they were told to go out in God's way they clung heavily to the earth, and whether they were content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter; the enjoyment of this life in the Hereafter is little.
If they did not go out, God would punish them with a painful punishment and replace them with another people, and they would not harm Him at all; God has power over all things.
They were told to go out, light and heavy, and to strive with their wealth and themselves in God's way; that is better for them, if they only knew.

Had it been a near gain and an easy journey, they would have followed you, but the distance seemed far to them; they will swear by God that, had they been able, they would have gone out with you, destroying themselves, and God knows that they are liars.

chapters.summary_md: The believers were asked why they clung heavily to the earth when told to go out in God's way, and warned of a painful punishment and replacement if they did not go [c1][c2]. They were told to go out, light and heavy, and to strive with their wealth and themselves, and the ayat say that some would swear they could not [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md:
The believers were asked what was wrong with them that when they were told to go out in God's way they clung heavily to the earth [c1]. They were asked whether they were content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter; the enjoyment of this life in the Hereafter is little [c1].

If they did not go out, God would punish them with a painful punishment and replace them with another people, and they would not harm Him at all; God has power over all things [c2].

They were told to go out, light and heavy, and to strive with their wealth and themselves in God's way; that is better for them, if they only knew [c3]. Had it been a near gain and an easy journey, they would have followed you, but the distance seemed far to them [c4]. They will swear by God that, had they been able, they would have gone out with you, destroying themselves, and God knows that they are liars [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat move from a question to a warning and then to a command, and end with a description of those who give excuses [c1][c2][c3][c4]. The phrase light and heavy is read in more than one way and is left as it stands [c3].
chapters.kids_md: The believers were told to go out in God's way, and some held back [c1]. The ayat say that going out and striving is better for them, if they knew [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat set the enjoyment of this life beside the Hereafter [c1]. Another is that the ayat describe excuses as sworn by those who did not go [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: where the believers were told to go, against whom, when, or how far the distance was; the ayat name no place or enemy.
- Not established: who the ones who swore were, or how many.
- Not established: what the light and heavy refer to; commentators read the phrase in more than one way.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name Tabuk, the opponents and the place and the season of the journey. The detailed accounts rest on biographical and historical sources (sira) and on later reports that the repository does not yet hold.

chapters.title_en: Those who stayed behind, and those excused

claims.statement_en: Those who were left behind rejoiced at staying behind the Messenger of God and disliked to strive with their wealth and themselves in God's way; they said: do not go out in the heat; they were told that the Fire of Hell is hotter, if they understood.
Let them laugh a little and weep much, as recompense for what they used to earn.

If God brought the Messenger back to a party of them and they asked leave to go out, he was to say: you will never go out with me and will never fight an enemy with me; you were content to sit the first time, so sit with those who stay behind.

When a surah was sent down telling them to believe in God and to strive with His Messenger, those of them with means asked leave and said: leave us to be with those who sit; they were content to be with those who stay behind, and their hearts were sealed, so they do not understand.

But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and themselves; for them are the good things, and they are the successful; God has prepared for them gardens with rivers beneath them, abiding there; that is the great triumph.
The excuse-makers among the desert nomads came to be given leave, and those who lied to God and His Messenger stayed behind; a painful punishment will strike those of them who disbelieve.
There is no blame on the weak, the sick, or those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to God and His Messenger; there is no way against those who do good; God is Forgiving, Merciful.

There is no blame either on those who came to him for mounts, and he said that he found nothing to carry them on; they turned away with tears flowing from sorrow that they could not find anything to spend.
The blame is only on those who ask leave while they are rich, content to be with those who stay behind; God has sealed their hearts, so they do not know.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat say that those who were left behind rejoiced at staying behind the Messenger of God, and that those of them with means asked leave to sit [c1][c4]. They say that there is no blame on the weak, the sick and those who find nothing to spend, and that the Messenger and those with him strove [c5][c7].
chapters.body_md:
Those who were left behind rejoiced at staying behind the Messenger of God and disliked to strive with their wealth and themselves in God's way [c1]. They said: do not go out in the heat; they were told that the Fire of Hell is hotter, if they understood [c1]. Let them laugh a little and weep much, as recompense for what they used to earn [c2].

If God brought the Messenger back to a party of them and they asked leave to go out, he was to say: you will never go out with me and will never fight an enemy with me; you were content to sit the first time, so sit with those who stay behind [c3]. When a surah was sent down telling them to believe in God and to strive with His Messenger, those of them with means asked leave and said: leave us to be with those who sit; their hearts were sealed, so they do not understand [c4].

But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and themselves; for them are the good things, and they are the successful; God has prepared for them gardens with rivers beneath them, abiding there; that is the great triumph [c5]. The excuse-makers among the desert nomads came to be given leave, and those who lied to God and His Messenger stayed behind; a painful punishment will strike those of them who disbelieve [c6].

There is no blame on the weak, the sick, or those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to God and His Messenger; there is no way against those who do good; God is Forgiving, Merciful [c7]. There is no blame either on those who came to him for mounts, and he said that he found nothing to carry them on; they turned away with tears flowing from sorrow that they could not find anything to spend [c8]. The blame is only on those who ask leave while they are rich, content to be with those who stay behind; God has sealed their hearts, so they do not know [c9].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat separate those who stayed behind by reason: some are condemned for choosing to sit, and others are cleared because they could not go [c4][c7][c8][c9]. The ayah on the Fire of Hell answers the excuse about the heat with a comparison [c1]. The ayat that describe the Messenger and those who believed with him say what is prepared for them [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Some people stayed behind and were glad, saying the heat was too great [c1]. The ayat say that the weak and the sick and those who had nothing to spend are not to blame [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat tell apart those who chose to sit from those who could not go and were sorry about it [c7][c8][c9]. Another is that the ayat set the excuse of the heat beside the Fire of Hell [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who stayed behind by name or how many; the ayat describe them and do not name them.
- Not established: when the surah was sent down that called them to believe and strive, or which surah is meant.
- Not established: how the Messenger answered those who came for mounts beyond the words the ayah records.
- Not established: what the day of the return to a party of them was.

chapters.title_en: The three who were left behind

claims.statement_en: God turned in mercy to the Prophet and the emigrants and the helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a party of them had almost swerved; then He turned to them; He is compassionate and merciful to them.

God turned also to the three who were left behind, until the earth, for all its breadth, closed in on them and their own souls closed in on them and they realised that there is no refuge from God except in Him; then He turned to them so that they might turn; God is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat say that God turned in mercy to the Prophet and the emigrants and the helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship [c1]. They say that God turned also to the three who were left behind, until the earth closed in on them, and that He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful [c2].
chapters.body_md:
God turned in mercy to the Prophet and the emigrants and the helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a party of them had almost swerved [c1]. Then He turned to them; He is compassionate and merciful to them [c1].

God turned also to the three who were left behind, until the earth, for all its breadth, closed in on them and their own souls closed in on them [c2]. They realised that there is no refuge from God except in Him; then He turned to them so that they might turn; God is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat name the hour of hardship and say the hearts of a party almost swerved before God turned to them [c1]. The three who were left behind are given a short account of their distress: the earth closing in, their own souls closing in, and the realisation that refuge is only with God [c2].
chapters.kids_md: God turned in mercy to the Prophet and the believers in a time of hardship [c1]. He also turned to three who had been left behind, when the earth felt too small for them [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat tie the hour of hardship to God's turning in mercy [c1]. Another is that the three found that there is no refuge from God except in Him, and God turned to them so that they might turn [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the three were by name, why they were left behind, or how long it lasted.
- Not established: what the hour of hardship was or how long it was; the ayah names it as the hour of hardship.
- Not established: whose hearts almost swerved, or why.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the three and the details of their story.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the journey, the preparations, those who stayed behind and the three. None is used in this draft.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: Tabuk, the Byzantines, and the date and route of the journey; the inventory title itself says the identification is from later tradition.
Not drafted: 9:40 (told in the draft for the emigration), 9:43-59 (the leave given, and the hypocrites' excuses, offerings and complaints), 9:84-85 and 9:94-96; these are for a later pass.
9:43 addresses the Prophet about leave given to those who stayed behind; it needs a scholar's wording before it is drafted and is left out for that reason.
The ayat give no numbers, no dates and no commanders; none are given in this draft.

chapters.title_en: When the help and the victory come

claims.statement_en: The surah speaks of the time when the help of God and the victory come.
The one addressed will see people entering God's religion in crowds.
He is told to glorify his Lord with praise and to ask His forgiveness, for He is ever accepting of repentance.

chapters.summary_md: The surah speaks of the time when the help of God and the victory come, and the one addressed sees people entering God's religion in crowds [c1][c2]. He is told to glorify his Lord with praise and to ask His forgiveness, for He is ever accepting of repentance [c3].
chapters.body_md:
The surah speaks of the time when the help of God and the victory come [c1]. The one addressed will see people entering God's religion in crowds [c2].

He is told to glorify his Lord with praise and to ask His forgiveness, for He is ever accepting of repentance [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The surah is built as a condition and a result: when the help and the victory come, and people enter in crowds, then glorify and ask forgiveness [c1][c2][c3]. It is stated as something that will come, and does not give the time [c1].
chapters.kids_md: God says that when His help and the victory come, and people enter His religion in crowds [c1][c2]. Then He tells the one addressed to praise his Lord and ask His forgiveness, because He accepts repentance [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the surah answers help and victory with praise and a request for forgiveness [c1][c3]. Another is that it closes on God as one who accepts repentance [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which victory is meant, where, when, or what led to it; the surah names neither the place nor the time.
- Not established: who the people entering in crowds were, or how many.
- Not established: how the surah is related in time to other events, or whether it speaks of one event or of a general promise.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the victory with a particular conquest, and the date and circumstances of the surah. The detailed accounts rest on biographical and historical sources (sira) and on later reports that the repository does not yet hold.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, on the circumstances of this surah and on the victory it is linked with. None is used in this draft.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the particular conquest and its place and date.
The word translated 'victory' (al-fath) is used in other surahs of other events; this draft does not equate them.

stories.title_en: The owner of a pair of gardens

chapters.title_en: A man with a pair of gardens

claims.statement_en: The ayah tells that a similitude (mathal) is to be struck for them: a pair of men, one of whom God gave a pair of vine gardens, surrounded with date palms, with crops between them.
Both gardens gave their produce and held back none of it, and God caused a river to flow through them.

The owner had fruit, and he told his companion, as he talked with him, that he had more wealth and a stronger following; he entered his garden while wronging himself and said that he did not think it would ever perish, that he did not think the final hour would come, and that if he were sent back to his Lord he would find something better than it.

His companion answered, as he talked with him, by asking whether he had disbelieved in the one who created him from dust, then from a drop, then shaped him as a man; he said that for his part God is his Lord and that he associates no one with his Lord.

The companion added that the owner should have said, on entering his garden, that it is as God wills and that there is no power except with God, though he saw that the companion had less wealth and fewer children.

The companion said that it might be that his Lord would give him something better than the owner's garden and would send something from the sky upon the garden so that it became bare, slippery ground, or that its water would sink into the earth so that the owner could not seek it.
The owner's fruit was encompassed, and he regretted what he had spent on the garden while it lay fallen on its trellises, and he said that he wished he had associated no one with his Lord.
The owner had no group to help him besides God and could not help himself; there, authority belongs to God, who is best in reward and best in outcome.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat give a similitude of a man to whom God gave a pair of gardens [c1][c2]. He spoke to his companion of his wealth and did not think the gardens would perish, and he later regretted what he had spent on them after his fruit was encompassed [c3][c7].
chapters.body_md:
The ayat tell that a similitude is to be struck for them: a pair of men, one of whom God gave a pair of vine gardens with date palms around them and crops between them [c1]. Both gardens gave their produce, and God caused a river to flow through them [c2].

The owner told his companion, as they talked, that he had more wealth and a stronger following [c3]. He entered his garden while wronging himself and said that he did not think it would ever perish, or that the final hour would come [c3]. He added that if he were sent back to his Lord he would find something better [c3].

The companion asked the owner whether he had disbelieved in the one who created him from dust, then from a drop, then shaped him as a man [c4]. He said that God is his Lord and that he associates no one with his Lord [c4]. He said the owner should have said, on entering his garden, that it is as God wills and that there is no power except with God [c5]. He said it might be that his Lord would give him something better than that garden, and would send something from the sky upon it, or that its water would sink into the earth [c6].

The owner's fruit was encompassed, and he regretted what he had spent on the garden while it lay fallen on its trellises, and he said that he wished he had associated no one with his Lord [c7]. He had no group to help him besides God, and he could not help himself [c8]. There, authority belongs to God, who is best in reward and best in outcome [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The text reports the owner's words and the companion's replies as speech and says nothing further about either man beyond what they say [c3][c4]. The ayah says the owner entered his garden while wronging himself, so his words about the garden are placed in that state [c3]. The thing sent from the sky is called husban in the Arabic, and the ayat do not explain what it would be [c6].
chapters.kids_md: A man had a pair of gardens with vines and date palms, and a river flowing through them [c1][c2]. His companion told him that he should have said that it is as God wills [c5]. Later his fruit was encompassed, and the garden lay fallen on its trellises [c7]. The man then wished that he had associated no one with his Lord [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the companion's reply links the owner's confidence in his wealth to remembering God, since he said the owner should have spoken of God's will on entering his garden [c5]. Another reading is that the ayat end with the owner wishing he had associated no one with his Lord, and with authority belonging to God [c7][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the pair of men were, where they lived or when; the ayat give no names, places, times or ages.
- Not established: how the fruit was encompassed, or what was sent from the sky; the word husban in 18:40 is left open here.
- Not established: whether the ayat describe a particular past event or are only an example. The ayah itself calls the passage a similitude (mathal), and this draft keeps to that.
- The senses of nafar in 18:34 (followers, kin or a group) and of walaya in 18:44 (authority or protection) are left open in this draft.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified for this similitude; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to it.
The wording of husban (18:40), nafar (18:34) and walaya (18:44) is left open; a scholar should choose how the page words them.

chapters.title_en: The garden and the oath to pick it early

claims.statement_en: God says that He tried them as He tried the owners of the garden, when they swore that they would pick its fruit in the morning and made no exception.
A visitation from their Lord went round the garden while they slept, and by morning it had become like al-sarim.

In the morning they called to one another to go early to their tilth if they meant to pick the fruit; they set off whispering to one another that no poor person should enter it that day; and they went early as people who thought themselves able.
When they saw the garden they said that they must have lost their way, and then said that rather they were deprived.
The one among them called awsatuhum said that he had told them, asking why they did not glorify God, and they said glory to their Lord, they had been wrongdoers.

They turned to blame one another and said woe to them, they had been transgressors, and that it might be that their Lord would give them something better in exchange, since they turned to their Lord in hope.
The ayah states that such is the punishment, and that the punishment of the hereafter is greater, if they knew.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat say that God tried them as He tried the owners of a garden, who swore to pick its fruit in the morning and made no exception [c1]. A visitation from their Lord went round the garden while they slept, and afterwards they said they had been wrongdoers [c2][c5].
chapters.body_md:
God says that He tried them as He tried the owners of the garden, when they swore that they would pick its fruit in the morning and made no exception [c1]. A visitation from their Lord went round the garden while they slept, and by morning it had become like al-sarim [c2].

In the morning they called to one another to go early to their tilth if they meant to pick the fruit [c3]. They set off whispering that no poor person should enter it that day, and they went early as people who thought themselves able [c3]. When they saw the garden they said that they must have lost their way, and then that rather they were deprived [c4].

The one among them called awsatuhum said that he had told them, and asked why they did not glorify God [c5]. They said glory to their Lord, they had been wrongdoers [c5]. They turned to blame one another and said woe to them, they had been transgressors [c6]. They said it might be that their Lord would give them something better in exchange, since they turned to their Lord in hope [c6].

The ayah states that such is the punishment, and that the punishment of the hereafter is greater, if they knew [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passage gives the owners' oath, their whispered plan and their later speech, and it reports all of this as their own words and actions [c1][c3][c6]. The ayat do not say what the visitation was, only that it came from their Lord and went round the garden while they slept [c2]. The closing ayah states a comparison between the punishment seen here and the punishment of the hereafter [c7].
chapters.kids_md: Some owners of a garden promised to pick its fruit early in the morning, and they made no exception [c1]. They had quietly agreed that no poor person should come in [c3]. A visitation came from their Lord while they slept, and in the morning the garden was changed [c2]. Then they said they had been wrongdoers, and that they hoped their Lord would give them something better [c5][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat connect what happened to the garden with the oath made without an exception and with the plan to keep a poor person out [c1][c3]. Another reading is that the owners are shown turning to their Lord in hope after they admitted they had been wrongdoers [c5][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the owners were, where the garden was, what it grew, how many of them there were, or when this happened; the ayat give none of this.
- Not established: what the visitation was or how it reached the garden.
- Not established: whether the ayat report a past event or give an example. The ayat do not use the word mathal here: they say that God tried them as He tried the owners of the garden. The classification of this item as a parable is the platform's, not the text's.
- Not established: who is meant by 'them' at the start of 68:17; the pronoun points to people addressed earlier in the surah, outside the ayat cited here.
- The words al-sarim (68:20, cut away or dark), awsatuhum (68:28, best or most moderate of them) and hard (68:25, resolve, prevention or anger) are read in more than one way; this draft leaves them open.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this passage.
The wording of al-sarim (68:20), awsatuhum (68:28) and hard (68:25) is left open; a scholar should choose how the page words them.

stories.title_en: The people of the town and the messengers

claims.statement_en: The ayah commands that a similitude be struck for them: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.
God sent to them two messengers, and they called them liars, so He strengthened them with a third, and they said that they were sent to them.

The people replied that the messengers were only humans like themselves and that the Merciful had sent nothing down, and that the messengers were only lying; the messengers said that their Lord knows that they were sent, and that their duty was only the clear delivery of the message.

The people said that they took the messengers as an evil omen and that they would stone them and a painful punishment would touch them from them; the messengers said that their omen was with them, asking whether it was because they were reminded, and said that rather they were a people who transgress.
A man came running from the farthest part of the city and told his people to follow the messengers, who ask no wage and are guided.

He said that he had no reason not to worship the one who created him and to whom they will be returned, and asked whether he should take gods besides Him whose intercession would not help him if the Merciful willed harm for him, for then he would be clearly in error.
He declared that he believed in their Lord and told them to hear him.
He was told to enter the garden, and he said that he wished his people knew how his Lord had forgiven him and made him one of the honoured.
God sent down no host from the sky upon his people after him and was not one to send one down; it was only one cry, and at once they were extinguished.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat tell that a similitude is struck of the companions of the town, to whom messengers came and were called liars [c1][c2]. A man came running from the farthest part of the city and told his people to follow the messengers, and afterwards one cry left his people extinguished [c5][c9].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah commands that a similitude be struck for them: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it [c1]. God sent to them two messengers, and they called them liars, so He strengthened them with a third [c2]. They said that they were sent to them [c2].

The people replied that the messengers were only humans like themselves, that the Merciful had sent nothing down, and that the messengers were only lying [c3]. The messengers said that their Lord knows that they were sent, and that their duty was only the clear delivery of the message [c3]. The people said that they took them as an evil omen and that they would stone them [c4]. The messengers said that their omen was with them, and that rather they were a people who transgress [c4].

A man came running from the farthest part of the city and told his people to follow the messengers, who ask no wage and are guided [c5]. He said that he had no reason not to worship the one who created him and to whom they will be returned [c6]. He asked whether he should take gods besides Him, whose intercession would not help him, and said that he would then be clearly in error [c6]. He declared that he believed in their Lord and told them to hear him [c7].

He was told to enter the garden, and he said that he wished his people knew how his Lord had forgiven him and made him one of the honoured [c8]. God sent down no host from the sky upon his people after him [c9]. It was only one cry, and at once they were extinguished [c9].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat use the word town for where the messengers came (36:13) and the word city for where the man came from (36:20) [c1][c5]. The messengers are first given as a pair, and then the ayah adds that God strengthened them with a third, without saying who the third was [c2]. The man's speech runs from his call to follow the messengers to his declaration of belief, and the ayat then report what he was told and what he said [c5][c6][c7][c8].
chapters.kids_md: Messengers came to a town, and the people said that they were only humans like themselves [c1][c3]. A man ran from the farthest part of the city and told his people to follow the messengers [c5]. He said that he believed in their Lord [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat stress that the messengers' duty was only the clear delivery of the message [c3]. Another reading is that the man's words link following the messengers with their asking no wage and being guided [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the name of the town, of the messengers, of the man or of his people, or when and where this happened; none is given.
- Not established: who the third messenger was, or what it means that the pair were strengthened.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the town, the messengers and the man are given names in later sources; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- Not established: whom the man addressed with the words 'so hear me' (36:25), or who told him to enter the garden (36:26); the ayat do not say.
- The ayah itself says that a similitude is to be struck (36:13). That this item is grouped with the parables is the platform's classification, and the ayat do not say whether the account describes a particular past event.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this passage.
The wordings to check first: the passive 'he was told' in 36:26 and the addressee of 36:25.

stories.title_en: The grain that grows seven spikes

claims.statement_en: The ayah gives a similitude: those who spend their wealth in the way of God are like a grain that grew seven spikes, with a hundred grains in each spike.
The ayah adds that God multiplies for whom He wills, and that God is vast and knowing.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens those who spend their wealth in the way of God to a grain that grew seven spikes, with a hundred grains in each spike [c1]. It adds that God multiplies for whom He wills [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah gives a similitude [c1]. Those who spend their wealth in the way of God are like a grain that grew seven spikes, and in each spike there is a hundred grains [c1]. The ayah adds that God multiplies for whom He wills, and that God is vast and knowing [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah names what is likened (spending wealth in the way of God) and what it is likened to (a grain and its growth) [c1]. It states the figures as part of the similitude and then says separately that God multiplies for whom He wills [c1][c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that spending wealth in the way of God is like a grain that grows seven spikes [c1]. In each spike there are a hundred grains [c1]. God gives more to whom He wills [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the similitude presents spending in the way of God as growth, as a single grain grows into many [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah closes by saying that God is vast and knowing [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what the ayah counts as spending in the way of God beyond its own words, or when and how the multiplying takes place.
- Not established: whether the figures in the similitude are to be read as exact quantities or as a picture of growth.
- The ayah itself calls the passage a similitude (mathal).
- The Arabic word sunbula is rendered 'spike' in this draft; a scholar may prefer another word for the part of the plant that holds the grains.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The word chosen for sunbula and the sense of 'multiplies for whom He wills' are for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The smooth rock with soil on it

chapters.title_en: The smooth rock with soil on it

claims.statement_en: The ayah tells those who believe not to cancel their charity with reminders of favours and with hurt, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in God and the last day.
His similitude is that of a smooth rock with soil on it; a heavy rain hits it and leaves it bare, and they have no power over anything they have earned.
The ayah ends by saying that God does not guide the disbelieving people.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah tells those who believe not to cancel their charity with reminders of favours and with hurt [c1]. It likens the one who spends to be seen by people to a smooth rock with soil on it that a heavy rain leaves bare [c1][c2].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah tells those who believe not to cancel their charity with reminders of favours and with hurt [c1]. This is like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in God and the last day [c1].

His similitude is that of a smooth rock with soil on it [c2]. A heavy rain hits it and leaves it bare, and they have no power over anything they have earned [c2]. The ayah ends by saying that God does not guide the disbelieving people [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives the comparison in steps: the believers are told what not to do, the one who spends to be seen is described, and then his similitude is given [c1][c2]. The rock and the soil are the picture, and the heavy rain is what leaves the rock bare [c2].
chapters.kids_md: God tells those who believe not to spoil their charity by reminding people of favours or by hurting them [c1]. A smooth rock with soil on it is left bare by a heavy rain [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayah links the cancelling of charity with reminders of favours, with hurt and with spending to be seen by people [c1]. Another reading is that the picture shows what seems to be there, the soil, being washed from bare rock [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who is meant by the one who spends to be seen by people beyond the description in the ayah; no person is named.
- Not established: what the soil stands for beyond the picture the ayah gives.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal) of this person.
- The Arabic words al-mann and al-adha are rendered 'reminders of favours' and 'hurt'; a scholar should check this wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The wording of al-mann and al-adha, and of safwan as a smooth rock, is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The garden on raised ground and the garden burned

claims.statement_en: The ayah gives a similitude of those who spend their wealth seeking God's approval and out of firmness within themselves: it is like a garden on raised ground (rabwa) that a heavy rain strikes, so that it gave its produce doubled, and if no heavy rain strikes it, then a light dew.
The ayah ends by saying that God sees what they do.

The next ayah asks whether any of those addressed would like to have a garden of date palms and vines, with rivers flowing beneath it and every kind of fruit in it, and then old age strikes him while his offspring are weak, and a whirlwind with fire in it strikes the garden and it burns.
The ayah ends by saying that thus God makes the signs clear to them, that they may reflect.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens those who spend their wealth seeking God's approval to a garden on raised ground that gave its produce doubled after a heavy rain [c1]. The next ayah asks whether anyone would like a garden that a whirlwind with fire in it burns, when old age has struck him and his offspring are weak [c3].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah gives a similitude of those who spend their wealth seeking God's approval and out of firmness within themselves [c1]. They are like a garden on raised ground that a heavy rain strikes, so that it gave its produce doubled [c1]. If no heavy rain strikes it, then a light dew falls [c1]. The ayah ends by saying that God sees what they do [c2].

The next ayah asks whether any of those addressed would like to have a garden of date palms and vines, with rivers flowing beneath it and every kind of fruit in it [c3]. It goes on that old age strikes him while his offspring are weak, and a whirlwind with fire in it strikes the garden and it burns [c3]. The ayah ends by saying that thus God makes the signs clear to them, that they may reflect [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The first ayah names what is likened (spending seeking God's approval and out of firmness within themselves) and what it is likened to (a garden on raised ground) [c1]. The next ayah is put as a question and does not itself say what the garden and the whirlwind stand for [c3]. The ayat close by saying that God sees what they do and that He makes the signs clear [c2][c4].
chapters.kids_md: Those who spend to seek God's approval are likened to a garden on raised ground [c1]. A heavy rain makes it give doubled produce, and if no heavy rain strikes it, a light dew falls [c1]. God sees what people do [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture of the garden on raised ground shows a garden that gives something either way, whether a heavy rain or a light dew falls on it [c1]. Another reading is that the picture of the burned garden is a question the listener is asked to consider, and that the ayat end by saying God makes the signs clear so that they may reflect [c3][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who is meant by those who spend beyond the description in the ayah; no person is named.
- Not established: who the man with the burned garden is, or what the fire and the whirlwind stand for; the ayah poses a question and gives no key.
- The first ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal). The next ayah does not use it: that it is grouped with the first as a parable is the platform's classification, not the text's.
- The words rabwa (raised ground) and tathbit min anfusihim (firmness within themselves, or confirming their own souls) are read in more than one way; this draft keeps the wording general.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The sense of tathbit min anfusihim and of rabwa, and whether 2:266 is part of the same similitude, are for a scholar to decide.

stories.title_en: The kindler of fire and the rain cloud

chapters.title_en: The kindled fire and the cloudburst

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that their similitude is that of one who kindled a fire; when it lit up what was around him, God took away their light and left them in darknesses, unable to see.
They are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not return.

The ayah then gives another picture, introduced by the word or: a cloudburst from the sky with darknesses, thunder and lightning in it, from whose thunderclaps they try to shut themselves away for fear of death, while God encompasses the disbelievers.

The lightning almost snatches away their sight; whenever it lights up for them they walk in it, and when it grows dark on them they stand still, and had God willed He would have taken away their hearing and their sight, for God has power over all things.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat give a picture of one who kindled a fire, whose light God took away and who was left in darknesses, and another of a cloudburst with darknesses, thunder and lightning [c1][c3]. In the picture of the cloudburst they walk when the lightning lights up for them and stand still when it grows dark [c4].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah says that their similitude is that of one who kindled a fire [c1]. When it lit up what was around him, God took away their light and left them in darknesses, unable to see [c1]. They are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not return [c2].

The ayah then gives another picture, introduced by the word or [c3]. It is a cloudburst from the sky with darknesses, thunder and lightning in it, and they try to shut themselves away from its thunderclaps for fear of death, while God encompasses the disbelievers [c3]. The lightning almost snatches away their sight [c4]. Whenever it lights up for them they walk in it, and when it grows dark on them they stand still [c4]. Had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight, for God has power over all things [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The pictures are joined by the word or, and the ayat do not say whether it presents an alternative or a further description of the same people [c3]. In the picture of the fire the light comes from a kindled fire and is taken away, and in the picture of the cloudburst it comes from the lightning and comes and goes [c1][c4]. The ayat call the people deaf, dumb and blind, and the closing ayah says that God could have taken away their hearing and their sight [c2][c4].
chapters.kids_md: A person kindled a fire, and it lit up what was around him [c1]. Then God took away their light and left them in darknesses [c1]. The next picture is a cloudburst with darkness, thunder and lightning [c3]. When the lightning lights up, they walk, and when it grows dark, they stand still [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture of the fire turns on light being given and then taken away [c1]. Another reading is that the picture of the cloudburst shows the same people walking when it is light and standing still when it is dark [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the pronoun their points to in 2:17; it refers to people described in ayat before 2:17, which are outside the ayat cited for this item.
- Not established: what the kindled fire and the cloudburst stand for beyond what the ayat themselves say about the people.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal) in the picture of the fire.
- The sense of the word or (aw) in 2:19 is read as an alternative or as an addition; this draft leaves it open.
- The Arabic of 2:19 also names what they put against the thunderclaps, and it is a part of the body; this draft says only that they shut themselves away.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The sense of aw in 2:19, and who the pronoun their covers in 2:17, are for a scholar to decide.

stories.title_en: The one who shouts to what hears only a call

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry.
They are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah gives the similitude of those who disbelieve as one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry [c1]. It adds that they are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says that the similitude of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry [c1]. They are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives the similitude in one sentence and then states how those who disbelieve are described [c1][c2]. What hears is described only by what it hears, a call and a cry, and the ayah does not name it [c1].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah gives a picture of one who shouts at something that hears only a call and a cry [c1]. It says that those who disbelieve are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not use reason [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture is about hearing a sound without understanding its meaning [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah links not using reason with being deaf, dumb and blind [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what is shouted at, since the ayah names it only as what hears nothing but a call and a cry.
- Not established: whether those who disbelieve are likened to the one who shouts or to what is shouted at; the comparison is read in both ways, and this draft keeps the ayah's own wording.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).
- The Arabic word for reason (yaqilun) is rendered 'use reason'; a scholar may prefer another wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
Who is likened to whom in 2:171 is a point of reading that a scholar should settle for the page.

stories.title_en: The wind with a biting frost

chapters.title_en: The wind with frost in it

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of what they spend in the life of this world is like a wind with sirr in it that struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves and destroyed it.
God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens what they spend in the life of this world to a wind with sirr in it that destroyed the tilth of a people who wronged themselves [c1]. It adds that God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says that the similitude of what they spend in the life of this world is like a wind with sirr in it [c1]. The wind struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves and destroyed it [c1]. God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives the similitude and then states who did the wrong: God did not wrong them, and they wrong themselves [c1][c2]. The Arabic word sirr is read as a biting frost or as a loud sound, and this draft leaves it open [c1].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah likens what they spend in the life of this world to a wind that destroyed the tilth of a people who wronged themselves [c1]. God did not wrong them [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayah shows spending that does not last, like tilth that the wind destroys [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah places the wrong with the people themselves, not with God [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who they are in this ayah; the pronoun points to people described in ayat before 3:117, which are outside the ayat cited for this item.
- Not established: where or when the tilth was struck, or whose it was; the people are not named.
- The word sirr is read as a biting frost or a loud sound; this draft leaves it open.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The sense of sirr, and who the pronoun they covers in 3:117, are for a scholar to decide.

chapters.title_en: The water, the foam and what stays

claims.statement_en: God sent down water from the sky, so valleys flowed, each according to its measure, and the flood carried a swelling foam.
From what they melt in the fire, seeking ornament or goods, there is foam like it.
The ayah says that thus God strikes the truth and the falsehood.
As for the foam, it goes as scum, while what benefits people stays in the earth; thus God strikes the similitudes.

chapters.summary_md: God sent down water from the sky, and the flood carried a swelling foam [c1]. The foam goes as scum, while what benefits people stays in the earth [c4].
chapters.body_md: God sent down water from the sky, so valleys flowed, each according to its measure, and the flood carried a swelling foam [c1]. From what they melt in the fire, seeking ornament or goods, there is foam like it [c2]. The ayah says that thus God strikes the truth and the falsehood [c3]. As for the foam, it goes as scum, while what benefits people stays in the earth [c4]. Thus God strikes the similitudes [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives pictures that end alike: the flood of water and the melting of metals in the fire both leave foam [c1][c2]. It then states the point: the foam goes as scum and what benefits people stays [c4]. The ayah ties the pictures to the truth and the falsehood in its own words and does not spell out which part stands for which [c3][c4].
chapters.kids_md: God sent down water from the sky, and the valleys flowed with it [c1]. The flood carried foam [c1]. The foam goes away as scum, and what benefits people stays in the earth [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayah sets what passes away, the foam, beside what stays, what benefits people, as a picture of falsehood and truth [c3][c4]. Another reading is that the ayah teaches by pictures of water and of fire that end in the same way [c1][c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which part of the pictures stands for the truth and which for the falsehood; the ayah says that God strikes them thus and gives no list.
- Not established: what is melted, since the ayah says only what they melt in the fire seeking ornament or goods.
- The ayah itself says that God strikes the similitudes (amthal).
- The sense of awdiya as valleys and of zabad as foam is taken from common usage; a scholar may prefer other words.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The mapping of the pictures to the truth and the falsehood is not stated in the ayah; a scholar should say how much the page may say.

stories.title_en: The good word and the evil word

chapters.title_en: The good word and the evil word as trees

claims.statement_en: The ayah asks whether one has seen how God struck a similitude: a good word is like a good tree, its root firm and its branch in the sky.
The tree gives its fruit at every time by the permission of its Lord, and God strikes similitudes for people that they may remember.
The similitude of an evil word is like an evil tree uprooted from the surface of the earth, with no steadiness.
God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the hereafter, and He leaves the wrongdoers astray, and God does what He wills.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat give a similitude of a good word as a good tree with a firm root and a branch in the sky, and of an evil word as an evil tree uprooted from the surface of the earth [c1][c3]. They add that God makes firm those who believe with the firm word [c4].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah asks whether one has seen how God struck a similitude: a good word is like a good tree, its root firm and its branch in the sky [c1]. The tree gives its fruit at every time by the permission of its Lord [c2]. God strikes similitudes for people that they may remember [c2].

The similitude of an evil word is like an evil tree uprooted from the surface of the earth, with no steadiness [c3]. God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the hereafter [c4]. He leaves the wrongdoers astray, and God does what He wills [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat pair a good word and an evil word with a good tree and an evil tree, the one firm and the other uprooted [c1][c3]. The good tree has a firm root and gives fruit at every time by the permission of its Lord [c1][c2]. The closing ayah turns from the trees to people and speaks of the firm word [c4].
chapters.kids_md: A good word is like a good tree with a firm root and a branch in the sky [c1]. It gives fruit at every time by the permission of its Lord [c2]. An evil word is like an evil tree uprooted from the surface of the earth, with no steadiness [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat set a good word beside an evil word through the picture of a good tree and an evil tree [c1][c3]. Another reading is that the closing ayah speaks of God making firm those who believe with the firm word [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which good word or which evil word is meant; the ayat name neither, and they do not name the kind of tree.
- Not established: what the firm word in 14:27 is; the ayah does not define it.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later commentary identifies the good word, the evil word and the firm word with particular sayings and with particular moments; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- The ayah itself says that God struck a similitude (mathal).

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: the reports that later commentary links to 14:24-27, to be found, graded by a named grader and linked by a scholar.
The wording of the firm word (14:27) and of the branch in the sky (14:24) is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: Deeds like ashes on a stormy day

chapters.title_en: Deeds like ashes on a stormy day

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes that the wind blows hard on a stormy day.
They have no power over anything of what they earned.
That, the ayah says, is the far error.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord to ashes that the wind blows hard on a stormy day [c1]. They have no power over anything of what they earned [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says that the similitude of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes [c1]. The wind blows hard on the ashes on a stormy day [c1]. They have no power over anything of what they earned [c2]. That, the ayah says, is the far error [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives the similitude in one sentence and then states what follows about those it describes: they have no power over what they earned, and this is the far error [c1][c2][c3]. The picture is of ashes, which are light, and of a wind that blows hard [c1].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord are like ashes [c1]. On a stormy day the wind blows hard on them [c1]. They have no power over anything of what they earned [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture shows deeds that cannot be gathered back once the wind has taken them [c1][c2]. Another reading is that the ayah calls this the far error [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which deeds are meant, or who in particular is meant by those who disbelieve in their Lord; no person is named.
- Not established: how the ayah relates to the other ayat on deeds that are lost; this draft cites only 14:18.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).
- The words ashtaddat bihi al-rih (the wind blew hard on it) and al-dalal al-baid (the far error) are rendered here in plain words; a scholar may prefer other wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The wording of the far error and of the wind blowing hard is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The owned slave and the one given provision

chapters.title_en: The owned slave and the one given provision

claims.statement_en: God struck a similitude: a slave who is owned and has power over nothing, and one to whom God gave good provision from Himself, so that he spends from it in secret and openly; the ayah asks whether they are equal.
The ayah says that all praise is for God, but that most of them do not know.
God also struck a similitude of a pair of men, one of whom is dumb, has power over nothing and is a burden on his master, and brings no good wherever he sends him.
The ayah asks whether he is equal to one who commands justice and is on a straight path.

chapters.summary_md: God struck a similitude of a slave who is owned and has power over nothing, and of one given good provision who spends from it in secret and openly, and asks whether they are equal [c1]. He also struck a similitude of a man who is dumb and a burden on his master, and asks whether he is equal to one who commands justice [c3][c4].
chapters.body_md:
God struck a similitude: a slave who is owned and has power over nothing, and one to whom God gave good provision from Himself, so that he spends from it in secret and openly [c1]. The ayah asks whether they are equal [c1]. It says that all praise is for God, but that most of them do not know [c2].

God also struck a similitude of a pair of men [c3]. One of them is dumb, has power over nothing and is a burden on his master, and brings no good wherever he sends him [c3]. The ayah asks whether he is equal to one who commands justice and is on a straight path [c4].
chapters.deep_md: Each similitude is built as a contrast followed by a question: are they equal [c1][c4]. The first contrast is between having power over nothing and spending from good provision given by God [c1]. The next is between one who brings no good and one who commands justice and is on a straight path [c3][c4].
chapters.kids_md: God struck a similitude of a slave who is owned and has power over nothing, and of one given good provision who spends from it in secret and openly [c1]. The ayah asks whether they are equal [c1]. It says that all praise is for God [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the first similitude sets having power over nothing beside spending from provision that God gave [c1]. Another reading is that the later similitude sets one who brings no good beside one who commands justice and is on a straight path [c3][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the men in these similitudes are; the ayat name no one and do not say whether the pictures are about particular persons.
- Not established: what the similitudes are about in the passage around them; the question are they equal is all the ayat state.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later sources link the pair of men to particular people; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- The ayat themselves use the word for a similitude (mathal) in both places.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The wording of abkam (dumb), kall (a burden) and of the straight path in 16:76 is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The town that was secure and content

claims.statement_en: God struck a similitude: a town that was secure and at ease, its provision coming to it in plenty from every place; it disbelieved in the favours of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear because of what they used to do.
A messenger from among them had come to them and they called him a liar, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.

chapters.summary_md: God struck a similitude of a town that was secure and at ease, with its provision coming in plenty from every place [c1]. It disbelieved in the favours of God, and God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear [c1].
chapters.body_md: God struck a similitude: a town that was secure and at ease, its provision coming to it in plenty from every place [c1]. It disbelieved in the favours of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear because of what they used to do [c1]. A messenger from among them had come to them and they called him a liar [c2]. The punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The first ayah describes the town as secure and supplied, and then at the point of hunger and fear [c1]. The next ayah says that a messenger from among them had come and was called a liar before the punishment seized them [c2]. The ayat do not name the town, the messenger or the punishment [c1][c2].
chapters.kids_md: God struck a similitude of a town that was secure and at ease, with its provision coming in plenty [c1]. The town disbelieved in the favours of God, and God made it taste hunger and fear [c1]. A messenger from among them had come, and they called him a liar [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat set security and plenty beside disbelief in the favours of God, and then hunger and fear [c1]. Another reading is that the ayat link the seizing by the punishment with calling the messenger a liar [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which town is meant, where or when it was, or who the messenger was; none is named.
- Not established: whether the similitude describes a particular past town or is an example.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later commentary links the town to a particular place; this draft does not repeat or vouch for it.
- The verb kafarat in 16:112 can be read as disbelieved or as was ungrateful; this draft keeps disbelieved in the favours of God and leaves the sense open.
- The ayah itself says that God struck a similitude (mathal).

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The sense of kafarat and the favours of God and of the garment of hunger and fear is for a scholar to decide.

stories.title_en: The woman who undid her yarn

chapters.title_en: The woman who undid her yarn

claims.statement_en: The ayah says not to be like her who undid her yarn into undone strands after it was made strong, taking your oaths as a means of deceit among you because one community is greater than another community.
God only tests you by it, and on the day of resurrection He will make clear to you that over which you used to differ.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah says not to be like her who undid her yarn after it was made strong, taking oaths as a means of deceit among you [c1]. It adds that God only tests you by it and will make clear on the day of resurrection that over which you used to differ [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says not to be like her who undid her yarn into undone strands after it was made strong [c1]. It goes on that they take their oaths as a means of deceit among them because one community is greater than another community [c1]. It adds that God only tests you by it, and that on the day of resurrection He will make clear to you that over which you used to differ [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah does not use the word for a similitude here [c1]. It gives a comparison by telling the listeners not to be like the woman, and it ties the picture to taking oaths as a means of deceit [c1]. The test and the clearing up of differences are stated in the later part [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says not to be like her who undid her yarn after it was made strong [c1]. It says that God only tests you by it [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture of undone strands is joined in the ayah with taking oaths as a means of deceit [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah ends by pointing to the day of resurrection, when God will make clear what they differed over [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the woman was, where she lived or when; no person is named.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later sources name the woman and tell an account about her; this draft does not repeat or vouch for it.
- Not established: what it refers to in 'God only tests you by it'; the pronoun is read as pointing to the picture, to the oaths or to one community being greater than another.
- The ayah does not use the word mathal. That this item is grouped with the parables is the platform's classification, not the text's; the ayah gives a comparison with 'not to be like'.
- The word ankathan (undone strands) and the clause one community is greater than another (arba min ummatin) are read in more than one way; this draft keeps the wording general.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The referent of the pronoun in 'tests you by it' and the sense of arba are for a scholar to decide.

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of those who take protectors besides God is like that of the spider, which took a house.
The ayah says that the frailest of houses is the house of the spider, if they knew.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens those who take protectors besides God to the spider, which took a house [c1]. It adds that the frailest of houses is the house of the spider, if they knew [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says that the similitude of those who take protectors besides God is like that of the spider, which took a house [c1]. It adds that the frailest of houses is the house of the spider, if they knew [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah names what is likened (those who take protectors besides God) and what it is likened to (the spider and its house) [c1]. It then states the point of the picture in one clause: the frailest of houses is the house of the spider [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that those who take protectors besides God are like the spider, which took a house [c1]. The frailest of houses is the house of the spider [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture compares reliance on protectors besides God with a house that is frail [c1][c2]. Another reading is that the ayah closes with the words if they knew [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the protectors are; the ayah says only protectors besides God and names none.
- Not established: what the house is made of or how the spider built it; the ayah says house and does not describe it.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).
- The Arabic awhan al-buyut is rendered 'the frailest of houses'; a scholar may prefer another wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The wording of awliya as protectors and of awhan as frailest is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: Those they invoke cannot create a fly

claims.statement_en: The ayah addresses people: a similitude is struck, so listen to it: those you call upon besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered for it.
If the fly takes something from them, they cannot rescue it from it; weak are the seeker and the sought.
They did not appraise God with His true appraisal; God is strong and mighty.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah addresses people with a similitude: those they call upon besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered for it [c1]. If the fly takes something from them, they cannot rescue it from it [c2].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah addresses people: a similitude is struck, so listen to it [c1]. Those you call upon besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered for it [c1]. If the fly takes something from them, they cannot rescue it from it [c2]. The ayah says that the seeker and the sought are weak [c2].

The next ayah says that they did not appraise God with His true appraisal [c3]. It adds that God is strong and mighty [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The similitude is introduced as something to be listened to, and its content is statements about those who are called upon besides God [c1][c2]. The words weak are the seeker and the sought close the picture, and the next ayah turns to how God was appraised [c2][c3]. The ayah does not say which one is the seeker and which the sought [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that those people call upon besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered for it [c1]. If the fly takes something from them, they cannot rescue it [c2]. God is strong and mighty [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture sets the creation of a fly beside those who are called upon besides God [c1]. Another reading is that the next ayah closes by saying that they did not appraise God with His true appraisal and that God is strong and mighty [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who those called upon besides God are; the ayah names none.
- Not established: what was taken by the fly or who held it; the ayah says something and does not name it.
- The words the seeker and the sought (al-talib wa-l-matlub) are read in more than one way, since the ayah does not say which is the fly and which the one called upon.
- The ayah itself says that a similitude is struck (duriba mathal).

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
Who the seeker and the sought are is for a scholar to decide.

claims.statement_en: God is the light of the heavens and the earth.

The similitude of His light is like a niche with a lamp in it, the lamp in a glass, the glass like a bright star, lit from a blessed olive tree that is neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost give light even if no fire touched it: light upon light.
God guides to His light whom He wills, and God strikes the similitudes for people, and God knows all things.
In houses that God has permitted to be raised and in which His name is remembered, there is glorifying of Him in the mornings and the evenings.
There are men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God, from establishing the prayer and from giving zakat; they fear a day on which hearts and sight are turned about.
The ayah states the purpose: that God may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty; and God provides for whom He wills without account.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah says that God is the light of the heavens and the earth, and gives a similitude of His light as a niche with a lamp in a glass [c1][c2]. The next ayat speak of houses in which God is remembered and of men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from remembering Him [c4][c5].
chapters.body_md:
God is the light of the heavens and the earth [c1]. The similitude of His light is like a niche with a lamp in it, the lamp in a glass, the glass like a bright star [c2]. The lamp is lit from a blessed olive tree that is neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost give light even if no fire touched it: light upon light [c2]. God guides to His light whom He wills, and God strikes the similitudes for people, and God knows all things [c3].

In houses that God has permitted to be raised and in which His name is remembered, there is glorifying of Him in the mornings and the evenings [c4]. There are men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God, from establishing the prayer and from giving zakat [c5]. They fear a day on which hearts and sight are turned about [c5]. The ayah states the purpose: that God may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty [c6]. God provides for whom He wills without account [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The similitude is built from named parts: a niche, a lamp, a glass, a star and an olive tree, and it ends with the words light upon light [c2]. The ayah then says that God guides to His light whom He wills [c3]. The ayat that follow speak of houses and of men, and the Arabic opens them with the word in, so that they can be read with the niche or as a new sentence [c4][c5].
chapters.kids_md: God is the light of the heavens and the earth [c1]. The ayah gives a picture of His light as a niche with a lamp in a glass, and the glass is like a bright star [c2]. God guides to His light whom He wills [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayah speaks of the light of God and then of those who remember Him in houses [c1][c4][c5]. Another reading is that the picture of light upon light is followed by the statement that God guides to His light whom He wills [c2][c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: what the niche, the lamp, the glass and the tree each stand for beyond what the ayah says.
- Not established: whose light the pronoun in 'His light' (nurihi) is read as; it is read as God's light, and some readings take it as the light of the believer. This draft keeps God's light.
- The attachment of 24:36 to the picture of the niche is read in more than one way; this draft treats the houses as a separate statement.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later commentary identifies the houses, the men and the blessed tree with particular buildings, people and trees; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- The ayah itself says that God strikes the similitudes (24:35).
- The phrase kawkab durri is rendered 'a bright star'; a scholar may prefer another wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: the reports that later commentary links to 24:35-38, to be found, graded by a named grader and linked by a scholar.
The wordings to check first: the attachment of 24:36, the pronoun in 'His light', and kawkab durri.

stories.title_en: The mirage and the layered darkness

chapters.title_en: The mirage and the darkness over the deep sea

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that those who disbelieve have deeds like a mirage in a plain: the thirsty one thinks it is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds God with him, who pays him his account in full; and God is swift in reckoning.

The ayah then gives a further picture, introduced by the word or: the deeds are like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is another wave, above which is a cloud: darknesses, some above others; when one reaches out he can hardly see what he reaches with.
The ayah ends by saying that whoever God gives no light has no light.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens the deeds of those who disbelieve to a mirage in a plain, which the thirsty one takes for water but finds to be nothing [c1]. It then gives a picture of darknesses over a deep sea, and says that whoever God gives no light has no light [c2][c3].
chapters.body_md:
