The ayah says that those who disbelieve have deeds like a mirage in a plain [c1]. The thirsty one thinks it is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing [c1]. He finds God with him, who pays him his account in full, and God is swift in reckoning [c1].

The ayah then gives a further picture, introduced by the word or: the deeds are like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is another wave, above which is a cloud: darknesses, some above others [c2]. When one holds out what is before him he can hardly see it [c2]. The ayah ends by saying that whoever God gives no light has no light [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives pictures joined by the word or, and the ayat do not say whether they are alternatives or further descriptions of the same deeds [c1][c2]. In the first the thirsty one finds nothing where he looked for water, and finds God with him [c1]. In the picture of the sea the darkness is layered, and the ayah closes with the statement about light [c2][c3].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that the deeds of those who disbelieve are like a mirage in a plain [c1]. The thirsty one thinks it is water, but when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing [c1]. The ayah also gives a picture of darknesses over a deep sea, with a wave above a wave and a cloud above them [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the mirage shows something that looks like water from far off and is found to be nothing on arrival [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah ends by saying that whoever God gives no light has no light [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which deeds are meant or who in particular is meant; no person is named.
- Not established: where the plain or the deep sea is, or what the layers of darkness stand for beyond the picture.
- The ayat do not use the word mathal here: they give similes with the word like. That this item is grouped with the parables is the platform's classification, not the text's.
- The sense of the word or in 24:40 is read as an alternative or as an addition; this draft leaves it open.
- The Arabic of 24:40 names a part of the body that reaches out; this draft says 'reaches out' and keeps that part general.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The sense of the word or in 24:40 and the wording of the reaching-out part in 24:40 are for a scholar to decide.

chapters.title_en: Those made to carry the Torah

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of those who were made to carry the Torah and then did not carry it is like the donkey carrying books.
The ayah says that bad is the similitude of the people who denied the signs of God, and that God does not guide the wrongdoing people.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah likens those who were made to carry the Torah and then did not carry it to the donkey carrying books [c1]. It adds that bad is the similitude of the people who denied the signs of God [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says that the similitude of those who were made to carry the Torah and then did not carry it is like the donkey carrying books [c1]. It adds that bad is the similitude of the people who denied the signs of God [c2]. It ends by saying that God does not guide the wrongdoing people [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah separates being made to carry the Torah from carrying it, and the similitude rests on that difference [c1]. The ayah then judges the similitude as bad for the people who denied the signs of God [c2]. The ayah does not name the people [c1][c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that some were made to carry the Torah and then did not carry it [c1]. It likens them to the donkey carrying books [c1].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture sets carrying books on one's back against carrying their meaning, since the ayah speaks of being made to carry the Torah and then not carrying it [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah closes with the statement that God does not guide the wrongdoing people [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who exactly were made to carry the Torah; the ayah names no people.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later commentary identifies the people with a particular community; this draft does not repeat or vouch for it.
- Not established: what is meant by carrying the Torah beyond the words of the ayah.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal), and the word asfar is rendered 'books'; a scholar may prefer another wording.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The wording of humilu (were made to carry) and of asfar is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The one given the signs who cast them off

claims.statement_en: The ayah commands that the news (naba) be recited to them of the one to whom God gave His signs and who slipped away from them, so Satan followed him and he was among the astray.
Had God willed, He would have raised him by the signs, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire.
His similitude is like the dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants.
The ayah says that this is the similitude of the people who denied the signs of God, and commands to relate the account so that they may reflect.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat tell of one to whom God gave His signs, who slipped away from them and was followed by Satan [c1]. His similitude is like the dog, which pants if it is attacked and pants if it is left alone [c3].
chapters.body_md:
The ayah commands that the news be recited to them of the one to whom God gave His signs and who slipped away from them [c1]. Satan followed him, and he was among the astray [c1].

Had God willed, He would have raised him by the signs, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire [c2]. His similitude is like the dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants [c3]. The ayah says that this is the similitude of the people who denied the signs of God [c4]. It commands to relate the account so that they may reflect [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat speak of the same matter in more than one way: as news (naba) to be recited, and as a similitude (mathal) [c1][c3]. The man is described by what he was given, what he did with it and what he followed, and the similitude of the dog is attached to him [c1][c2][c3]. The ayah then widens the similitude to the people who denied the signs [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God gave His signs to one man, and he slipped away from them [c1]. Satan followed him [c1]. The ayah likens him to the dog, which pants if it is attacked and pants if it is left alone [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat describe one who was given the signs and slipped away from them, and say that God could have raised him by them [c1][c2]. Another reading is that the ayat close by telling that the account is to be related so that they may reflect [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the man is; the ayat give no name, place, time or people.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later sources give the man a name and tell an account about him; this draft does not repeat or vouch for it.
- Not established: how the signs were given, or in what way he slipped away from them; the ayah says only that he did.
- The ayat call the account news (naba) and also use the word for a similitude (mathal) for his state; this draft keeps both words.
- The sense of the pant of the dog as a likeness to the man is not spelled out by the ayah beyond the comparison.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The wording of insalakha (slipped away) and akhlada ila al-ard (clung to the earth) is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The life of this world like rain

chapters.title_en: The life of this world like rain

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of the life of this world is like water that God sent down from the sky, with which the plants of the earth, from which people and cattle eat, mingled, until the earth took its adornment and was adorned, and its people thought they were able over it, then His command came to it by night or by day, and He made it a reaped field, as if it had not been there the day before.
The ayah adds that thus God makes the signs clear for a people who reflect.

The ayah commands that a similitude of the life of this world be struck for them: like water that God sent down from the sky, with which the plants of the earth mingled, and it became dry stubble that the winds scatter; and God has power over all things.

The ayah says to know that the life of this world is play, amusement, adornment, boasting among you and rivalry in wealth and children, like a rain whose growth pleased the kuffar; then it dries, and you see it yellow, then it becomes broken stubble.
The ayah adds that in the hereafter there is severe punishment and forgiveness from God and approval, and that the life of this world is only the enjoyment of delusion.

chapters.summary_md: The ayat in different surahs liken the life of this world to rain and to what grows from it, which then becomes a reaped field, dry stubble or broken stubble [c1][c3][c4]. The last of them adds that in the hereafter there is severe punishment and forgiveness from God and approval [c5].
chapters.body_md:
In one ayah, the similitude of the life of this world is like water that God sent down from the sky, with which the plants of the earth mingled [c1]. The earth took its adornment and was adorned, and its people thought they were able over it, then His command came to it by night or by day, and He made it a reaped field, as if it had not been there the day before [c1]. Thus God makes the signs clear for a people who reflect [c2].

In another ayah, a similitude of the life of this world is to be struck for them, like water that God sent down from the sky, with which the plants of the earth mingled [c3]. It became dry stubble that the winds scatter, and God has power over all things [c3].

In a further ayah, the life of this world is play, amusement, adornment, boasting among you and rivalry in wealth and children [c4]. It is like a rain whose growth pleased the kuffar; then it dries, and you see it yellow, then it becomes broken stubble [c4]. In the hereafter there is severe punishment and forgiveness from God and approval, and the life of this world is only the enjoyment of delusion [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat share the picture of water from the sky and the plants that grow with it, and each ends it differently: a reaped field, dry stubble scattered by the winds, and broken stubble [c1][c3][c4]. Only 10:24 and 18:45 speak of a similitude by that word, while 57:20 compares the life of this world to rain with the word like and lists what it is [c1][c3][c4]. The word kuffar in 57:20 is read as the disbelievers or as the farmers, and the ayah does not settle it [c4].
chapters.kids_md: The ayat say that the life of this world is like rain from the sky, and like the plants that grow with it [c1][c3]. The plants later become dry stubble [c3]. God has power over all things [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat compare the life of this world to rain and to what grows from it, which then dries and is scattered or broken [c1][c3][c4]. Another reading is that the last ayah sets the life of this world beside the hereafter, where there is severe punishment and forgiveness from God and approval [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: whether the ayat are statements of one similitude or separate similitudes; they come from different surahs and the ayat do not say.
- Not established: when the reaping or the drying takes place; 10:24 says by night or by day, and no more.
- The word kuffar in 57:20 is read as disbelievers or as farmers; this draft keeps the Arabic word.
- The ayat 10:24 and 18:45 use the word for a similitude (mathal); 57:20 gives a likeness with the word like and states what the life of this world is.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The sense of kuffar in 57:20 and the wording of zukhruf (adornment) in 10:24 are for a scholar to decide.

stories.title_en: The man shared among quarrelling partners

chapters.title_en: The partners and the one man

claims.statement_en: God struck for them a similitude from themselves: do you have, among those you own, partners in what God provided for you, so that you are equal in it, fearing them as you fear one another? Thus God makes the signs clear for a people who use reason.
God struck a similitude: a man in whom are quarrelling partners, and a man wholly for one man; the ayah asks whether they are equal in likeness.
The ayah says that all praise is for God, but that most of them do not know.

chapters.summary_md: One ayah gives a similitude from themselves and asks whether they have partners among those they own, equal with them in what God provided [c1]. Another gives a similitude of a man in whom are quarrelling partners and a man wholly for one man [c2].
chapters.body_md:
God struck for them a similitude from themselves [c1]. It asks whether they have, among those they own, partners in what God provided for them, so that they are equal in it, fearing them as they fear one another [c1]. Thus God makes the signs clear for a people who use reason [c1].

In another ayah, God struck a similitude: a man in whom are quarrelling partners, and a man wholly for one man [c2]. The ayah asks whether they are equal in likeness [c2]. It says that all praise is for God, but that most of them do not know [c3].
chapters.deep_md: Each similitude is built as a question the listeners can answer from their own life [c1][c2]. The first begins with the words from themselves, and the other contrasts one man belonging to quarrelling partners with one man belonging wholly to a single master [c1][c2]. The ayat are in different surahs, and they do not say whether they are one similitude or separate similitudes [c1][c2].
chapters.kids_md: God struck a similitude from themselves about partners among those they own [c1]. God also struck a similitude of a man in whom are quarrelling partners and a man wholly for one man [c2]. The ayah asks whether they are equal [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the first similitude asks whether anyone treats those they own as equal partners in what God provided [c1]. Another reading is that the later similitude sets a man pulled by quarrelling partners beside a man wholly for one man [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the people addressed are, or what the partners stand for; the ayat state the pictures as questions and give no key.
- Not established: whether the ayat are one similitude or separate similitudes.
- The ayat themselves use the word for a similitude (mathal) in both places.
- The Arabic of 30:28 speaks of those whom the right hands possess; this draft says 'those you own' and keeps the wording general.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to these ayat.
The wording of shuraka mutashakisun (quarrelling partners) and salaman (wholly for one) is for a scholar to confirm.

stories.title_en: The blind and deaf, and the seeing and hearing

chapters.title_en: The blind and deaf, and the seeing and hearing

claims.statement_en: The ayah says that the similitude of both groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing.
The ayah asks whether they are equal in likeness, and asks whether they will not remember.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah gives the similitude of both groups as the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing [c1]. It asks whether they are equal in likeness [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah says that the similitude of both groups is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing [c1]. It asks whether they are equal in likeness [c2]. It asks whether they will not remember [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah places the comparison between both groups as a pair of pairs: the blind with the deaf and the seeing with the hearing [c1]. It ends with questions, whether they are equal and whether they will not remember [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that both groups are like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing [c1]. It asks whether they are equal [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture joins losing sight with losing hearing, and having sight with having hearing [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah ends with a question about remembering [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which groups are meant in this ayah; it says both groups, and the ayat that say which are outside the ayah cited here.
- Not established: which group is likened to which half of the picture; this draft keeps the ayah's own wording.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
Which group stands for which half of the picture is for a scholar to decide.

stories.title_en: The one who was dead and was given life and light

chapters.title_en: The one who was dead and was given life

claims.statement_en: The ayah asks whether one who was dead, and whom God gave life and made for him a light by which he walks among people, is like one whose similitude is in the darknesses, from which he does not come out.
The ayah says that thus what they used to do was made to seem fair to the disbelievers.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah asks whether one who was dead and whom God gave life and made a light for, by which he walks among people, is like one whose similitude is in the darknesses [c1]. It adds that what they used to do was made to seem fair to the disbelievers [c2].
chapters.body_md: The ayah asks a question [c1]. It asks whether one who was dead, and whom God gave life and made for him a light by which he walks among people, is like one whose similitude is in the darknesses, from which he does not come out [c1]. The ayah says that thus what they used to do was made to seem fair to the disbelievers [c2].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah is a question, and it sets states side by side: given life and light, and darknesses from which there is no coming out [c1]. The first person walks among people by the light, and the ayah uses the word for a similitude (mathal) of the one in the darknesses [c1]. The ayah closes by saying what was made to seem fair to the disbelievers [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah asks about one who was dead and whom God gave life and a light to walk among people by [c1]. It asks whether he is like one who is in the darknesses and does not come out [c1].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayah sets life and light beside darknesses from which there is no coming out [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah ends by saying that what they used to do was made to seem fair to the disbelievers [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the one who was dead and the one in the darknesses are; the ayah names no one.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later commentary names the persons it takes them to be; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- Not established: whether dead is meant of the body or of the state of belief; this draft keeps the ayah's word and leaves the sense open.
- The ayah uses the word for a similitude (mathal) of the one in the darknesses, and puts the whole as a question.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: none identified; a scholar should say whether any should be linked to this ayah.
The sense of mayyitan (dead) and the grammar of the question in 6:122 are for a scholar to decide.

stories.title_en: The sown seed in the Torah and the Injil

chapters.title_en: The similitude in the Torah and in the Injil

claims.statement_en: Muhammad is the messenger of God, and those with him are firm against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves; you see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and approval.
Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration.
The ayah says that this is their similitude in the Torah.

Their similitude in the Injil is like a seed that put forth its shoot, then strengthened it, then it grew thick and stood upright on its stalk, pleasing the sowers, so that God may enrage the disbelievers through them.
God has promised those among them who believed and did righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.

chapters.summary_md: The ayah describes those with Muhammad and says that this is their similitude in the Torah [c1][c3]. Their similitude in the Injil is like a seed that put forth its shoot and grew thick and stood upright on its stalk [c4].
chapters.body_md:
Muhammad is the messenger of God, and those with him are firm against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves [c1]. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and approval [c1]. Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration [c2]. The ayah says that this is their similitude in the Torah [c3].

Their similitude in the Injil is like a seed that put forth its shoot, then strengthened it, then it grew thick and stood upright on its stalk, pleasing the sowers, so that God may enrage the disbelievers through them [c4]. God has promised those among them who believed and did righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The ayah gives a description of those with Muhammad and then names the Torah and the Injil as the places for their similitude [c1][c3][c4]. The picture in the Injil is of a seed that goes through stages: a shoot, strengthening, thickening and standing upright on its stalk [c4]. The ayah ends with a promise of forgiveness and a great reward to those among them who believed and did righteous deeds [c5].
chapters.kids_md: The ayah says that Muhammad is the messenger of God, and that those with him are merciful among themselves [c1]. It says that you see them bowing and prostrating [c1]. Their similitude in the Injil is like a seed that put forth its shoot and grew thick and stood upright on its stalk [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the picture of the seed shows growth in stages, from a shoot to standing upright on its stalk [c4]. Another reading is that the ayah joins this picture to a description of those with Muhammad as bowing and prostrating and seeking bounty from God and approval [c1][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who those with him are by name; the ayah names no one except the messenger.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later sources identify those with him with particular people and events; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- Not established: what the Torah and the Injil say of them; this draft cites the Quran only and does not quote those books.
- The ayah can be read as that is their similitude in the Torah, and their similitude in the Injil is like a seed, or as one similitude stated for both books; this draft follows the first reading and leaves the other open.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal) in both places.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: the reports that later commentary links to 48:29, to be found, graded by a named grader and linked by a scholar.
The wordings to check first: the division of the clause about the Torah and the Injil, and the word sima (mark) with its place on the faces.

stories.title_en: The examples given: the wives of Nuh and Lut, the wife of Fir'awn and Maryam

chapters.title_en: The examples for those who disbelieved and those who believed

claims.statement_en: God struck as a similitude for those who disbelieved the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut; both were under righteous servants of God's servants and betrayed them, so they availed them nothing against God, and they were told to enter the fire with those who enter.

God struck as a similitude for those who believed the wife of Fir'awn, when she asked her Lord to build for her a house with Him in the garden, and to save her from Fir'awn and his deeds, and to save her from the wrongdoing people.
God also gave Maryam, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, so that God breathed into it of His spirit, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His books, and was of the devout.

chapters.summary_md: God struck as a similitude for those who disbelieved the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut [c1]. He struck as a similitude for those who believed the wife of Fir'awn, and also gave Maryam, daughter of Imran [c2][c3].
chapters.body_md:
God struck as a similitude for those who disbelieved the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut [c1]. Both were under righteous servants of God's servants and betrayed them, so they availed them nothing against God, and they were told to enter the fire with those who enter [c1].

God struck as a similitude for those who believed the wife of Fir'awn [c2]. She asked her Lord to build for her a house with Him in the garden, and to save her from Fir'awn and his deeds, and to save her from the wrongdoing people [c2].

God also gave Maryam, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, so that God breathed into it of His spirit [c3]. She believed in the words of her Lord and His books, and was of the devout [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat give examples in groups: for those who disbelieved, the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut, and for those who believed, the wife of Fir'awn and Maryam [c1][c2][c3]. The first group are described as under righteous servants and as betraying them, and the ayah does not say how they betrayed them [c1]. The wife of Fir'awn is given in her own request to her Lord, and Maryam is given in what she guarded and what she believed [c2][c3].
chapters.kids_md: God gave examples for those who believed [c2]. One is the wife of Fir'awn, who asked her Lord to build for her a house with Him in the garden [c2]. Another is Maryam, daughter of Imran, who believed in the words of her Lord and His books [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayat give examples of both kinds: wives under righteous servants who betrayed them, and a wife and a woman who asked, guarded and believed [c1][c2][c3]. Another reading is that the ayah says the wives who betrayed availed them nothing against God, even though both were under righteous servants [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how the wives of Nuh and Lut betrayed their husbands; the ayah says only that they betrayed them.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later sources give personal names to the wives of Nuh and Lut and to the wife of Fir'awn and tell accounts about them; this draft does not repeat or vouch for them.
- Not established: where or when the wife of Fir'awn made her request, or what became of her; the ayah gives only her request.
- The ayah ends the example of Maryam with 'breathed into it'; the pronoun is read in more than one way, and this draft keeps the ayah's wording.
- The ayat themselves use the word for a similitude (mathal) of the wives; 66:12 continues the list with and Maryam.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: the reports that later commentary links to 66:10-12, to be found, graded by a named grader and linked by a scholar.
The wordings to check first: fa-khanatahuma (betrayed them) in 66:10, and the pronoun in fihi (into it) in 66:12.

stories.title_en: The first words of revelation: the command to read

claims.statement_en: The passage opens with a command to read in the name of the Lord of the one addressed, who created.
God created the human being from an alaq, a word often rendered a clinging thing or a clot.
The command to read is repeated, with the statement that the Lord of the one addressed is the most generous.
God is the one who taught by the pen and taught the human being what he did not know.

chapters.summary_md: The passage opens with a command to read in the name of the Lord who created [c1]. It says that He created the human being from an alaq [c2], that He is the most generous [c3], and that He taught by the pen and taught the human being what he did not know [c4].
chapters.body_md:
The passage opens with a command to read in the name of the Lord of the one addressed, who created [c1].

It says that God created the human being from an alaq, a word often rendered a clinging thing or a clot [c2]. The command to read is then repeated, with the statement that the Lord of the one addressed is the most generous [c3].

The passage ends by saying that God is the one who taught by the pen and taught the human being what he did not know [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The command to read is given without saying what is to be read [c1]. The passage joins creation [c2], generosity [c3] and teaching by the pen [c4] to one and the same Lord [c1]. The word alaq is kept in Arabic here because it is read in more than one way [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The passage tells us to read in the name of our Lord, who created [c1]. It says that God taught by the pen [c4]. It says that God taught the human being what he did not know [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage ties reading and learning to the name of the Lord who created [c1][c4]. Another is that what a human being comes to know is presented as something God taught [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: that these verses are the first revelation. The inventory title calls them traditionally the first; the verses themselves do not say so.
- Not established: when, where or how these words came, who spoke them to the one addressed, or who the one addressed is. The verses name no one.
- Not established: what the one addressed was to read. The verse gives no object.
- The Arabic alaq is read in more than one way; this draft keeps the Arabic word beside a common rendering and decides nothing.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the occasion, the place and the circumstances in which these verses came. None is used in the story texts.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the beginning of revelation and on the occasion of these ayat, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.
Whether these verses were the first to be revealed is a matter of later tradition; the inventory title says so with the word traditionally. A scholar should decide how the page words this.
The sense of alaq is for the reviewer; the draft gives a common rendering and the Arabic word.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The Night of Power and the sending down of the Quran

claims.statement_en: God says that He sent it down in the Night of Power; the verse does not name what 'it' is.
The verse asks the one addressed what would let him know what the Night of Power is.
The Night of Power is better than a thousand months.
The angels and the Spirit come down in it, by the permission of their Lord, with every matter.
It is peace until the rising of dawn.

chapters.summary_md: God says that He sent it down in the Night of Power [c1]. The Night of Power is better than a thousand months [c3], and the angels and the Spirit come down in it by the permission of their Lord [c4]. It is peace until the rising of dawn [c5].
chapters.body_md:
God says that He sent it down in the Night of Power; the verse does not name what it is [c1]. The verse then asks the one addressed what would let him know what the Night of Power is [c2].

The Night of Power is better than a thousand months [c3]. The angels and the Spirit come down in it, by the permission of their Lord, with every matter [c4]. It is peace until the rising of dawn [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passage answers its own question by saying what the night is better than [c2][c3]. It speaks of a coming down of the angels and the Spirit, and says that it happens by the permission of their Lord [c4]. The last verse describes the night as peace and gives its end as the rising of dawn [c5].
chapters.kids_md: God says that He sent it down in the Night of Power [c1]. This night is better than a thousand months [c3]. The angels and the Spirit come down in it, by the permission of their Lord [c4]. It is peace until the dawn rises [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage invites attention to a single night by saying what it is better than [c3]. Another is that peace is how the passage describes the night [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which night this is, in which month, or how a believer would know it. The verses give none of this.
- Not established: what the thousand months measures, or how a night can be better than that; the verse says only that it is.
- Not established: what 'it' refers to in 97:1. Other chapters of this story speak of the Quran being sent down, and the inventory groups them; this verse does not name it.
- Not established: what 'every matter' includes, or who the Spirit is; the verse names the Spirit beside the angels and says no more here.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the date of the night and the identification of the Spirit. Neither is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: God swears by the clear Book and says that He sent it down in a blessed night.
God says that He has always been one who warns.
In that night every wise matter is made distinct, as a command from God, who says that He has always been one who sends.
It is a mercy from the Lord of the one addressed, who is the one who hears and knows.

chapters.summary_md: God swears by the clear Book and says that He sent it down in a blessed night [c1]. In it every wise matter is made distinct, as a command from Him [c3]. It is a mercy from the Lord of the one addressed [c4].
chapters.body_md:
God swears by the clear Book and says that He sent it down in a blessed night [c1]. He says that He has always been one who warns [c2].

In that night every wise matter is made distinct, as a command from God, who says that He has always been one who sends [c3]. It is a mercy from the Lord of the one addressed, who is the one who hears and knows [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The night is called blessed [c1], and the passage says that in it every wise matter is made distinct [c3]. The passage ties the sending down to warning [c1][c2] and to a command from God [c3]. It ends by naming the whole as mercy [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God says that He sent it down in a blessed night [c1]. God says that He has always been one who warns [c2]. It is a mercy from our Lord, who hears and knows [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage presents the sending down of the Book as warning and as mercy together [c2][c4]. Another is that it speaks of a night as blessed without describing what happens to it [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: that the blessed night here is the night of power of the previous chapter. The verses do not say so; the inventory and later readers group them.
- Not established: what the letters at the opening of the surah mean, or what 'made distinct' covers.
- Not established: what 'it' is in 44:3 beyond the clear Book that God swears by; whether it is the whole Quran or a part is not said.
- Not established: when the blessed night was or in what month.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of this night with the night of power. It is not used in the story texts.

chapters.title_en: The month of the sending down

claims.statement_en: The month of Ramadan is the one in which the Quran was sent down, as guidance for the people and as clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion.
God says that He wants ease for them and does not want hardship for them.
The verse gives as aims that they complete the period, that they magnify God for having guided them, and that they give thanks.

chapters.summary_md: The Quran was sent down in the month of Ramadan, as guidance for the people and as clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion [c1]. God says that He wants ease for them and not hardship [c2].
chapters.body_md:
The month of Ramadan is the one in which the Quran was sent down, as guidance for the people and as clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion [c1].

The verse says that God wants ease for them and does not want hardship for them [c2]. It gives as aims that they complete the period, that they magnify God for having guided them, and that they give thanks [c3].
chapters.deep_md: This verse names the month in which the sending down took place [c1]. It describes the Quran by the words guidance, clear proofs of the guidance, and the criterion [c1]. It links the month to ease and to gratitude [c2][c3].
chapters.kids_md: The Quran was sent down in the month of Ramadan [c1]. It is guidance for the people [c1]. God says that He wants ease for us and not hardship [c2].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the verse joins the sending down of the Quran to thanks for having been guided [c1][c3]. Another is that it states ease as God's wish [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: the night of the month in which the sending down took place, or whether the sending down here is the same event as in the other chapters; the verse says only that the Quran was sent down in the month.
- Not established: whether 'sent down' here means all at once or in parts. Another story speaks of parts.
- The verse goes on to speak about fasting in this month and about those who are sick or travelling. Those provisions are not restated here; this draft gives no judgement on them, and a scholar should decide whether and how the page presents them.
- The Arabic word translated 'the criterion' (furqan) is read in more than one way and is left as a rendering for the reviewer.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the Night of Power, on the sending down of the Quran in the month, and on the date of the night, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.

The chapters rest on separate passages. The verses do not say in so many words that the blessed night, the Night of Power and the month are one event; the inventory groups them, and a scholar should decide how the page states the link.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the date of the Night of Power and the identification of the Spirit named in the passage.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The Quran sent down in parts

claims.statement_en: God says that He separated the Quran into parts so that the one addressed might recite it to the people over a period, and that He sent it down in stages.
Those who disbelieved asked why the Quran was not sent down upon him all at once.
The verse answers that it is so in order that God may make firm the heart of the one addressed with it, and says that God set it out in measured sequence.

chapters.summary_md: God says that He separated the Quran into parts, so that it might be recited to the people over a period [c1]. Those who disbelieved asked why it was not sent down all at once [c2], and the answer given is that God makes firm the heart of the one addressed with it [c3].
chapters.body_md:
God says that He separated the Quran into parts so that the one addressed might recite it to the people over a period, and that He sent it down in stages [c1].

Those who disbelieved asked why the Quran was not sent down upon him all at once [c2]. The verse answers that it is so in order that God may make firm the heart of the one addressed with it, and says that God set it out in measured sequence [c3].
chapters.deep_md: The verses at 17:106 and 25:32 speak of the same manner of sending down [c1][c3]. The verse at 17:106 gives a purpose of the parts: recitation to the people over a period [c1]. The verse at 25:32 records an objection and gives a purpose of its own: making firm the heart [c2][c3]. The words for separating, for a period and for measured sequence are read in more than one way [c1][c3].
chapters.kids_md: God sent the Quran down in parts, not all at once [c1]. Some people who did not believe asked why it was not sent down all at once [c2]. The answer is that God makes the heart of the one who receives it firm with it [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage presents the staged sending down as a kindness to the heart of the one who received it [c3]. Another is that it presents it as a help for reciting to the people over a period [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how many parts there were, how long the sending down lasted, or the intervals between the parts. The verses say only 'over a period' and 'in stages'.
- Not established: who the people were who asked why it was not sent down all at once, or when they asked.
- The Arabic verb in 17:106 can be read as 'separated' or as 'made distinct'; the draft keeps 'separated' and a scholar should decide.
- The Arabic word rendered 'set out in measured sequence' can also mean 'recited slowly'; this draft keeps the wider rendering.
- Not established: how this relates to the verses that speak of the Quran being sent down in a night or a month. The verses here do not mention a night.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the manner and order in which the parts came. None is used in the story texts.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the staged sending down of the Quran and on the occasions of particular parts, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.

How the staged sending down fits with the sending down in a night or a month is a question of interpretation; the verses do not answer it. A scholar should decide whether the page says anything about it.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The wrapped one and the cloaked one

claims.statement_en: The passage opens with a call to the one addressed by the word al-muzzammil, often rendered the wrapped one.
The one addressed is told to stand through the night except for a little: half of it, or a little less than that, or more than that; and to recite the Quran in measured fashion.
God says that He will cast upon the one addressed a weighty word.
The rising of the night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech.
By day the one addressed has long occupation.
The one addressed is told to remember the name of his Lord and to devote himself to Him with complete devotion.

chapters.summary_md: The passage calls on the one addressed as the wrapped one [c1]. He is told to stand through the night except for a little, and to recite the Quran in measured fashion [c2]. God says that He will cast upon him a weighty word [c3], and he is told to remember the name of his Lord and devote himself to Him [c6].
chapters.body_md:
The passage opens with a call to the one addressed by the word al-muzzammil, often rendered the wrapped one [c1].

He is told to stand through the night except for a little: half of it, or a little less than that, or more than that; and to recite the Quran in measured fashion [c2]. God says that He will cast upon him a weighty word [c3].

The passage says that the rising of the night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech [c4], and that by day he has long occupation [c5]. He is told to remember the name of his Lord and to devote himself to Him with complete devotion [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The call and the commands are addressed to one person, whom the verses do not name [c1]. The commands are about the night [c2], and the passage gives reasons from the night and the day [c4][c5]. The weighty word that God will cast upon him is not described [c3]. The passage ends with remembrance and devotion [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The passage calls to someone who is wrapped up, and tells him to stand through the night except for a little [c1][c2]. He is told to recite the Quran slowly and clearly [c2]. He is told to remember the name of his Lord [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage joins the quiet of the night to speech that is more upright [c4]. Another is that it places remembrance of the Lord's name beside the long occupation of the day [c5][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who is addressed. The call is by a title and the verses name no one.
- Not established: why the one addressed is called the wrapped one, or what he was wrapped in; the verses give no circumstance.
- Not established: what the weighty word is, or when it was cast.
- Not established: for whom the standing through the night was meant beyond the one addressed, or for how long. The later verses of the same surah are outside this draft.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identity of the one addressed and the occasion of the call. Neither is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: The passage opens with a call to the one addressed by the word al-muddaththir, often rendered the cloaked one.
The one addressed is told to arise and warn.
He is told to magnify his Lord.
He is told to purify his garments; the Arabic word is read in more than one way.
He is told to keep away from ar-rujz, a word whose sense is disputed.
He is told not to give in order to gain more; the phrase is read in more than one way.
He is told to be patient for the sake of his Lord.

chapters.summary_md: The passage calls on the one addressed as the cloaked one [c1]. He is told to arise and warn [c2], to magnify his Lord [c3], and to be patient for the sake of his Lord [c7].
chapters.body_md:
The passage opens with a call to the one addressed by the word al-muddaththir, often rendered the cloaked one [c1].

He is told to arise and warn [c2], and to magnify his Lord [c3]. He is told to purify his garments; the Arabic word is read in more than one way [c4]. He is told to keep away from ar-rujz, a word whose sense is disputed [c5], and not to give in order to gain more, a phrase that is also read in more than one way [c6].

The passage ends by telling him to be patient for the sake of his Lord [c7].
chapters.deep_md: A series of short commands follow one another, and the passage gives no reason for any of them [c2][c3][c4][c5][c6][c7]. Some of them are read in more than one way: the word for garments, the word ar-rujz, and the phrase about giving in order to gain more [c4][c5][c6]. The warning has no stated object [c2].
chapters.kids_md: The passage calls to someone covered up, and tells him to arise and warn [c1][c2]. He is told to magnify his Lord [c3]. He is told to be patient for the sake of his Lord [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage places patience for the sake of the Lord at the end of a series of commands [c7]. Another is that the commands to warn and to magnify the Lord stand side by side [c2][c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who is addressed, or why he is called the cloaked one. The call is by a title and the verses name no one.
- Not established: whom or what he was to warn; the verse has no object.
- Not established: what ar-rujz refers to, whether the garments in 74:4 are clothing or something else, or what the phrase about giving in order to gain more refers to.
- Not established: whether this passage came before or after the previous chapter's; the chapters follow the inventory order.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identity of the one addressed and the occasion of the call. Neither is used in the story texts.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the occasion of the calls, on who was addressed and on the order of the passages, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.
The titles al-muzzammil and al-muddaththir are in the Arabic as calls; their sense (wrapped, cloaked) is a rendering. The verses do not describe the condition of the one addressed.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identity of the one addressed in both passages. The inventory title gives an identification that the verses themselves do not.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The vision described in the surah of the star

chapters.title_en: The companion who has not strayed

claims.statement_en: God swears by the star when it falls.
God says that the companion of those addressed has neither strayed nor erred.
He does not speak out of desire.
It is nothing but a revelation that is being revealed.

chapters.summary_md: God swears by the star when it falls [c1]. He says that the companion of those addressed has neither strayed nor erred [c2], and that he does not speak out of desire [c3]. It is nothing but a revelation being revealed [c4].
chapters.body_md:
God swears by the star when it falls [c1].

He says that the companion of those addressed has neither strayed nor erred [c2]. He does not speak out of desire [c3]. It is nothing but a revelation that is being revealed [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The passage opens with an oath and then makes a series of statements about the companion [c1][c2][c3]. The last statement says what 'it' is, and does so by the word revelation [c4]. The verse does not say what 'it' refers to [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God swears by the star when it falls [c1]. God says that the companion has not strayed and has not erred [c2]. He does not speak out of desire [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage separates what is said out of desire from what is revealed [c3][c4]. Another is that it begins by setting the companion's honesty before anything else is said [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the companion is. The verse says 'your companion' and gives no name.
- Not established: what 'it' refers to in 53:4, or whether 'the star when it falls' is a star, a group of stars, or something else; the Arabic word and its verb are read in more than one way.
- Not established: when or where the words were first heard.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the companion and the occasion. Neither is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: The companion was taught by one who is strong in power.
God revealed to His servant what He revealed.
The heart did not lie about what it saw.
The verse asks the listeners whether they will dispute with him about what he sees.

chapters.summary_md: The passage says that the companion was taught by one who is strong in power [c1]. It says that God revealed to His servant what He revealed [c2], that the heart did not lie about what it saw [c3], and asks whether they will dispute with him about what he sees [c4].
chapters.body_md:
The passage says that the companion was taught by one who is strong in power [c1].

It says that God revealed to His servant what He revealed [c2]. The heart did not lie about what it saw [c3]. The verse then asks the listeners whether they will dispute with him about what he sees [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The passage names a teacher only by a quality, strong in power, and does not name him [c1]. It does not say what God revealed, only that He revealed what He revealed [c2]. It speaks of the heart and of what was seen, and of a dispute about what is seen [c3][c4].
chapters.kids_md: The passage says that the companion was taught by one who is strong in power [c1]. God revealed to His servant what He revealed [c2]. The verses say that his heart did not lie about what it saw [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage treats what was revealed and what was seen as true and asks the listeners not to dispute it [c3][c4]. Another is that it leaves what was revealed unspecified [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the teacher is. The verses give a quality and no name; later readers differ on who is meant, and the draft takes no side.
- Not established: who 'his servant' is, what was revealed to him, or what the heart saw; the verses say 'what He revealed' and 'what it saw'.
- This chapter leaves out 53:6-9, which speak of where the teacher stood and how near he came. They are left out on purpose, because they invite a picture; a scholar should decide whether the page should present them and in what words.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the teacher and of the one who saw. Neither is used in the story texts.

chapters.title_en: At the lote tree of the farthest limit

claims.statement_en: The verse says that he saw him on another descent, a word that can also be read as another occasion.
It was at the lote tree of the farthest limit, near which is the garden of refuge.
This was when the lote tree was covered by what covered it.
The sight did not swerve and did not exceed.
He saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord.

chapters.summary_md: The passage says that he saw him on another descent [c1], at the lote tree of the farthest limit, near which is the garden of refuge [c2]. It says that the sight did not swerve and did not exceed [c4], and that he saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord [c5].
chapters.body_md:
The passage says that he saw him on another descent, a word that can also be read as another occasion [c1].

It was at the lote tree of the farthest limit, near which is the garden of refuge [c2]. This was when the lote tree was covered by what covered it [c3].

The sight did not swerve and did not exceed [c4]. He saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passage does not say who is seen; the pronoun is not resolved in the verse [c1]. It names a place by its names, the lote tree of the farthest limit and the garden of refuge [c2]. What covered the lote tree is not said [c3]. The passage closes with what the sight did not do and with what was seen, signs of his Lord [c4][c5].
chapters.kids_md: The passage says that he saw something on another occasion [c1]. It was at the lote tree of the farthest limit, near the garden of refuge [c2]. He saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage describes what was seen as signs of the Lord and not as an end in itself [c5]. Another is that it speaks of a sight that did not swerve and did not exceed [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: whom he saw, or what he saw. The pronoun in 53:13 is not resolved here, and 'the greatest signs' are not listed.
- Not established: what covered the lote tree, where the tree is, or what 'the farthest limit' is a limit of.
- Not established: when this took place or how it relates to any journey; the verses do not say.
- The Arabic word for 'descent' can be read as a descent or as an occasion; the draft gives both.
- This chapter does not describe the one seen or the manner of the sight, and no verse here does.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the one seen and the occasion. Neither is used in the story texts.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the vision, on the identity of the one who taught and the one seen, and on the occasion, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.

This story is drafted with the greatest restraint. It states only what the verses say, names no angel, describes no one, and leaves out 53:6-9, which speak of position and nearness. A scholar should decide whether and how to include them.
Whether the one who taught (53:5) and the one seen (53:13) are the same, and who they are, is a question the verses leave to interpretation; the draft does not decide it.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identity of the companion, of the teacher and of the one seen, and the occasion of the passage.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: The passage tells that someone frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him.
The verse asks the one addressed what would let him know: perhaps the blind man might purify himself.
He might also be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him.
As for the one who considers himself in no need, the one addressed attends to him.
It is not upon the one addressed if that one does not purify himself.
As for the one who came to the one addressed striving, and he fears, the one addressed is distracted from him.

chapters.summary_md: The passage tells that someone frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him [c1]. It says that the blind man might purify himself or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him [c2][c3]. It speaks of the one who came striving, and fears, and from whom attention was turned [c6].
chapters.body_md:
The passage tells that someone frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him [c1].

The verse then asks the one addressed what would let him know: perhaps the blind man might purify himself [c2], or he might be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him [c3].

As for the one who considers himself in no need, the one addressed attends to him [c4]. It is not upon the one addressed if that one does not purify himself [c5]. And as for the one who came to the one addressed striving, and he fears, the one addressed is distracted from him [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The passage begins by speaking of someone who frowned and turned away, and goes on to speak directly to the one addressed [c1][c2]. It sets one person beside another: one who considers himself in no need and is attended to, and one who came striving and fearing and is not [c4][c6]. It names the possible benefit to the blind man as purifying himself and being reminded [c2][c3], and says what is not upon the one addressed [c5].
chapters.kids_md: The passage tells of a blind man who came, and of someone who frowned and turned away [c1]. It says that the blind man might have been reminded, and that the reminder would have helped him [c3]. It speaks of the one who came striving and fearing [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage turns attention toward the one who comes striving and fearing [c6]. Another is that it sets the one who considers himself in need of nothing beside the one who comes seeking [c4][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the blind man is. The verses say only 'the blind man' and give no name.
- Not established: who frowned and turned away. The first verses use a verb with 'he', and the verses that follow speak to 'you'; that they are the same person is an inference from the change of address, and the draft does not state it.
- Not established: who the one is who considers himself in no need, where this took place, or when.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the blind man, the identity of the one who frowned and the occasion. None is used in the story texts, and this draft names no one.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the occasion of these ayat, on the identity of the blind man and on who is addressed, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.

The verses do not say that the one who frowned and the one addressed are the same; the inventory title reads them so. A scholar should decide how the page words this, and whether it should name anyone.
The Arabic verb rendered 'purify himself' and the verb rendered 'be reminded' are kept close to the Arabic; their fuller sense is for the reviewer.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The jinn who listened to the Quran

chapters.title_en: A group of the jinn listens

claims.statement_en: God says that He directed to the one addressed a group of the jinn, who were listening to the Quran.
When they were present they said to one another to be silent, and when it was finished they turned back to their people as warners.
They said to their people that they had heard a book sent down after Musa, confirming what was before it, and guiding to the truth and to a straight path.
They called on their people to respond to the caller of God and to believe in him, so that God would forgive them part of their sins and protect them from a painful punishment.
Whoever does not respond to the caller of God cannot frustrate God on the earth, has no protectors besides Him, and is in clear error.

chapters.summary_md: God says that He directed a group of the jinn to the one addressed, and they listened to the Quran [c1]. They turned back to their people as warners [c2], and said that they had heard a book sent down after Musa, guiding to the truth [c3]. They called on their people to respond to the caller of God and to believe [c4].
chapters.body_md:
God says that He directed to the one addressed a group of the jinn, who were listening to the Quran [c1]. When they were present they said to one another to be silent, and when it was finished they turned back to their people as warners [c2].

They said to their people that they had heard a book sent down after Musa, confirming what was before it, and guiding to the truth and to a straight path [c3]. They called on their people to respond to the caller of God and to believe in him, so that God would forgive them part of their sins and protect them from a painful punishment [c4].

They added that whoever does not respond to the caller of God cannot frustrate God on the earth, has no protectors besides Him, and is in clear error [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passage reports what the jinn said to one another and to their people, not what they saw [c2][c3]. They describe what they heard as a book sent down after Musa that confirms what came before it [c3]. Their call has a promise and a warning: forgiveness and protection for those who respond, and clear error for those who do not [c4][c5]. They do not name the caller of God [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God says that a group of the jinn listened to the Quran [c1]. They told one another to be silent while they listened [c2]. Then they went back to their people and told them what they had heard [c2][c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage shows listeners who first listen in silence and then go back to their people to tell them [c2]. Another is that it records the jinn describing the book as guiding to the truth and a straight path [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: how many were in the group. The verse says 'a group' and gives no number.
- Not established: where or when this happened, or how the jinn came to be directed to the one addressed.
- Not established: who 'the caller of God' is, or what 'after Musa' says about the book beyond what the jinn say of it.
- Not established: that this group is the same as the one in the next chapter. The verses do not say so.
- This chapter describes no jinn; the verses do not.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the place and the occasion. Neither is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: The one addressed is told to say that it has been revealed to him that a group of the jinn listened, and said that they had heard a wondrous Quran.
It guides to the right course, so they believed in it, and they would never associate anyone with their Lord.
Some of them are righteous and some are otherwise, for they were on divided paths.
When they heard the guidance they believed in it; whoever believes in his Lord need not fear loss or burden.
Some of them submit and some deviate; those who submit have sought the right course.
As for those who deviate, they are fuel for Hell.

chapters.summary_md: The one addressed is told to say that a group of the jinn listened and said that they had heard a wondrous Quran, which guides to the right course, and that they believed in it [c1][c2]. They said that, when they heard the guidance, they believed [c4], and that some of them submit and some deviate [c5].
chapters.body_md:
The one addressed is told to say that it has been revealed to him that a group of the jinn listened, and said that they had heard a wondrous Quran [c1]. It guides to the right course, so they believed in it, and they would never associate anyone with their Lord [c2].

They said that some of them are righteous and some are otherwise, for they were on divided paths [c3]. When they heard the guidance they believed in it; whoever believes in his Lord need not fear loss or burden [c4].

They said that some of them submit and some deviate, and that those who submit have sought the right course [c5]. As for those who deviate, they are fuel for Hell [c6].
chapters.deep_md: Here the speech of the jinn is given to the one addressed as something revealed to him [c1]. They describe the Quran by its effect: it guides to the right course [c2]. They then describe themselves as divided, and say what follows for those who believe and for those who deviate [c3][c4][c5][c6]. The verses of this surah that are not used here speak of other matters; this chapter keeps only what the jinn say of the Quran and of themselves [c1][c3].
chapters.kids_md: The one addressed is told to say that a group of the jinn listened and said that they had heard a wondrous Quran [c1]. They said that it guides to the right course, so they believed in it [c2]. They said that, when they heard the guidance, they believed [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage shows a hearing that ends in belief, and a statement that those who believe in their Lord need not fear loss or burden [c2][c4]. Another is that the jinn describe themselves honestly as divided into those who submit and those who deviate [c3][c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: that this group is the same as the group in the previous chapter. The verses do not say so.
- Not established: how many there were, where or when, or how the one addressed learned of it; the verse says that it was revealed to him.
- Not established: what 'divided paths' (72:11) looks like among the jinn.
- This chapter leaves out 72:3-10 and 72:12, which speak of other things, among them the sky and what the jinn say of it; a scholar should decide whether any belongs here.
- This chapter describes no jinn; the verses do not.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the occasion and the place. Neither is used in the story texts.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the jinn who listened, on the place and the occasion, and on whether the passages speak of one group or more, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.
The chapters rest on separate passages. The verses do not say that the group of 46:29 and the group of 72:1 are the same; the inventory groups them.
A point for the reviewer: the statement of 72:15 about those who deviate is the jinn's own speech and is kept in the chapter only as such.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The Spirit brings down the revelation

chapters.title_en: A named angel and the Spirit

claims.statement_en: The one addressed is told to say: whoever is an enemy to a certain angel whom the verse names, it is he who brought it down upon the heart of the one addressed, by the permission of God, confirming what was before it and as guidance and good news for the believers.
Whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers and angels whom the verse names, God is an enemy to the disbelievers.
The one addressed is told to say that the Holy Spirit brought it down from his Lord with the truth, to make firm those who believe, and as guidance and good news for those who submit.
It is the revelation sent down by the Lord of the worlds, and the trustworthy Spirit came down with it.
It came down upon the heart of the one addressed, so that he might be one of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue.

chapters.summary_md: The verses speak of who brought the revelation down [c1][c3][c4]. One passage names an angel as the one who brought it down upon the heart of the one addressed, by the permission of God [c1]. Another says that the Holy Spirit brought it down from his Lord with the truth [c3], and another that the trustworthy Spirit came down with it [c4], upon the heart of the one addressed, in a clear Arabic tongue [c5].
chapters.body_md:
The one addressed is told to say: whoever is an enemy to a certain angel whom the verse names, it is he who brought it down upon the heart of the one addressed, by the permission of God, confirming what was before it and as guidance and good news for the believers [c1]. The next verse says that whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers and angels whom the verse names, God is an enemy to the disbelievers [c2].

The one addressed is also told to say that the Holy Spirit brought it down from his Lord with the truth, to make firm those who believe, and as guidance and good news for those who submit [c3].

In other verses the revelation is called the revelation sent down by the Lord of the worlds, and the trustworthy Spirit came down with it [c4]. It came down upon the heart of the one addressed, so that he might be one of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passages use different names or titles for the one who brought it down: an angel whom the verse names [c1], the Holy Spirit [c3] and the trustworthy Spirit [c4]. In each case the verses give the revelation as from God, whether by His permission [c1], from the Lord [c3] or sent down by the Lord of the worlds [c4]. In each case the verses place it upon the heart of the one addressed [c1][c5]. Whether the names speak of one being is not stated in the verses [c1][c3][c4].
chapters.kids_md: The verses say that an angel brought the revelation down upon the heart of the one addressed, by the permission of God [c1]. They also say that the Holy Spirit brought it down from his Lord with the truth [c3]. It came in a clear Arabic tongue [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passages put the source of the revelation with the Lord and describe the one who brings it as acting by His permission [c1][c4]. Another is that they present the revelation as guidance and good news for those who believe and submit [c1][c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: that the angel of 2:97, the Holy Spirit of 16:102 and the trustworthy Spirit of 26:193 are one being. The verses use these names and titles in separate places and do not say that they name one; the draft states each as the verse says it.
- The angels named in the Arabic of 2:97-98 are referred to here without their names; see the story-level notes.
- Not established: how the revelation was brought, what the heart refers to, or how the Arabic tongue relates to the bringing.
- This chapter describes no angel; the verses do not.
- Not established: when or in what circumstances these verses were first said. The passage at 2:97-98 speaks of enmity without saying whose.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the people who were hostile, the occasion of 2:97-98, and the identification of the Holy Spirit and the trustworthy Spirit with the named angel. None is used in the story texts.

claims.statement_en: The Quran is the word of an honoured messenger, one who has power with the Lord of the Throne, of established standing, obeyed there, and trustworthy.
The companion of those addressed is not mad.
He saw him on the clear horizon.
He does not withhold the unseen; the Arabic word is read as 'withholding' or as 'suspected'.
It is not the word of an accursed devil.
The companion was taught by one who is strong in power.

chapters.summary_md: The verses say that the Quran is the word of an honoured messenger, one who has power with the Lord of the Throne and is trustworthy [c1]. They say that the companion of those addressed is not mad [c2], and that it is not the word of an accursed devil [c5]. In another verse they say that the companion was taught by one who is strong in power [c6].
chapters.body_md:
The verses say that the Quran is the word of an honoured messenger, one who has power with the Lord of the Throne, of established standing, obeyed there, and trustworthy [c1].

They say that the companion of those addressed is not mad [c2], and that he saw him on the clear horizon [c3]. They say that he does not withhold the unseen; the Arabic word is read as withholding or as suspected [c4]. They say that it is not the word of an accursed devil [c5].

In another verse the companion is described as taught by one who is strong in power [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The honoured messenger is described by his standing and his trust and in no other way: he has power with the Lord of the Throne, he is obeyed there and is trustworthy [c1]. The verses do not name him, nor the one seen on the horizon [c1][c3]. They deny madness of the companion and deny that the revelation is the word of an accursed devil [c2][c5]. The verse at 53:5 gives a teacher a quality in the same way, strong in power, without a name [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The verses say that the Quran is the word of an honoured messenger, who is trustworthy [c1]. They say that the companion is not mad [c2]. They say that it is not the word of an accursed devil [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the passage describes the messenger by standing and trust and not by form [c1]. Another is that it answers charges made against the revelation and denies them plainly [c2][c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: who the honoured messenger is, who the one seen on the horizon is, or who the teacher strong in power is. None is named in these verses.
- Not established: that the honoured messenger of 81:19 is the same as the angel of 2:97, the holy spirit of 16:102 or the teacher of 53:5. The verses do not say so.
- Not established: what 'the clear horizon' is, when the sighting took place, or what 'the unseen' covers.
- This chapter describes no one; the verses give a standing and a trust, nothing more.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the honoured messenger, of the one seen and of the teacher, and the occasion. None is used in the story texts.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated reports on the identity of the Spirit, of the angel named in 2:97 and of the honoured messenger, each with a named grader. None is used in this draft.

A note on the validator: the shared anchor fixture lists the Arabic name of the angel of 2:97 under tradition names (written for another story, where the verses do not name him). Here 2:97-98 name him in the Arabic, so the draft could not write his name in the story texts and writes 'a certain angel whom the verse names'. A scholar and an editor should restore the name on the page, where it is anchored in 2:97-98.

This story is drafted with restraint. It states what each verse says, depicts no angel, and does not say that the names and titles in these verses name one being; the inventory title does. A scholar should decide how the page words the link.
The word read as 'withholding' or 'suspected' in 81:24 is read in more than one way in the tradition of recitation; the draft keeps both.
Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the identification of the honoured messenger, of the Holy Spirit and of the trustworthy Spirit with the angel named in 2:97.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

stories.title_en: The change of the direction of prayer

claims.statement_en: God says that the foolish among the people will say: what has turned them from the qibla they were facing?
The answer given is that the east and the west belong to God, and that He guides whom He wills to a straight path.
God made them a community in the middle, so that they might be witnesses over the people and the messenger a witness over them.
God made the qibla they were on only in order to know who follows the messenger from who turns back on his heels.
It was hard except for those whom God guided; God would not let their faith be lost, and He is kind and merciful to the people.

chapters.summary_md: God says that the foolish among the people will ask what has turned them from the qibla they were facing [c1]. The answer is that the east and the west belong to God and that He guides whom He wills to a straight path [c2]. God made them a community in the middle, so that they might be witnesses over the people [c3].
chapters.body_md:
God says that the foolish among the people will say: what has turned them from the qibla they were facing? [c1] The answer given is that the east and the west belong to God, and that He guides whom He wills to a straight path [c2].

God made them a community in the middle, so that they might be witnesses over the people and the messenger a witness over them [c3]. God made the qibla they were on only in order to know who follows the messenger from who turns back on his heels [c4]. It was hard except for those whom God guided; God would not let their faith be lost, and He is kind and merciful to the people [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The question is put as something the foolish will say, and the answer is given first as a statement about the east and the west [c1][c2]. The verse at 2:143 gives a reason for the earlier qibla: it was a means of knowing who follows the messenger [c4]. It adds that the change was hard except for those whom God guided, and that God would not let their faith be lost [c5]. The verses do not name the earlier qibla or the new one in these verses [c1][c4].
chapters.kids_md: God says that some people will ask why the believers turned from the direction they were facing [c1]. The answer is that the east and the west belong to God [c2]. God says that He would not let their faith be lost, and that He is kind and merciful to the people [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the answer places every direction with God before it speaks of any change [c2]. Another is that the passage connects the earlier direction with a test of who follows the messenger [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established: which qibla the believers had been facing, when and where the change was made, or how it was carried out. The verses say 'the qibla they were on' and name neither.
- Not established: who the foolish are. The verse says 'the foolish among the people'.
- The word qibla means the direction faced; these verses do not use the word prayer. How it relates to prayer is for the reviewer.
- Not established: what the community 'in the middle' implies beyond the purpose the verse gives.
